The Essentials on the Amitabha Sūtra is an extremely important treatise in the study and practice of the Pure Land. Master Yinguang held it in the highest esteem and taught:

“The Great Collection Sūtra says: ‘In the Dharma-ending age, of the countless millions who cultivate, rarely one attains the Way; only by relying on the recitation of the Buddha's name can one be released from birth and death.’ From this it is known that the single practice of Buddha-recitation is the way cultivated alike by the highest sages and the humblest mortals, the practice walked by the wise and the foolish alike. It is easy to take up yet leads to high attainment; little effort is spent yet results come quickly. Because it relies wholly on the Buddha's power, its benefit is surpassing, going beyond the ordinary paths of teaching. The ancients said: ‘To seek the Way through other gates is like an ant climbing a high mountain; to be reborn through Buddha-recitation is like a sail boat running before a fair wind.’ This may be called the finest description of it. If you wish to investigate it, the Amitabha Sūtra has the Essentials composed by Master Ōuyi, in which both principle and practice reach their utmost — it is the foremost commentary since the Buddha spoke this scripture, wonderful beyond measure and accurate beyond measure. Even if an ancient Buddha appeared in the world again to re-comment on this sūtra, he could not surpass it.”
The annotation follows. The headings in the text are added by the annotator and do not belong to the original Essentials.
The Amitabha Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha

[Note] The Amitabha Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha is the essential teaching the World-Honored One spoke of His own accord without being asked, a profound scripture praised by all the Buddhas of the ten directions, the supreme expedient of ultimate means, and the final destination of the most complete and sudden teaching.

In this scripture the World-Honored One teaches beings to hold solely the name of Amitabha Buddha, so as to cultivate the practice of the Pure Land, cross beyond the three realms horizontally, be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, fully realize the three non-regressing stages, and accomplish Buddhahood in a single lifetime. Practice is established upon the vow, and the vow is born of faith. Therefore the scripture first sets forth in detail the sublime adornments of the primary and companion worlds to arouse faith; next it especially urges beings to seek rebirth there, to arouse the vow; and then it directly reveals the practice of holding the Name, to establish practice. In this scripture the World-Honored One especially reveals how to ensure rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss: faith, vow, and the holding of the Name, with a mind single and undivided. Thereby the fundamental doctrine of the Pure Land school is established.

The ninth patriarch of the Pure Land school, Master Ōuyi, says in the ‘Clarifying the Aim’ section of this Essentials: “Faith is faith in oneself and faith in the Other, faith in cause and faith in effect, faith in particulars and faith in principle; the vow is to weary of the Sahā world and to long for the Land of Ultimate Bliss; practice is to hold the Name and single-mindedly stay undivided.”

The twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, Master Chewu, says: “Single-mindedness is the final home of pure karma and the great gate of the Pure Land. If one has not entered this gate, in the end he is not secure. How can the student fail to be diligent!” (From the Sayings of Master Chewu)

[The Three Non-regressions] First, non-regression in stage: not falling back from the stage one has reached by cultivation. Second, non-regression in practice: not falling back from the practice one has undertaken. Third, non-regression in mindfulness: not turning back from right mindfulness.

There are two Chinese translations of the Amitabha Sūtra. The first is the Amitabha Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, translated by Master Kumārajīva in the Yao Qin period, commonly called the Qin translation; the second is the Sūtra on the Praise of the Pure Land Buddha's Reception, translated by Master Xuanzang in the Tang dynasty, commonly called the Tang translation. Responding to the inclination of the common people toward economy, Master Kumārajīva translated primarily by meaning, with few words yet rich content, subtle and fluent. Master Xuanzang, by contrast, used a word-for-word direct translation, accurate and complete, preserving the original as far as possible. When one studies the meaning of the scripture closely, comparing the two translations against each other yields a deeper and more accurate understanding.
For example, in the Amitabha Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha:

“Śāriputra! If a good man or good woman hears of Amitabha Buddha and holds fast to His name, for one day, or two days, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven days, with a mind single and undivided, then when that person approaches the end of life, Amitabha Buddha together with the holy multitude will appear before him; at the moment of death, with a mind unconfused, he will at once be reborn in the Pure Land of Amitabha Buddha's Sukhāvatī.”
In this passage, students of the Pure Land are greatly concerned with one question: what is the state of ‘single-mindedness’? Over the long years, opinions have been many and the dispute endless.
The wording of the Sūtra on the Praise of the Pure Land Buddha's Reception is:

“Śāriputra! If those good men or good women of pure faith, having heard the name of this Amitāyus Buddha of boundless, measureless, inconceivable merit, and the meritorious adornments of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, ponder it after hearing it, and for one day and night, or two or three, or four or five, or six or seven, maintain their recollection without confusion, then when such good men or good women come to the end of life, Amitāyus Buddha, together with his countless disciples of the Śrāvaka assembly and the multitude of bodhisattvas, will surround and come before him, and with compassionate aid keep his mind undistracted. Once he has relinquished his life, he will follow the Buddha's assembly and be born in the pure Buddha-land of Amitāyus's Land of Ultimate Bliss.”
Set the two side by side and it is clear: ‘single-mindedness’ is precisely ‘maintaining recollection without confusion.’

In the Sūtra on the Praise of the Pure Land Buddha's Reception, the World-Honored One taught: “You beings should all believe and receive the merit of this praised, inconceivable Buddha-land and the Dharma-gate by which all Buddhas take beings under their protection.” Therefore, reciting the Buddha's name is the gate by which all the Buddhas take beings under their protection, and in this scripture the World-Honored One specifically and clearly reveals how to cultivate this Dharma-gate.

After the World-Honored One had spoken the passage “If those good men or good women of pure faith, having heard the name of this Amitāyus Buddha of boundless, measureless, inconceivable merit, and the meritorious adornments of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, ponder it after hearing it, and for one day and night, or two or three, or four or five, or six or seven, maintain their recollection without confusion, then when such good men or good women come to the end of life, Amitāyus Buddha, together with his countless disciples of the Śrāvaka assembly and the multitude of bodhisattvas, will surround and come before him, and with compassionate aid keep his mind undistracted; once he has relinquished his life, he will follow the Buddha's assembly and be born in the pure Buddha-land of Amitāyus's Land of Ultimate Bliss,” he immediately said: “If those good men or good women of pure faith, having heard the name of this Amitāyus Buddha of inconceivable merit and the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, should all believe and receive it, make the vow, and
practice as the Buddha has spoken
, they will be born in that Buddha-land.”

Here the World-Honored One sets forth faith, vow, and practice with perfect clarity: faith is ‘believing and receiving’; the vow is ‘making the vow’; practice is ‘cultivating as the Buddha has spoken.’

When faith and vow remain only in the head, they are nothing but an idea. They must be put into practice to be true faith and deep vow. So true faith and deep vow necessarily lead to earnest practice. Without earnest, vigorous cultivation, how can one realize what one believes? How can one fulfill what one vows? Faith and vow without effort are only hollow faith and shallow vow.

In the Sūtra on the Praise of the Pure Land Buddha's Reception, the World-Honored One, again and again and a third and fourth time, charged beings to ‘cultivate as the Buddha has spoken’, and clearly told us that if one merely cultivates as the Buddha has spoken, one is received by all the Buddhas of the ten directions and will surely be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, never regressing and swiftly realizing Buddhahood. His earnest concern overflows in the words. The World-Honored One taught:

If those good men or good women of pure faith, having heard the name of this Amitāyus Buddha of inconceivable merit and the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, should all believe and receive it and make the vow,
cultivating as the Buddha has spoken
, they will be born in that Buddha-land.”
Whoever practices as the Buddha has spoken

, all will surely be irretrievable from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and all will surely be born in the pure Buddha-land of Amitāyus Buddha's Land of Ultimate Bliss. Therefore, Śāriputra, all you beings, should
believe and receive and understand the words of me and of the Buddhas of the ten directions
, and with diligence,
practice as the Buddha has spoken
, without raising any doubt.”
Whoever practices as the Buddha has spoken

, all will surely be irretrievable from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and all will surely be born in the pure Buddha-land of Amitāyus Buddha's Land of Ultimate Bliss. Therefore, Śāriputra, if those good men or good women of pure faith, all should with deep faith and understanding aspire to be reborn in the pure Buddha-land of Amitāyus's Land of Ultimate Bliss, and
not act with lax abandon

In this defiled, tolerant, enduring world, in this evil age of the five defilements, if there are good men or good women of pure faith, who hear of this Dharma — a thing extremely hard to believe in all the worlds — and are able to give rise to faith and understanding, accept, uphold, proclaim, and
cultivate in accordance with the teaching

, then know that such persons are exceedingly rare, and that in the presence of measureless Buddhas they have planted good roots. At the end of life such persons will surely be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and enjoy the Great Vehicle's Dharma-pleasure of that pure Buddha-land adorned with various meritorious excellencies.”
Question: The Sūtra on the Praise of the Pure Land Buddha's Reception says ‘after hearing it, ponder it.’ How should one ponder?

Answer: By reciting the Buddha's name (holding fast to the Name). The Prajñā Sūtra of Mañjuśrī says: “Good men and good women who wish to enter the single-practice samādhi should dwell in a quiet place, abandon all distracted thoughts, not seize upon appearances, fasten the mind upon a single Buddha, and single-mindedly call on His name.”

Question: I too know that faith, vow, and the holding of the Name with a mind single and undivided can lead to rebirth at ease, and I admire it endlessly. The problem is, how can an ordinary person attain such a high state?

Answer: Single-mindedness is in fact maintaining recollection without confusion (see the Tang translation of the Amitabha Sūtra, the Sūtra on the Praise of the Pure Land Buddha's Reception), that is, as Master Ōuyi says: “It is clear and distinct, neither drowsy nor scattered.” (From the Master Ōuyi Pure Land Collection

Occasional Talks in the Brahma Chamber) Such a state — so long as the method is correct and one works diligently — everyone can attain. This is why it is said that the Pure Land Dharma-gate is a gate at which ten thousand who cultivate, ten thousand are reborn.
Question: How does one attain single-mindedness in Buddha-recitation?
Answer:
Aware Buddha-Recitation
and
Investigating Buddha-Recitation
both set forth the concrete methods for attaining single-mindedness in Buddha-recitation.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin
[Note] This scripture (the Amitabha Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha) was translated in the Yao Qin period by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva.

[Yao Qin] There have been three Qin dynasties in history. The first was the Qin state of the Warring States period, down to the Qin dynasty in which Qin Shi Huang unified the world. The second Qin dynasty was in the period of the Sixteen Kingdoms of the Five Barbarians, its ruler being Fu Jian. The third Qin dynasty was that in which Fu Jian's general, Yao Chang, killed Fu Jian and set up on his own; its realm was also called Qin. Later, to distinguish it from Fu Jian's Qin dynasty, people called it the Yao Qin, also known as the Later Qin. [Śāriputra] That is, Śāriputra. [Tripitaka] The word ‘Tripitaka’ means the canon of sūtras, the canon of vinaya, and the canon of śāstra-s. The sūtra canon is the scriptures spoken by the Buddha; the vinaya canon is the precepts established by the Buddha; the śāstra canon consists of the Abhidharma (meaning the dharma that is incomparable) and other treatises spoken by the Tathāgata, and the various śāstra-s composed by the Buddha's disciples. [Tripitaka Master] A bhikṣu versed in all three divisions of the canon. [Kumārajīva] (

CE), rendered into Chinese as ‘Boy of Youth’, originally a man of India, grew up in Kucha (located between Kuqa and Shaya counties of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region). After leaving the home life, he mastered the Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstra-s. In the third year of the Hongshi era of Yao Xing of the Later Qin (in the year

CE), he arrived at Chang'an and translated scriptures in the Xiaoyao Garden. The sūtras and śāstra-s he translated before and after amount to over three hundred eighty scrolls. In the fifteenth year of the Hongshi era of the Yao Qin (in the year
CE), he passed away in Chang'an. After his cremation, his tongue did not burn, showing that the scriptures he translated were absolutely reliable and without error.

Explained by the Western-realm Monk Ōuyi Zhixu

[Note] The Essentials on the Amitabha Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha was composed by the ninth patriarch of the Pure Land school, the eminent monk of the late Ming and early Qing, Master Ōuyi. This work is terse in words yet rich in meaning, and penetrating in both principle and practice; it is the first among the Ten Essentials of the Pure Land.

[Ōuyi Zhixu] (1599–1655), an eminent monk of the Ming dynasty and the ninth patriarch of the Pure Land school. A native of Mudu in Wu County (Jiangsu), he was of the common surname Zhong, his style name being Zhixu and his dharma name Ōuyi, with the additional sobriquet ‘the man of the eight noes.’ Because in his later years he dwelt on Lingfeng (Hang County, Zhejiang), where he built a temple, founded a society, and wrote books, the world knows him as Master Ōuyi of Lingfeng. In youth he was fond of Confucian learning and vowed to exterminate Buddhism and Daoism. At seventeen, happening to read Great Master Lianchi's Records of Self-Knowledge and Random Notes from the Bamboo Window, he burned the anti-Buddhist treatises he had written and turned to Buddhism. While observing mourning for his father, he heard the Sūtra of the Primal Vows of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, and the resolve to leave the home life first arose in him. At twenty-two he devoted himself exclusively to Buddha-recitation. The next year he made the forty-eight vows and called himself the ‘great layman of the Long.’ At twenty-four he respectfully took tonsure under Master Xueling, a follower of Great Master Hanshan. Master Ōuyi once studied the Huayan, Tiantai, and Consciousness-only teachings, wishing to unify Chan, doctrine, and vinaya, and to synthesize the systems of the various Buddhist schools; yet in practice he inclined chiefly toward Buddha-recitation. He advocated fusing the three teachings of Buddhism, Daoism, and Confucianism. His disciple Master Chengshi compiled his posthumous works, the Collected Treatises of Master Ōuyi of Lingfeng, in ten scrolls (abbreviated as the Lingfeng Collected Treatises).

When the Master was fifty-six he fell ill. He left instructions that after his cremation, his bones should be ground and mixed with flour, and distributed to birds, beasts, and fish, to bind all beings in the joy of the Dharma. Seated cross-legged at the corner of his rope bed, he raised his hand toward the west and passed away. Three years after his nirvāṇa, his disciples cremated him in accordance with the rites. On opening the shrine, they saw that his hair had grown to cover his ears, his face was as in life, and he sat cross-legged majestic. After the cremation, his teeth were all intact. Therefore they did not dare follow his instruction to grind the bones and mix them with flour, but reverently enshrined his relics and built a stūpa to the right of the great hall on Lingfeng.

[The Ten Essentials of the Pure Land] These are the ten scrolls of Pure Land essentials selected by Master Ōuyi, including: the Essentials on the Amitabha Sūtra; the Rite of Repentance and Vows for Rebirth in the Pure Land; the Two Gates of Resolving Doubts and Practicing the Vow for Rebirth in the Pure Land; the Gate of the Beginner's Samādhi of the Sūtra of the Contemplation of Amitāyus; the Rite of Practice and Vow for Upholding the Amitabha Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha; the Ten Doubts of the Pure Land; the Treatise on the Jewel-King Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation; the Questions on the Pure Land; the Direct Pointers of the Jewel-King Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation; the Pure Land Poems of the Western Studio; the Treatise on Birth in the Pure Land and Non-Birth; the Dharma Sayings of the Pure Land; and the Combined Treatise on the West.

[Essentials] Now, the Buddhas, out of compassion for the deluded multitudes, teach them in accordance with their capacities. Although returning to the source is not two, the expedient means are many. Yet among all expedients, to seek the most direct and the most complete and sudden, there is none better than Buddha-recitation and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. Again, among all Buddha-recitation Dharma-gates, to seek the most simple and most secure, there is none better than faith, vow, and the single holding of the Name. Therefore the three Pure Land sūtras circulate together in the world, yet the ancients alone set the Amitabha Sūtra as a daily recitation. Is this not because they saw that the single practice of holding the Name pervades all three roots of capacity, gathers both separate and ultimate truth without leaving anything out, embraces both the Chan school and the doctrinal schools without exception, and is indeed utterly inconceivable?

[Note] The Buddha-recitation Dharma-gate is the most direct, most complete, and most sudden of all Dharma-gates, and faith, vow, and the holding of the Name is again the most simple, most easy, and most secure within the Buddha-recitation Dharma-gates.

[Now] A word of opening. [Returning to the source] Returning to the true, still, original source (nirvāṇa). [Although returning to the source is not two, the expedient means are many] Though all cultivation is for returning to the origin and the source (returning to the source), the specific methods of practice (expedient means) are many. [The three Pure Land sūtras] The three scriptures on which the Pure Land school relies: the Amitabha Sūtra, the Sūtra of the Contemplation of Amitāyus, and the Longer Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra. [Chan school and doctrinal schools] ‘The school' refers to the Chan school; apart from the Chan school, the other nine schools (the Kośa school, the Satyasiddhi school, the Tiantai school, the Huayan school, the True Word school, the Dharmalakṣaṇa school, the Three Treatises school, the Pure Land school, and the Vinaya school) are all called ‘the doctrinal schools.’

[Essentials] From ancient times, commentaries have never been lacking in writers, but with the passage of time works are lost, and few survive. The Venerable Yunchi composed the Commentary and Sub-commentary, vast, subtle, and refined. Master Youxi wrote the Circle-Completion Commentary, profound, high, and broad. These two, like the sun and moon in mid-heaven, are seen by all who have eyes. But as the words are rich and the meaning elaborate, their bounds are hard to fathom, so that beginners of shallow understanding may find it difficult to reach faith and vow. Therefore, not measuring my own dullness, I have again composed this Essentials. I do not presume to differ from the two elders, nor need I force agreement with them. It is like viewing a peak from the side and seeing a ridge, or from across and seeing a range; though none of these exhausts the true appearance of Mount Lu, yet each may count as seeing Mount Lu for oneself.
[Note] This explains the reasons for composing the Essentials.

[Writers have never been lacking] In every age those who wrote commentaries were not wanting. [Yunchi] The eminent Ming monk, Great Master Lianchi, the eighth patriarch of the Pure Land school. [Venerable] The sense of ‘my teacher’; it is the title monks use for their own teacher. [The Venerable Yunchi] Though they had never met, Master Ōuyi honored Great Master Lianchi as his personal teacher. [Commentary and Sub-commentary] The Commentary on the Amitabha Sūtra, with its sub-commentary, composed by Great Master Lianchi. [Youxi] The eminent Ming monk, Master Chuandeng. [Circle-Completion Commentary] The Circle-Completion Commentary on the Brief Explanation of the Amitabha Sūtra, composed by Master Chuandeng. [Now] A word of opening. [Beginner] One who has just begun to study. [Difficult to reach faith and vow] Hard for one to rely upon it to arouse faith and make the vow.
[Essentials] Now, to explain the scriptural text, [I set forth] the fivefold profound meaning.

[Note] ‘Profound meaning’ means that, before expounding the scriptural text, one first clarifies the deep and subtle principle this scripture sets forth. This is the outline of the scripture, so that the reader first grasps the whole, then studies the text; when the net is lifted the mesh spreads open, and it is easy to grasp and understand. ‘The fivefold profound meaning,’ also called the fivefold profound discussion. When Great Master Zhizhe of the Tiantai school preached Buddhist scriptures, he always set up the fivefold profound meaning: one, explaining the title — explaining the scripture's title; two, discerning the essence — discerning the aim of the scripture; three, clarifying the aim — setting forth the purpose of cultivation; four, discussing the function — from the aim, discussing the scripture's function (its fruition); five, judging the teaching — judging whether the doctrinal meaning is great or small, provisional or real.
[Great and small] The Great Vehicle and the Small Vehicle. [Provisional and real] A teaching suited to a given time is called ‘provisional’; an ultimate and unchanging teaching is called ‘real.’

[Essentials] First, explaining the name. This scripture takes as its name the speaker and the one spoken of. ‘Buddha’ is the teaching lord of this world who speaks, namely Śākyamuni, who, mounted on the power of the great compassionate vow, was born in this evil world of the five defilements and, enlightened first, awakens those after him; there is no dharma he does not know, no thing he does not see. ‘Spoke’ means delight in what he holds within. The Buddha's heart is to deliver beings; when the causes of beings' Buddhahood are ripe, he speaks for them this hard-to-believe Dharma, so that they may be ultimately delivered, and therefore he is delighted. ‘Amitabha’ is the guide of that land spoken of, who with the forty-eight vows draws in beings of faith, vow, and Buddha-recitation to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and ever to abide at the stage of non-regression. The Sanskrit ‘Amitabha’ is here rendered ‘Buddha of Measureless Life’, and also ‘Buddha of Measureless Light.’ In sum, his merit, wisdom, spiritual powers, miraculous abilities, the adornments of his primary and companion worlds, and his teaching and transformation of beings — each and all are measureless. All words that come from the Buddha's golden mouth are generically called ‘sūtra.’ Set against the preceding five characters, this makes a title combining the general and the particular. Teaching, practice, and principle each, in turn, have their general and particular, as is extensively set forth in the Tiantai canon.

[Note] [Explaining the name] To explain the title ‘The Amitabha Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha.’ [Combining general and particular as the title] In the six characters of the title ‘The Amitabha Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha,’ there is a distinction of general and particular. The first five characters differ from the titles of other scriptures and are particular; the last character is common to the titles of all scriptures and is general. So the title ‘The Amitabha Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha’ combines general and particular into a single title. [Teaching, practice, and principle each have their general and particular, as extensively set forth in the Tiantai canon] Besides the title, teaching, practice, and principle also each have general and particular; the meaning is vast, as set forth in the Tiantai Canon. [Tiantai] The name of a mountain in Tiantai County, Taizhou Prefecture, Zhejiang Province; in the Sui dynasty, Great Master Zhizhe dwelt on this mountain and founded a school, and the later age named his school the Tiantai school after it, abbreviated as Tiantai or the Tai school.

[Essentials] Second, discerning the essence. All Mahāyāna sūtras take the reality of all things as their true substance. The nature of the single thought-mind present before us is not within, not without, not in the middle; it is not past, not present, not future; not blue, yellow, red, or white, not long, short, square, or round; not scent, not taste, not touch, not dharma. Seek it and it cannot be found, yet one cannot say it is nothing. It creates the hundred realms and the thousand suchnesses, yet one cannot say it is something. It is apart from all discrimination, thought, language, and letters, while discrimination, thought, language, and letters are not, apart from this, a self-nature of their own. In sum, apart from all marks, it is at once all dharmas. Being apart, it is without marks; being at once all dharmas, it is not without marks. Being unable to name it, one forcibly calls it the reality of all things.

[Note] [Discerning the essence] To discern the aim of the scripture. [The reality of all things] The true appearance; all Mahāyāna sūtras take the reality of all things as the true substance. The Buddha Treasury Sūtra says: “What is called the reality of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, with nothing existing.” [One thought] ‘Thought’ means a thought of the mind. If a common person's thought, arising as the sense faculties meet their objects, is born and perished from moment to moment, this is a deluded thought; if it is apart from faculties and objects, a thought that is true, pure, bright, and subtle, empty, transparent, and spiritually penetrating, then it is the thought of the Tathāgata's right knowledge. [Mind-nature] That is, the substance of our own mind — the self-nature. [Not scent, not taste, not touch, not dharma] Here scent, taste, touch, and dharma are the last four of the six sense objects (form, sound, scent, taste, touch, and dharma).

[Essentials] The substance of the reality of all things is neither still nor luminous, yet again it is still and ever luminous, luminous and ever still. Still while luminous is forcibly named the land of eternal still light; luminous while still is forcibly named the pure dharmakāya. Again, luminous-and-still is forcibly named the dharmakāya, and still-and-luminous is forcibly named the recompense body. Again, the still-and-luminous of the nature-endowed merit is named the dharmakāya, and the still-and-luminous of the cultivated merit is named the recompense body. Again, the luminous-and-still of the cultivated merit is named the enjoyment body, and the still-and-luminous of the cultivated merit is named the transformation body. Stillness and luminosity are not two; body and land are not two; nature and cultivation are not two; the true and the responsive are not two — none is other than the reality of all things. The reality of all things is not two, and again is not not-two. Therefore, with its whole substance it becomes the primary world and the companion world, the Dharma and the recompense, self and other. Even the speaker and the spoken, the deliverer and the delivered, the believer and the believed, the vower and the vowed, the holder and the held, the born and the birth-place, the praiser and the praised — none is other than what is stamped by the true seal of the reality of all things.

[Note] The stillness-and-luminosity, body-and-land, nature-and-cultivation, true (dharmakāya) and responsive (transformation body), principle and practice set forth above are all non-dual, because in terms of the reality of all things, they differ not. Master Ōuyi then further clarifies: the reality of all things is not only not-two, but also not not-two.

[The reality of all things is not two, and again not not-two] The Buddha Treasury Sūtra says: “What is called the reality of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, with nothing existing.” Since the reality of all dharmas is ultimately empty with nothing existing, to speak of it as two or as not-two both become idle talk. Hence it is said: “The reality of all things is not two, and again is not not-two.” [The true seal of the reality of all things] ‘True seal’ means the seal of the true Dharma. [Dharma seal] The seal and testament of the Buddha's Dharma — this is the seal of truth handed down from Buddha to Buddha, the standard of the Dharma; what does not accord with the Dharma seal is not the Buddha's Dharma. The Small Vehicle uses the ‘three Dharma seals’ to authenticate: the seal that all conditioning is impermanent, the seal that all dharmas are without self, and the seal of the stillness of nirvāṇa. The Great Vehicle uses the ‘seal of the reality of all things’ to authenticate, also called the seal of the reality of all dharmas. Because the reality of all dharmas already embraces the impermanence of all conditioning, the selflessness of all dharmas, and the stillness of nirvāṇa, it is called the single Dharma seal or the single seal of the reality of all things. Since the Great Vehicle takes as its basis the teaching of the principle of the reality of all dharmas, whatever teaching is apart from the reality of all dharmas is Mara's teaching. In the Lotus Sūtra, the Buddha says: “I, adorned in body with marks, radiate light over the world, revered by the measureless assembly, and proclaim for them the seal of the reality of all things.” The Numerical Dictionary of the Tripitaka says: “The Mahāyāna sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata are all authenticated by the principle of the reality of all things. Outsiders cannot mix in, the Māras cannot overthrow. If it has the seal of the reality of all things, it is the Buddha's teaching; if it lacks the seal of the reality of all things, it is Mara's teaching.” Great Master Zhizhe's Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra says: “The Small Vehicle sūtras which are stamped with the three seals of impermanence, no-self, and nirvāṇa are the Buddha's teaching; cultivating them, one attains the Way; without the three Dharma seals, they are Mara's teaching. The Mahāyāna sūtras have only the single Dharma seal — the reality of all dharmas — and are called the sūtras of ultimate meaning; by them one attains the great Way; without the seal of the reality of all things, they are Mara's teaching.” In the Sentence and Phrase of the Lotus Sūtra, he further says: “The Buddhas awaken to the mark of reality, and mounted on this real way appear in the world. So that beings may attain this reality — for this sole matter — they appear in the world, and for nothing else. Apart from the reality of all dharmas, all is named Mara's activity.”

[Essentials] Third, clarifying the aim. The aim is the essential path of cultivation, the pivot of attaining the essence, and the guiding principle of the myriad practices. When the net is lifted, the meshes spread open; when the collar is taken, the sleeves and the breast are drawn in. Therefore, after the essence, the aim should be discerned.

This sūtra takes faith, vow, and the holding of the Name as the essential method of practice. Without faith, the vow cannot be stirred; without the vow, practice cannot be guided; without the wonderful practice of holding the Name, the vow cannot be fulfilled and the faith cannot be realized.

The sūtra first sets forth the primary and companion worlds to give rise to faith; then urges the making of the vow to guide practice; then reveals the holding of the Name to arrive straightway at non-regression. Faith is faith in oneself and faith in the Other, faith in cause and faith in effect, faith in particulars and faith in principle; the vow is to weary of the Sahā world and to long for the Land of Ultimate Bliss; practice is to hold the Name and single-mindedly stay undivided.

[Note] ‘Clarifying the aim’ — to set forth the essential path of cultivation. This sūtra takes faith, vow, holding the Name, and single-mindedness as the essential path of cultivation. Based on the meaning of the scripture, Master Ōuyi gave a clear definition of ‘faith, vow, and the holding of the Name’: “Faith is faith in oneself and faith in the Other, faith in cause and faith in effect, faith in particulars and faith in principle. The vow is to weary of the Sahā world and long for the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Practice is to hold the Name and single-mindedly stay undivided.” Whenever ‘faith, vow, and the holding of the Name’ is mentioned in the Essentials, its meaning is: faith — faith in oneself and in the Other, in cause and in effect, in particulars and in principle; vow — wearying of the Sahā world and longing for Sukhāvatī; practice — holding the Name and single-mindedly undivided. Reading ‘without the wonderful practice of holding the Name, the vow cannot be fulfilled and the faith cannot be realized’ and ‘practice is to hold the Name, single-mindedly undivided’ continuously together, the concrete meaning is: without the wonderful practice of holding the Name in single-mindedness, the vow cannot be fulfilled and the faith cannot be realized. Therefore the point of landing and the concrete expression of deep faith and firm vow lie in the wonderful practice of holding the Name in single-mindedness.

[The pivot of attaining the essence] To carry through the purpose of cultivation is the key (pivot) to comprehending (attaining) the scripture's aim (essence). Here ‘the essence’ is the true substance of the section on discerning the essence — the reality of all things; Master Ōuyi says: “All Mahāyāna sūtras take the reality of all things as their true substance.” [Pivot] The opening and closing of a door depend on the pivot (the turning axis on the door); the release of a crossbow depends on the trigger (the release mechanism of the bow, also called the trigger). ‘Pivot’ refers to the key of a matter.
Question: There is a saying:
“If one has true faith and firm vow, even reciting the Buddha's name with a scattered mind will surely lead to rebirth.”
Is this saying correct?
Answer: “If one has true faith and firm vow, even reciting the Buddha's name with a scattered mind will surely lead to rebirth” —
this is simply an absurdity!
It is a tearing apart of faith and vow from practice.
Faith, vow, and practice are a single whole, linked ring to ring and inseparable; the relationship among them is:
faith stirs the vow, and the vow guides practice; practice fulfills the vow, and practice verifies faith.
Faith and vow without effort are hollow practice and shallow vow.
Hence Master Ōuyi taught:
“This scripture
takes faith, vow, and the holding of the Name as the essential method of practice. Without faith, the vow cannot be stirred; without the vow, practice cannot be guided;
without the wonderful practice of holding the Name, the vow cannot be fulfilled and the faith cannot be realized
Many of the makers of absurdities about how one can be reborn,
the feature common to them all
, is precisely the tearing apart of faith and vow from practice. Some even proclaim: as long as one has faith and vow, one is reborn! Faith itself is rebirth!
The Buddha and the patriarchs have again and again taught us to
recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly
, and again and again charged us to
cultivate as the Buddha has spoken
(see
The Sūtra on the Praise of the Pure Land Buddha's Reception, Annotated
). Therefore, one of true faith and firm vow must certainly cultivate as the Buddha has spoken and recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly (see
Single-Minded Buddha-Recitation, Not Scattered-Mind Buddha-Recitation
). The one who recites with a scattered mind is precisely the one who, dreading difficulty and suffering, acts contrary to the teaching of the Buddha and the patriarchs,
and this is the very concrete expression of faith untrue and vow unreal
(see further the teaching of the great master Yongming, a manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, below). Therefore,
the one who recites with a scattered mind,
is as the great master Yongming says:
“The power of faith is slight.”
Therefore, in one who recites with a scattered mind, the faith and vow are certainly not true and firm.
The situation of ‘reciting with a scattered mind and yet having true faith and firm vow’ simply does not exist;
it is a false proposition
, just as a brave warrior who shrinks back before battle does not exist.

‘If one has true faith and firm vow, even reciting the Buddha's name with a scattered mind can lead to rebirth’ means: reciting with a scattered mind and yet having true faith and firm vow can also lead to rebirth. But since the situation of ‘reciting with a scattered mind and yet having true faith and firm vow’ does not exist at all, how can the matter of rebirth or non-rebirth even be addressed?
Therefore,
‘If one has true faith and firm vow, even reciting with a scattered mind will surely lead to rebirth’ is simply an absurdity.
The great master Yongming
in
the Collected Works Returning All Goodness to One
taught:
“If in words and deeds one does not correspond,
the power of faith being slight
, without a mind of thought after thought continuing, but with an intention of frequent interruption
(that is, scattered-mind Buddha-recitation)
Relying on his idleness
, hoping for rebirth at the end of life, but shielded by the obstacles of karma, he fears he will scarcely meet a good friend; urged on by wind and fire,
right mindfulness is not established
[Fear of failing to find a good spiritual friend] One may be unable to meet a great good spiritual friend who can support him in sustaining right mindfulness at the moment of death.
In this passage, Master Yongming clearly points out: why does one practice Buddha-recitation with a scattered mind (
“without a mind of thought succeeding thought in unbroken continuity, but with an intent that is interrupted again and again”
)? It is because
“his words and actions are out of accord, and his power of faith is slight”
Therefore, one whose words match his actions and whose faith and vows are sincere will certainly practice Buddha-recitation with a single-minded heart.
But to practice Buddha-recitation with a scattered mind shows precisely that this person is
“out of accord in word and action, with but slight power of faith”
. Moreover, Master Yongming specially points out that scattered-mind Buddha-recitation is the practice of a slothful person; if one continues in this sloth (
“relying on his indolence”
), then at the moment of death
“when wind and fire press upon him, right mindfulness is not accomplished,”
therefore he cannot attain rebirth.
[Words and actions out of accord] Words and deeds do not match: while in speech one claims to have true faith and sincere vows, in actual conduct one is indolent (neither genuine nor earnest):
“without a mind of thought succeeding thought in unbroken continuity, but with an intent that is interrupted again and again.”
Therefore the crucial point is this: can scattered-mind Buddha-recitation accomplish right mindfulness at death? For right mindfulness at death is the key to rebirth.
On this point, Master Daochuo teaches:
“The wise diligently gather in the mind, so that at death the intent does not scatter
(and thereby, accomplishing right mindfulness at death, they attain rebirth).
But one who does not train the mind in single-minded concentration will surely be scattered at death
(and so, failing to accomplish right mindfulness at death, they revolve in the six realms).
See
Master Daochuo’s Teachings on the Pure Land
.) Past patriarchs and great masters all taught in this way without exception.
Therefore, Master Yongming then teaches:
“Why is this so? Now is the cause, and the moment of death is the fruit; the cause must be genuine, and then the fruit will not be false.
If one would have the ten recitations at death accomplished
(that is, to accomplish the ten recitations in unbroken continuity at death),
then one must prepare the bridge and the ferry
that is, one must make full preparation in advance)
, gathering all merit together and dedicating it to that time
(dedicating it to the moment of death),
so that thought after thought is not deficient
(thought succeeding thought in unbroken continuity);
then one may be free of worry.”
(from the Collected Works of the Common Return of All Good)”
[Accomplishing the ten recitations at death] To accomplish the ten recitations in unbroken continuity at death. (See
“Ten Recitations at Death, Rebirth through the Unbroken Continuity”
.) [But yuban jinliang] One must make full preparation in advance. “Jinliang” (the bridge and the ferry): a ferry crossing and a bridge; “yuban jinliang” means to make full preparation in advance.

In the foregoing teaching, Master Yongming sets forth clearly the causal relationships between faith-and-vows and practice, and between practice and rebirth: faith and vows are the cause, and practice is the fruit; practice is the cause, and rebirth is the fruit. Therefore,
“the cause must be genuine, and then the fruit will not be false.”
The relationship among these three—faith, vows, and practice—is this:
faith awakens vows, vows guide practice; practice fulfills vows, and practice validates faith.

Q: An article says: “Master Miaolian, who passed away a few years ago, having practiced the Pratyutpanna samādhi ten times in twenty years, made his forty-ninth great vow: those who practice Buddha-recitation with a scattered mind can also attain rebirth.” Is this true?

A: As far as I know, Master Miaolian’s forty-ninth great vow is: “All who have seen my face, heard my teaching, or even heard my name, I will deliver so that they too reach the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss; if they are not reborn there in this life, I will surely return to guide them, until at last they are reborn there.” It is not: “those who practice Buddha-recitation with a scattered mind can also attain rebirth.” You can verify this on the internet.

If anyone truly made the forty-ninth great vow “those who practice Buddha-recitation with a scattered mind can also attain rebirth,” he would be slandering the Buddha, calling Amitabha Buddha to account for not receiving beings who practice Buddha-recitation with a scattered mind. Such a person, who does not himself understand the Dharma, would audaciously make so great a vow as to set himself above Amitabha Buddha!
In fact,
at the moment of death of every living being, Amitabha Buddha is there to welcome him,
including those beings who practiced Buddha-recitation with a scattered mind.
It is only that beings without right mindfulness at death cannot see it, and so, following their own deluded thoughts, they go on to take rebirth according to their karma.
Therefore, one must have right mindfulness at death in order to see Amitabha Buddha come to welcome him, and then follow the Buddha to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
On this principle, Master Zhongfeng, honored as the Ancient Buddha of Jiangnan, teaches in the Three Hours of Mindfulness:
“Though it is said that Amitabha draws beings to rebirth, one should believe
that it is but the mind itself manifesting;
through the mutual response between the practitioner’s appeal and the Buddha’s compassion,
in the end
(after all)
it is not obtained from outside.

[Only the mind itself manifesting] That Amitabha Buddha comes to welcome (draw) beings is but the mind itself manifesting; this is owing to the mutual response between the practitioner’s appeal and the Buddha’s compassion, and not anything obtained from outside. Thus only one with right mindfulness at death can see the Buddha come, while the others nearby cannot. For those dying beings lacking right mindfulness at death, because their own minds are turbid and confused and lack the response of right mindfulness (the unbroken continuity of the ten recitations), naturally the Buddha’s welcome does not appear within the mind, and so they do not see the Buddha come—not that Amitabha Buddha has failed to come.
Therefore, whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has right mindfulness at death
(the ten recitations in unbroken continuity at death).
This is why
Master Shandao, the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, and Master Yongming, also the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, both earnestly teach:
one must accomplish the ten recitations in unbroken continuity at death
(see
“The Eighteenth Vow”
This is indeed the teaching of Amitabha Buddha!
[The mutual response between appeal and compassion] The appeal of the practitioner and the response of Amitabha Buddha interpenetrate each other.

As for the principle of the mutual response at death between the practitioner’s appeal and the Buddha’s compassion, Master Yinguang, the manifestation of Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, teaches in his Preface to the Guide to Pure Karma for Beginners:

“The mind of beings is like water, and Amitabha Buddha is like the moon. When beings’ faith and vows are complete and they move the Buddha with utmost sincerity, the Buddha responds to them, just as when the water is clear the moon appears. If the mind is not pure, is not utterly sincere, and accords with greed, hatred, and delusion, going against the Buddha, then it is like turbid, agitated water: although the moon does not fail to shine upon it, yet it cannot receive the moon’s bright reflection.”

Translation: The mind of beings is like water, and Amitabha Buddha is like the moon. When beings’ faith and vows are complete and they move the Buddha with utmost sincerity, the Buddha responds to them, just as when the water is clear and still the moon appears (a metaphor for how a pure mind of right mindfulness evokes the Buddha’s welcome). If the mind is not pure, is not utterly sincere, and accords with greed, hatred, and delusion, going against the Buddha, then it is like turbid, agitated water: although the Buddha-moon shines upon it without fail (a metaphor for the Buddha always welcoming every dying being), yet it cannot brightly reflect the image (a metaphor for how an agitated, turbid mind cannot evoke the Buddha’s welcome;
instead it follows its own deluded thoughts and goes on to take rebirth according to its karma

“Only when the water is clear and still does it appear; when the water is turbid and agitated it is hidden. The moon indeed has no preference or rejection; the reason it does not appear is that the water, dark and turbid and rushing, has no way to receive its reflection.”

Translation: Only when the water is clear and still does the moon’s reflection appear; when the water is turbid and agitated the moon’s reflection does not appear. The moon indeed shines without preference or rejection; the reason its reflection does not appear is that the water, dark and turbid and rushing, has no way to receive it. (Metaphor: only those beings with right mindfulness at death can see the Buddha’s welcome; beings without right mindfulness at death cannot see it. The Buddha indeed welcomes every dying being without preference or rejection; that beings without right mindfulness at death do not see the Buddha’s welcome is because
their own minds are dark and turbid
and scattered,
and so
they follow their own deluded thoughts and go on to take rebirth according to their karma

Therefore, for a practitioner of Buddha-recitation, single-minded right mindfulness at death is of utmost importance. The thousand recitations and the ten thousand recitations, extending even to reciting the Buddha’s name all day and all year, are nothing but making this single thought of Buddha-recitation familiar,
so as to ensure that at death this thought continues unbroken, evoking the Buddha’s welcome.
Hence Master Shandao, the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, and Master Yongming, also the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, both earnestly teach:
one must accomplish the ten recitations in unbroken continuity at death
(see
“The Conditions for Rebirth”
This is the word of the sages! If one will not listen to the words of Amitabha Buddha, whose words will one listen to?

[Unbroken continuity] The thought of Buddha-recitation succeeds one after another without intermingling with deluded thoughts. [The word of the sages] This is what the sages have spoken, correct and without error, altogether worthy of belief and acceptance.
[Essential Explanation] To believe in oneself is to believe that this present single thought-mind is in itself neither the fleshy heart nor the shadow of perceived objects;
(in time)
it has neither beginning nor end, and
(in space)
it has no boundary; through the whole day it follows conditions, and through the whole day it remains unchanging.

[Note] To believe in oneself is to take the original mind as one’s own mind, and not to take the fleshy heart (the physical heart) or the deliberating mind (the shadow of the six sense objects) as one’s own mind.
[The deliberating mind] The mind that grasps at sense objects and gives rise to all manner of discrimination and grasping and rejecting.

[Essential Explanation] The lands as numerous as dust motes in the space of the ten directions are all things that appear within my single thought-mind. Though I am confused and deluded, if a single thought turns the mind back, I will surely be reborn in the Pure Land inherently present within my own mind, with no further doubt. This is called believing in oneself.

[Note] The lands as numerous as dust motes in the space of the ten directions are all originally things that appear within my single thought-mind. Since all things are manifested by my own mind, the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is of course also manifested by my own mind. Although we are confused and inverted, the original mind is not lost; if a single thought turns the mind back, we will surely be reborn in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss inherently present within our own minds. With no further doubt about this, it is called believing in oneself.

[Essential Explanation] To believe in another is to believe that Śākyamuni Tathāgata never speaks falsely, that Amitabha Buddha’s vows are never empty, and that the Buddhas of the six directions, with their broad and long tongues, never speak two ways. Following the true teachings of all the Buddhas, resolve with determination to seek rebirth, with no further doubt. This is called believing in another.

[Note] [The broad and long tongue] One of the thirty-two marks. The tongue is broad and long, soft, red, and thin, able to cover the face up to the hairline. When the tongue bears such a mark, one’s speech is surely true.

[Essential Explanation] To believe in the cause is to deeply believe that even scattered recitation of the Buddha’s name is still a seed of Buddhahood; how much more so, then, one who is single-minded and undisturbed—how could he fail to be reborn in the Pure Land? This is called believing in the cause.
[Note] Here the Master clearly points out: scattered recitation of the Buddha’s name is a seed of Buddhahood.

[A seed of Buddhahood] This plants the distant cause of Buddhahood. For example, when the Blessed One was in the world, an old man came to the Buddha, desiring to leave home and cultivate the Way. The Buddha happened to be away, and all the great disciples, who possessed the knowledge of past lives, saw that the old man had, for eons, planted no roots of goodness; even if he left home now he would gain but little benefit, so they would not permit him. The old man felt ashamed of his deep obstructions and was greatly grieved. When the Buddha returned and saw him, he allowed him to leave home, and before long the old man attained arhatship. The great disciples were all amazed and asked the Buddha why. The Buddha said: Your knowledge of past lives extends only to events within eighty thousand kalpas. This old man,
beyond eighty thousand kalpas,

was a woodcutter who went into the mountains to gather firewood. On the way he met a fierce tiger and, terrified, fled up a tree. The tiger followed, biting at the trunk until it was nearly half way through. The woodcutter, in desperation and at a loss, involuntarily called out “Namo Buddha.” Because of the root of goodness from the merit of that recitation of the Buddha’s name, he is able now to leave home and cultivate the Way.

[Essential Explanation] To believe in the fruit is to deeply believe that the gathering of all the good in the Pure Land is born from the samādhi of Buddha-recitation, just as planting melons yields melons and planting beans yields beans, and just as a shadow must follow a form and an echo must answer a sound; it is never in vain. This is called believing in the fruit.

[Note] To believe in the fruit is to deeply believe that being reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss and gathering together in one place with all the superior good people all come from the samādhi of Buddha-recitation.

[The gathering of all the good] The Amitabha Buddha Sūtra says: “Śāriputra! Beings who hear this should make the vow to be reborn in that land. Why is this? So that they may gather together in one place with all such superior good people.” [Samādhi] In Chinese it is rendered “concentration” (ding), meaning to settle the mind in one place. The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says: “When the good mind dwells in one place without wavering, this is called samādhi.”

[Essential Explanation] To believe in matters is to deeply believe that, because this present single thought is inexhaustible, the worlds in the ten directions manifested by the mind are likewise inexhaustible. There truly is a Land of Ultimate Bliss beyond a hundred thousand koṭi lands, supremely pure and adorned, unlike the fables of Master Zhuang. This is called believing in matters.
[Note] To believe in matters is to deeply believe that the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, like the world we now dwell in, truly exists, and is not like the fables in the Zhuangzi.

[Essential Explanation] Faith in principle means deeply believing that the ten billion lands do not in fact lie outside the present thought-moment of one's own single mind, because the mind-nature of this present single thought truly has no outside. And deeply believing that the dependent and proper retributions, the host and the companions, of the Western [Pure Land] are all reflections manifested within this present single thought. The whole of phenomena is precisely principle; the whole of the deluded is precisely the true; the whole of cultivation is precisely the nature; the whole of the other is precisely the self. Because my mind pervades all, the Buddha's mind also pervades all, and the mind-nature of all living beings also pervades all. It is like a thousand lamps in a single room: each light pervades the others, layer upon layer each enfolds the rest, and none obstructs another. This is called faith in principle.

[Note] Faith in principle means deeply believing that the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is manifested within the present thought-moment of one's own single mind. 'Dependent and proper retributions, host and companions' broadly designates everything in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[The single thought-moment of the present mind] the thought of a single present moment. 'Single' (jie) describes what is most minute and most small: 'jie' carries the sense of weak and small, and 'er' is a particle. [Dependent and proper retributions, host and companions] Here 'dependent' (the dependent retribution) refers to the four lands of the Land of Ultimate Bliss (the Land of Sages and Commoners Together, the Land of Expedient Liberation with Remainder, the Land of Real Reward and Adornment, and the Land of Eternally Quiescent Light), and 'proper' (the proper retribution) refers to Amitabha Buddha and the living beings there; 'host' is Amitabha Buddha, and 'companions' are the living beings there (bodhisattvas, shravakas, humans, and gods). [The whole of phenomena is precisely principle, the whole of the deluded is precisely the true, the whole of cultivation is precisely the nature, the whole of the other is precisely the self] Here 'whole' (quan) means thorough and penetrating. When one has truly penetrated, one realizes the non-duality of phenomena and principle, of the true and the deluded, of nature and cultivation, and of self and other, and one can all the more realize the non-duality of mind and land.

[Essential Explanation] Having thus believed, one sees that the Saha world is the defilement evoked by one's own mind, and since one's own mind is defiled, one ought in principle to turn from it in loathing. The Land of Ultimate Bliss is the purity evoked by one's own mind, and since one's own mind is pure, one ought in principle to rejoice in and seek it. One must loathe defilement and renounce it to the very end, only then is there nothing further to renounce. One must rejoice in purity and seek it to the very end, only then is there nothing further to seek. Therefore the Miaozong says: if taking and rejecting reach their utmost, they are not a different track from neither taking nor rejecting. Suppose one does not engage in taking and rejecting but merely exalts non-taking and non-rejecting: that is to cling to principle and abandon phenomena. Since phenomena are abandoned, the principle too is not complete. If one understands that the whole of phenomena is precisely principle, then taking too is precisely principle and rejecting too is precisely principle. Each taking and each rejecting is nothing other than the Dharma-realm. Hence, following faith, the vow is made clear.

[Note] Once deep faith is established, an earnest vow is therefore born: to turn from the Saha world in loathing and to rejoice in and seek the Land of Ultimate Bliss. This loathing and turning away, this rejoicing and seeking (one's own mind leaving defilement and seeking purity), should be carried out on the level of phenomena; one must not cling to principle and abandon phenomena.
[Miaozong] the Miaozong Chao, a commentary on the Sutra of Contemplation of Immeasurable Life, written by the Venerable Siming of the Song dynasty; abbreviated as the Miaozong Chao.

[Essential Explanation] As for the words 'holding the Name single-mindedly and without confusion': the Name calls forth the virtue, and the virtue is inconceivable; therefore the Name is also inconceivable. The merit of the Name is inconceivable; hence even scattered recitation becomes the Buddha-seed, and holding it fast brings one to non-retrogression. Yet the various sutras set forth Pure Land practices in thousands of different ways. Such methods as contemplating an image, contemplative visualization, worship and offering, the fivefold repentance, and the six recollections: when any one of these practices is accomplished, one is reborn in the Pure Land. Only the one method of holding the Name gathers in the widest range of capacities and is the easiest to take up. Therefore Shakyamuni, the Compassionate Honored One, spoke it without being asked, and singled it out especially for the greatly wise Shariputra. It may be called the first among expedients, the unsurpassed among the definitive teachings, and the most perfect and sudden among the perfect and sudden. Hence it is said: cast a pure pearl into turbid water, and the turbid water cannot but become clear; cast the Buddha's Name into a scattered mind, and the scattered mind cannot but become Buddha.

[Note] The practitioner holds the Name single-mindedly and without confusion. The practices of the Pure Land are thousands of different kinds, yet the one method of holding the Name gathers in the widest range of capacities and is the easiest to take up; it may be called the first among expedients, the unsurpassed among the definitive teachings, and the most perfect and sudden among the perfect and sudden.

[Scattered recitation becomes the Buddha-seed; holding it fast brings one to non-retrogression] This is the abbreviated style common in classical Chinese, which echoes the preceding text: scattered recitation of the Name is still a seed of Buddhahood, while one who holds the Name single-mindedly and without confusion is reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and ascends directly to the stage of non-retrogression. [The fivefold repentance] The Tiantai Master Zhiyi, for the sake of those cultivating the Lotus Samadhi, established five methods of repentance: first, repentance, revealing one's past transgressions and cautioning against them in the future; second, entreaty, entreating the Buddhas of the ten directions to turn the Dharma-wheel; third, sympathetic joy, rejoicing in and praising all roots of goodness, one's own and others'; fourth, dedication, directing the merit one has cultivated toward living beings and toward the Buddha-way; fifth, vow-making, making the four universal vows to guide the four preceding practices. [The six recollections] mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Sangha, mindfulness of the precepts, mindfulness of giving, and mindfulness of the heavens.

[Essential Explanation] Faith, vows, and holding the Name are taken as the true cause of the One Vehicle; the four kinds of Pure Land are taken as the wondrous fruit of the One Vehicle. When the cause is set forth, the fruit must follow; therefore faith, vows, and holding the Name are made the core of the sutra. The characteristics of those four kinds of Pure Land are set out in detail in the Miaozong Chao and in the Profound Meaning of the Brahma Net Sutra, and are not fully described here. When the proper retribution section of the text is explained below, they will be briefly indicated.

[Note] Once again it is pointed out that faith, vows, and holding the Name single-mindedly and without confusion are the core of this sutra. It is especially important to note that in this section Master Ouyi has already given a clear definition of faith, vow, and practice: faith is faith in oneself and faith in the other, faith in cause and faith in effect, faith in phenomena and faith in principle; the vow is to turn from the Saha world in loathing and to rejoice in and seek the Land of Ultimate Bliss; the practice is to hold the Name single-mindedly and without confusion. Therefore wherever the later text speaks of 'faith,' it means faith in oneself and faith in the other, faith in cause and faith in effect, faith in phenomena and faith in principle; wherever it speaks of 'vow,' it means to turn from the Saha world in loathing and to rejoice in and seek the Land of Ultimate Bliss; and wherever it speaks of 'practice,' 'holding the Name,' or 'holding fast,' it means to hold the Name single-mindedly and without confusion.

[The four kinds of Pure Land] also called the four Buddha-lands or the four lands: the Land of Sages and Commoners Together, the Land of Expedient Liberation with Remainder, the Land of Real Reward and Adornment, and the Land of Eternally Quiescent Light. The Land of Sages and Commoners Together is the land where ordinary beings dwell together with the sages who manifest bodies and speak the Dharma in order to transform living beings. The Land of Expedient Liberation with Remainder is the land where the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas who have not yet realized the Dharma-body dwell. The Land of Real Reward and Adornment is the land where the Buddha's reward-body dwells together with the bodhisattvas on the stages above the ground. The Land of Eternally Quiescent Light is the land of quiescence revealed by the Buddha's pure Dharma-body.

On the three bodies and four lands, Master Shengan explains in his Annotated Essay on the Western Pure Land: 'Question: There is only one Western [Pure Land]; why divide it into four lands? And there is only one Buddha; why are there three bodies? Is this not to hack apart and tear asunder (the ancient form of the particle ye)? Answer: It is like there being only one moon, yet its light and shadow differ; or again like there being only one mirror, yet its reflections differ in image and in brightness. When did it ever hack apart the light and shadow, or tear asunder the mirror images? The Dharma-body is like the moon, the reward-body like its light, the transformation-body like its shadow. Eternally Quiescent Light is like the substance of the mirror, Real Reward like the mirror's light, and Expedient [Liberation] and Sages and Commoners Together like the images in the mirror. In the Buddha there is only the one Dharma-nature body, dwelling in the Land of Eternally Quiescent Light. For the bodhisattvas of the ten grounds and the thirty minds (the ten abodes, ten practices, and ten dedications, called the thirty minds), he manifests the perfect and complete reward-body and dwells in the Land of Real Reward. For shravakas and bodhisattvas he manifests the superior and inferior bodies and dwells in the Land of Expedient [Liberation]. For ordinary beings and bodhisattvas who have newly aroused the mind he manifests the inferior response-body and dwells in the Land of Sages and Commoners Together.'

[The superior and inferior bodies] the superior response-body and the inferior response-body. The Tiantai school divides the Buddha's response-body into two kinds, superior and inferior. The superior is called the superior response-body, the body manifested for bodhisattvas on the first ground and above. The inferior is called the inferior response-body, such as the sixteen-foot Buddha-body manifested for ordinary beings before the grounds and for the followers of the two vehicles. [Before the grounds] before the first ground. Before the grounds one is an ordinary-being bodhisattva; only on the grounds does one become a Dharma-body bodhisattva.
[Essential Explanation] Fourth, clarifying the power and function. This sutra takes rebirth and non-retrogression as its power and function.

[Note] 'Discussing the function' means discussing the power and function (the fruit and effect) of a sutra on the basis of its core teaching. This sutra takes rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and the direct ascent to the stage of non-retrogression as its power and function. The sutra says: 'Living beings born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are all avaivartika.'

[Avaivartika] translated into Chinese as non-retrogression. It means that merit and roots of goodness increase ever more and never fall away or turn back, until Buddhahood is attained. Ordinarily a bodhisattva must pass through one great asamkhya kalpa of cultivation before reaching this stage of non-retrogression.

[Essential Explanation] Rebirth takes place in four lands, and each is discussed in nine grades. Let us briefly clarify the characteristics of gaining rebirth in the four lands. If one holds the Name and has not yet cut off view-and-thought delusion, then whether one is scattered or concentrated, one is reborn in the Land of Sages and Commoners Together in three grades and nine ranks. If one holds the Name to the point of single-mindedness in phenomena, and view-and-thought delusion falls away of itself, then one is reborn in the Pure Land of Expedient Liberation with Remainder. If one reaches single-mindedness in principle and bursts through one grade of ignorance, or even through forty-one grades, then one is reborn in the Pure Land of Real Reward and Adornment and also partially realizes the Land of Eternally Quiescent Light. If ignorance is utterly cut off, that is the supreme Real Reward and ultimate Quiescent Light.

[Note] [Each is discussed in nine grades] The Land of Sages and Commoners Together is divided into nine grades according to the lightness or heaviness of view-and-thought delusion; the Land of Expedient Liberation with Remainder is divided into nine grades according to the lightness or heaviness of dust-and-sand delusion; and the Land of Real Reward and Adornment and the Land of Eternally Quiescent Light are divided into nine grades according to the lightness or heaviness of ignorance-delusion. [Whether one is scattered or concentrated] 'Scattered' here means that although one has not attained concentration in Buddha-recitation, one has already reached the point where false thoughts arise but do not continue. [The three delusions] view-and-thought delusion, dust-and-sand delusion, and ignorance-delusion. View-delusion is the deluded error of ordinary beings in their views, such as the five wrong views: the view of a self, extreme views, wrong views, the view of grasping at views, and the view of grasping at precepts. Thought-delusion is the deluded error of ordinary beings in their thinking, such as the afflictions of greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt. These two delusions are the root by which living beings drift through the three realms and suffer birth and death to no purpose; cut them off, and one can end birth and death and escape the three realms. Dust-and-sand delusion is the delusion of bodhisattvas. When a bodhisattva transforms and delivers living beings, if he does not master the immeasurable Dharma-gates, as numberless as dust and sand, he cannot complete the work of teaching and transforming living beings; hence it is called dust-and-sand delusion. Ignorance-delusion is fundamental ignorance; it can obscure the principle of the Middle Way and the real mark, and when it is utterly cut off, one becomes a Buddha. Among the three delusions, view-and-thought is coarse, dust-and-sand is middling, and ignorance is subtle.

[Essential Explanation] Non-retrogression has four meanings. First, non-regression of mindfulness: breaking through ignorance, revealing the Buddha-nature, being born directly in the Real Reward, and partially realizing the Quiescent Light. Second, non-regression of practice: view-and-thought having fallen away and dust-and-sand also broken through, one is born in the Land of Expedient [Liberation] and advances toward the ultimate fruit. Third, non-regression of stage: carrying one's karma and attaining rebirth, one dwells in the Land of Sages and Commoners Together, is received in a lotus calyx, and forever leaves behind the conditions of retrogression. Fourth, ultimate non-retrogression: whether with a sincere mind or a scattered mind, with mind or without mind, understanding or not understanding, if the Name of Amitabha Buddha, or the names of the Buddhas of the six directions, or the title of this sutra merely passes once through the ear, then even after a thousand myriad kalpas one will in the end be delivered and freed by this cause. It is like hearing the drum smeared with poison: far and near, all perish; or taking a little diamond: it is certain never to be dissolved.

[Note] Non-retrogression has four meanings. First, non-regression of mindfulness: thought after thought flows into the Tathagata's ocean of fruition, one breaks through ignorance, reveals the Buddha-nature, is born directly in the Pure Land of Real Reward and Adornment, and also partially realizes the Land of Eternally Quiescent Light. Second, non-regression of practice: view-and-thought delusion having been cut off and dust-and-sand delusion also broken through, one is born in the Land of Expedient [Liberation], constantly cultivates the practice of delivering living beings, and seeks the Buddha-way above. Third, non-regression of stage: carrying one's karma and attaining rebirth in the Land of Sages and Commoners Together, because one is born by transformation in a lotus, one forever leaves behind the conditions of falling back. Fourth, ultimate non-retrogression: whether one recites with a sincere mind or a scattered mind, with mind or without mind, or understanding the meaning or not, so long as the Name of Amitabha Buddha, or the names of the Buddhas of the six directions, or the title of this sutra (the Buddha Speaks of Amitabha Sutra) passes once through the ear, it is stored in the alaya-consciousness and becomes a Buddha-seed that is forever indestructible. Even after a thousand myriad kalpas, when the roots of goodness have ripened, one will in the end be delivered and freed by this cause. The universality of gaining deliverance through hearing the Name is like hearing the sound of the drum smeared with poison: far and near, greed, anger, and delusion all perish; and the Buddha-seed planted by hearing the Name endures forever indestructible, like taking a little diamond, which is certain never to vanish with the passage of time.

[The drum smeared with poison] This drum is smeared with a poison such that all who hear its sound die. Chan uses it as a metaphor for the master's pivotal words, which cause students to extinguish greed, anger, and delusion. Chan Master Quanhuo said: 'The purport of our teaching is like the drum smeared with poison. Strike it once, and all who hear it, far and near, perish.' (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)

[Essential Explanation] Furthermore, those who merely carry their karma and are born in the Pure Land of Sages and Commoners Together and realize the stage of non-regression are all equal to the bodhisattvas of the stage of one more birth
(all equal to the bodhisattvas awaiting the Buddha-stage who are one birth from Buddhahood)
, and all will in one lifetime surely fill the Buddha-stage
(all attain Buddhahood in one lifetime)

. Now, to dwell in one place together with the highest good: this is to be born in the Land of Sages and Commoners Together and yet already to transcend horizontally into the upper three lands. To fill the Buddha-stage in one lifetime: this is the non-regression of stage, and already to have perfectly realized the three kinds of non-regression. Such power and function were never before found in a thousand sutras and ten thousand treatises. Compared with the sudden enlightenment of the true cause, which is merely a gradual step out of the dust and can only hope for the Buddha-stage if one does not fall back life after life, it is not to be spoken of in the same day. How can those of the teachings and the Chan lineage fail to ponder this?
[Those of the teachings and the Chan lineage] Here 'teachings and lineage' refers to the Chan lineage and the teachings below it.

[Essential Explanation] Fifth, the teaching category. This sutra belongs to the Mahayana bodhisattva collection. It was further spoken without being asked, and is empowered by the Buddha's thoroughly great compassion; it can cause living beings of the Dharma-ending age who are beset by many obstacles to ascend directly to non-retrogression by relying on it. Therefore, when in the future the sutras and the Dharma are utterly extinguished, this sutra will be especially preserved to remain in the world for a hundred years, broadly delivering conscious beings. It is the agada medicine that holds all illnesses at once, absolute and perfectly fused, inconceivable. The profound treasury of the Avatamsaka, the secret marrow of the Lotus, the heart-essence of all Buddhas, and the compass of the ten thousand practices of the bodhisattvas all do not go beyond this. Were one to wish to praise it at length, a kalpa would not suffice to exhaust it; the wise will know it for themselves.

[Note] The teaching category of this sutra is that it belongs to the Mahayana bodhisattva collection; it is the profound treasury of the Avatamsaka, the secret marrow of the Lotus, the heart-essence of all Buddhas, and the compass of the ten thousand practices of the bodhisattvas.

[Classification of the teachings] discerning whether a teaching is great or small, provisional or real. [The bodhisattva collection] the general name for the Mahayana sutras. Because it contains the methods by which Mahayana bodhisattvas cultivate the cause and realize the fruit, it is called the 'bodhisattva collection.' [Collection] the Buddha's gathering in and receiving of living beings through his compassionate teaching. [Living beings] also called sentient beings, namely all animals that possess consciousness. [Conscious beings] those who possess a mind-consciousness, that is, living beings. [The agada medicine] also called the medicine of immortality. This medicine is wondrous and its value is immeasurable; taken, it clears away all illnesses. [The compass] an instrument used in ancient China to determine direction, equivalent to the modern compass.

blocks.text: 1. The Assembly of the Dharma Gathering

inline.s: [Essential Explanation] Entering the text, it divides into three parts: first, the introductory section; second, the core section; third, the circulation section. These three are named the good beginning, the good middle, and the good end. The introduction is like the head, in which the five sense organs are all present. The core is like the body, in which the organs are complete. The circulation is like the hands and feet, by which movement is not impeded. Therefore when Zhiyi explained the Lotus Sutra, he took the whole of the first chapter as the introduction and the last eleven and a half chapters as the circulation. Again, at one time the two gates of the original and the manifested were each divided into three sections, so that the five chapters beginning with the 'Dharma Master' were all circulation for the manifested gate. For the introduction must raise the guiding principle of a sutra, and the circulation ensures that the gift of Dharma is not blocked; their importance is no small matter. Later people did not understand this, and whenever a passage of the scripture touched even slightly on principle, they judged it to belong to the core section, so that the introduction and the circulation were left as mere empty convention. How then could it be said that the first words are good and the last words are good?
[Note]

The scripture text divides into three great parts: first, the introductory section; second, the core section; third, the circulation section.
