The introductory section sets forth the causes and conditions that gave rise to this sutra. The core section is the main exposition of this sutra. The circulation section enumerates the benefits of receiving and upholding this sutra and urges and praises its reception, upholding, reading, recitation, and circulation. Master Ouyi stresses here that one must not slight the introductory section and the circulation section.

[Zhiyi] whose name was Zhiyi, the first patriarch of the Tiantai school. This school takes the Lotus Sutra, the Nirvana Sutra, the Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra, and the Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom as its main texts, and clarifies the wondrous principle of the threefold contemplation of one mind. [At one time] The Tiantai Contemplation Sutra Commentary says: 'Here we do not discuss whether the time was long or short, real or provisional; when the exposition of this sutra was concluded, the whole of it is called one time.' [The two gates of the original and the manifested] the gate of the original ground and the gate of the manifested trace, abbreviated as the original gate and the manifested gate. This was established by the Tiantai Master Zhiyi, and afterward every commentator on the Lotus Sutra without exception divided it broadly into the original gate and the manifested gate. 'Original' means the original ground of having attained Buddhahood long ago; 'manifested' means the trace manifested by a recent attainment. The original gate refers to the original ground of the Tathagata's having attained the Way in the distant past; the manifested gate refers to the traces manifested by the Tathagata's recently shown Buddhahood for the sake of teaching living beings.
A1. The introductory section: B1. The general introduction; B2. The particular introduction
B1. The general introduction: C1. Identifying the time and place of the assembly; C2. Citing the great assembly who heard together
C1. Identifying the time and place of the assembly

[Common Introduction] This is the introduction common to all sutras (“Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was at …”). For example, the first passage of this sutra (“Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was at the Jetavana Grove in the garden of Anathapindada in the kingdom of Sravasti, together with a great assembly of bhiksus, twelve hundred and fifty …”) is the common introduction. The common introduction is also called the confirmation introduction, because it possesses the six matters of faith, hearing, time, teacher, place, and assembly, which prove that what is spoken in the sutra is true and credible. These six matters are also called the Six Accomplishments; the possession of these six conditions accomplishes the Dharma-assembly.

[Six Accomplishments] In the common introduction of the sutras six matters are set forth to attest that the sutra was truly spoken by the Buddha himself. Taking this sutra’s common introduction as the example: first, “Thus” is the accomplishment of faith — the Buddha spoke thus; second, “I have heard” is the accomplishment of hearing — heard by me (Ananda) with my own ears, not handed down by hearsay; third, “At one time” is the accomplishment of time — the moment when teacher and students meet and the capacities and the teaching coincide; fourth, “The Buddha” is the accomplishment of the teacher — the master of the teaching; fifth, “at the Jetavana Grove in the garden of Anathapindada in Sravasti” is the accomplishment of place — the site of the teaching; sixth, “together with a great assembly of bhiksus, twelve hundred and fifty” is the accomplishment of the assembly — the multitude who heard. Because it clearly states that this sutra was personally heard by the compiler (Ananda) from the Buddha, and sets out the master, time, place, and those present, it causes beings to know the sutra is without error and so to arouse faith; hence it is also called the confirmation introduction.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was at the Jetavana Grove in the garden of Anathapindada in the kingdom of Sravasti.

[Essential Explanation] “Thus” marks faith and accord. “I have heard” marks the lineage of transmission. “At one time” marks the meeting of capacity and occasion. “The Buddha” marks the teacher. “Sravasti and the rest” marks the place where the sutra was taught.

[Note] “Thus” is the accomplishment of faith; “I have heard” is the accomplishment of hearing; “At one time” is the accomplishment of time; “The Buddha” is the accomplishment of the teacher; “at the Jetavana Grove in the garden of Anathapindada in Sravasti” is the accomplishment of place.

[At one time] That time. This refers to the time when the Buddha spoke this sutra, that is, the moment when teacher and students meet and the capacities and the teaching coincide. As the Tathagata speaks the Dharma, it extends to gods and humans; compiled and handed down, it spreads throughout the world; because the record of year, month, and day is hard to make identical, the phrase “at one time” is used to record it. [Teacher and students] Teacher and students, master and disciples. [Capacity and teaching coincide] “Capacity” is the disposition of the listeners; “teaching” is the Buddha’s imparting of the teaching. The capacities of sentient beings differ, so the Buddha, according to their capacity, imparts teaching of greater or lesser depth. “Capacity and teaching coinciding” means that the roots of the audience and the Buddha’s teaching respond to and accord with one another.

[Essential Explanation] The wondrous principle of reality, unchanged through past and present, is called “Thus”. Relying on the principle of reality, to recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Pure Land, with certainty not mistaken, is called “So”. Reality is neither self nor no-self; Ananda does not destroy the provisional name, so he still says “I”. The ear-faculty gives rise to ear-consciousness, directly hearing the perfect sound, like space imprinting space — this is called “heard”.
[Note] This explains “Thus have I heard”.

[Provisional name] A false and unreal name. Dharmas originally have no name; people provisionally assign them. The name is unreal and not in accord with the substance. [Ananda does not destroy the provisional name] Ananda has no longer the view or pride of self; to conform to the world he does not destroy the provisional name “I”, so without self he still says “I”. [Like space imprinting space is called hearing] The hearing is empty and what is heard is empty; hence like space imprinting space is called hearing. This principle is thoroughly taught in the prajna sutras. The Diamond Sutra says: “Every characteristic is false and vain.” (See the
Essential Explanation of the Diamond Sutra
article.) The Heart Sutra says: “No eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, object of thought.” (See the
Essential Explanation of the Heart Sutra
article.)

[Essential Explanation] Time has no real dharma; because teacher and students meet and the speaking and the hearing are complete, it is called “at one time”. Enlightening oneself and enlightening others, with enlightenment and practice complete, a great teacher of gods and humans — this is called “the Buddha”.
[Note] [Time has no real dharma] Time is an illusion.

[Essential Explanation] Sravasti means “renowned for possessions”, the name of a great kingdom of central India, capital of King Prasenajit. That king’s son was named Jeta, meaning “victory”. The king’s minister was named Sudatta, meaning “Feeder of the lone and widowed”. The Elder Anathapindada covered the prince’s park with gold and offered it to the Buddha and the monks. Prince Jeta, moved with admiration, gave the remaining strip of ground that had not been covered. Hence the whole is called the Jetavana Grove in the garden of Anathapindada.

[Note] [Kingdom of Sravasti] In present-day northwest India, on the south bank of the Rapti river; the king then was Prasenajit. [Jeta Grove] The grove of Prince Jeta. [Anathapindada] The Elder Anathapindada (“elder” is a respectful title for the virtuous and eminent). He was Sudatta, a wealthy merchant of the Sravasti capital, kind and charitable, fond of giving to the orphaned and widowed (“orphaned” — those who have lost their parents; “widowed” — those who have lost their spouse; together, the poor with none to rely on), so he won the fine name “Anathapindada”. [Garden] A wooded park. [Jetavana Grove in the garden of Anathapindada] A park in the Sravasti capital where Sakyamuni Buddha taught this sutra. The trees belonged to Prince Jeta, the land to the Elder Anathapindada; together they offered them to the Buddha, hence the name, meaning the prince’s grove and the elder’s garden, where the Buddha often taught. The story of their joint offering: when the Buddha taught in Magadha, the elder begged him to come to Sravasti to save the people, and the Buddha consented. The elder searched and found Prince Jeta’s park most suitable, so wished to buy it. The prince jested: “Cover the ground with gold to a depth of five inches, and I will sell.” The elder agreed and did so. Moved by his sincerity, the prince said: “What men prize most is gold; he can spend his whole fortune to buy land to build a park for the monks — how could I lack anything and not take part?” He then of himself resolved to make the offering, asking to void the earlier pact. The elder would not. The prince said: “You have been allowed the ground for the gold; we have not spoken of the trees. The ground is yours, the trees mine; let us together complete the work and simply present the offering.” When the Buddha came he told Ananda: “The garden the elder bought; the grove the prince gave. With one mind they together honored the merit. From now on this place should be called the Jetavana Grove in the garden of Anathapindada.”
C2: Drawing in the great assembly to hear together — D1: the assembly of hearers; D2: the assembly of bodhisattvas; D3: the assembly of gods and humans.

[Essential Explanation] The hearers are placed first because of their renounced appearance, because they always follow, and because the Buddha’s Dharma depends on the sangha for transmission. The bodhisattvas are placed in the middle because their appearance is not fixed, because they do not always follow, and because they represent the meaning of the Middle Way. The gods and humans are placed last because of their worldly appearance, because the wise and the ordinary are mingled in their ranks, and because their office is that of external protection.
[Note] This explains why the hearers (the great assembly of bhiksus) are placed first, the bodhisattvas in the middle, and the gods and humans last.
D1: The assembly of hearers: E1: setting out the class and declaring the number;
E3: listing the names of the foremost
E1: Setting out the class and declaring the number
Together with a great assembly of bhiksus, twelve hundred and fifty.

[Essential Explanation] “Great bhiksu” means one who has received the complete precepts and left home. “Bhiksu” is Sanskrit with three meanings: first, “mendicant” — one bowl sustains the body, he stores nothing, and seeks only the essential liberation; second, “destroyer of evil” — with right wisdom he destroys the evil of affliction, not falling into love and views; third, “terror of Mara” — setting his mind on the precepts, when the rite of ordination is accomplished Mara is terrified. “Sangha” in full is sangha, translated “harmonious assembly”: together realizing the unconditioned liberation is the harmony of principle; bodies dwelling together, mouths without dispute, minds rejoicing together, views understood alike, precepts cultivated alike, benefits shared alike — the harmony of matters. The twelve hundred and fifty: the three Kasyapas, teachers and disciples, were in all a thousand; Sariputra’s
(i.e., Sariputra)

and Maudgalyayana’s teachers and disciples were two hundred; Yasas and the rest were fifty. All, having attained liberation earlier after the Buddha’s enlightenment, were moved by his deep kindness and always followed him.
[Note] [Twelve hundred and fifty] These twelve hundred and fifty great bhiksus were the Buddha’s constant attendants. According to the Sutra of Past and Present Cause and Effect, volume four

, of these: the small group headed by Yasas was fifty; the teachers and disciples of Uruvilva Kasyapa, five hundred; of Nadi Kasyapa, two hundred and fifty; of Gaya Kasyapa, two hundred and fifty; of Sariputra, one hundred; of Mahamaudgalyayana, one hundred. These first served non-Buddhist teachers and later, receiving the Buddha’s guidance, attained the fruit; moved by his kindness, at every assembly they followed without leaving, so they were called the constant attendants. Hence the sutras often say “twelve hundred and fifty together”. [Together] Together, in one place.
E2: Showing their rank and praising their virtues
All are great arhats, well known to the multitude.

[Essential Explanation] “Arhat” also contains three meanings: first, “worthy of offerings” — the fruit of the mendicant; second, “slayer of thieves” — the fruit of destroying evil; third, “no rebirth” — the fruit of the terror of Mara. Moreover, there are the three kinds of wisdom-liberated, both-liberated, and doubt-free liberation; here it is the doubt-free liberation, hence they are called great. Again, they are originally dharmakaya great beings who manifest as hearers, and who realize this inconceivable Dharma of the Pure Land, hence they are called great. Turning the wheel with the Buddha, broadly benefiting gods and humans, so they are well known to the multitude.

[Note] The arhat is the highest fruit of the vehicle of hearers. The Sanskrit word “arhat” contains the meanings of slayer of thieves, no rebirth, and worthy of offerings. “Slayer of thieves” is to slay completely the thieves of affliction; “no rebirth” is to be freed from birth and death and no longer receive a future existence; “worthy of offerings” is to be worthy of the offerings of gods and humans.
E3: Listing the names of the foremost

The elders Sariputra, Mahamaudgalyayana, Mahakasyapa, Mahakatyayana, Mahakausthila, Revata, Cudapanthaka, Nanda, Ananda, Rahula, Gavampati, Pindola Bharadvaja, Kalodayin, Mahakapphina, Bakkula, Anuruddha, and such great disciples.
[Essential Explanation] Both in virtue and in years they are venerable, hence elders. The Venerable Shenzi
(i.e., Sariputra)
is foremost in wisdom among the hearers. The Venerable Maudgalyayana
(i.e., Mahamaudgalyayana)
is foremost in supernatural powers. The Venerable Kassapa
(i.e., Mahakasyapa)
has a body that emits golden light and transmitted the mind-seal as the first patriarch, foremost in ascetic practice. The Venerable Katyayana
(i.e., Mahakatyayana)
, of Brahman stock, foremost in debate. The Venerable Mahakausthila
(i.e., Mahakausthila)
, foremost in answering questions. The Venerable Revata
(i.e., Revata)
, foremost in freedom from disorder. The Venerable Cudapanthaka
(i.e., Cudapanthaka)
, because of dull faculties could hold but one verse, yet his eloquence was inexhaustible, foremost in meaning. The Venerable Nanda
(i.e., Nanda)
, the Buddha’s own younger brother, foremost in deportment. The Venerable Ananda
(i.e., Ananda)
, the Buddha’s younger cousin and his attendant, foremost in learning. The Venerable Rahula
(i.e., Rahula)
, the Buddha’s son, foremost in secret practice. The Venerable Gavampati
(i.e., Gavampati)
, from past evil speech received this remnant retribution, foremost in heavenly offerings. The Venerable Pindola Bharadvaja
(i.e., Pindola Bharadvaja)
, long dwelling in the world, foremost in the field of merit. The Venerable Kalodayin
(i.e., Kalodayin)
, the Buddha’s emissary, foremost in teaching. The Venerable Mahakapphina
(i.e., Mahakapphina)
, foremost in knowledge of the constellations. The Venerable Bakkula
(i.e., Bakkula)
, foremost in longevity. The Venerable Anuruddha
(i.e., Anuruddha)
, also the Buddha’s younger cousin, foremost in the heavenly eye.

[Note] [Virtue and years] Virtue and the years of the precepts (the number of years since a bhiksu received the complete precepts). [Shenzi] The Chinese translation of Sariputra. The Sanskrit sari is translated as “body” and putra as “son”.

[Essential Explanation] These constant attendants are originally dharmakaya great beings who manifest as hearers and act as the assembly of influence. Now hearing the merit of the Pure Land’s embracing, they gain the benefit of the highest truth, increase the Way and diminish birth, purify their own Buddha-land, and so are also called the assembly of the occasion.

[Note] These constant attendants are originally dharmakaya great beings who manifest as hearers and act as the assembly of influence. Now hearing the merit of the Pure Land’s embracing, they gain the benefit of the highest truth, and so increase their realization of the dharmakaya and break through ignorance, purifying their own mental land; hence they are also called the assembly of the occasion.

[Assembly of influence] One of the four assemblies. The Buddhas and dharmakaya bodhisattvas, to assist Sakyamuni’s teaching, manifest bodies like shadows and echoes to uphold the Dharma-site. [Four assemblies] The initiators, who set the teaching in motion; the assembly of the occasion, who benefit upon hearing; the assembly of influence, bodhisattvas from other lands who assist in proclaiming the Dharma; and the assembly of connection, beings of dull faculties and little merit. [Highest truth siddhanta] One of the four siddhantas. [Four siddhantas] Four universal bestowals of Dharma: the worldly siddhanta — speaking of shallow matters to make listeners rejoice and accept; the individual siddhanta — examining the capacities and speaking the Dharma each needs, to arouse right faith; the remedial siddhanta — to the angry teaching the contemplation of compassion, to the deluded dependent origination, to the obstructed Buddha-recitation, thus bestowing Dharma medicines to remove the evil illnesses of beings; the highest-truth siddhanta — when the occasion is ripe, speaking of the real character of all dharmas, to enable beings to enter the Way of the sages. [Increase the Way and diminish birth] “Way” is the Middle-Way dharmakaya; “diminish birth” is to lessen the growth of ignorance. [Purify their own Buddha-land] To purify the Buddha-land of one’s own mind.
D2: The assembly of bodhisattvas
Together with the bodhisattvas, great beings: Manjusri, prince of the Dharma, the bodhisattva Ajita, the bodhisattva Gandhahasti, the bodhisattva Ever Vigorous, and such great bodhisattvas.

[Essential Explanation] A bodhisattva, great being, is called one of great resolve who has accomplished sentient beings; a title for one whose compassion and wisdom both operate and who benefits self and others. The Buddha is king of the Dharma; Manjusri succeeds to the Buddha’s family and so is called prince of the Dharma, foremost in wisdom among the bodhisattvas. Without brave and true wisdom one cannot realize the Pure Land Dharma gate, so he is placed first
(that is, placed first)
. Maitreya
(i.e., the bodhisattva Ajita)
will become a Buddha in the future, now dwelling at equal enlightenment
(the bodhisattva of equal enlightenment)
, and takes as his chief task the ultimate adornment and purification of the Buddha-land, so he is listed next. The “Never Resting” one
(Gandhahasti is translated “Never Resting”)
, because he practices through vast eons without pausing. The “Ever Vigorous” one
(the bodhisattva Ever Vigorous)

, because he benefits self and others without weariness. These bodhisattvas of deep attainment must all seek rebirth in the Pure Land, because never apart from seeing the Buddha, hearing the Dharma, and drawing near to the sangha, they can speedily perfect bodhi.
D3: The assembly of gods and humans
And Sakra, lord of the devas, and so on, with countless assemblies of gods and humans.
[Essential Explanation] Sakra, lord of the devas, is called the “lord of the Trayastrimsa heaven”. “And so on”: below, equal to the four kings
(i.e., the heaven of the four kings)

, above, equal to Yama, Tusita, Nirmita, and Paranirmitavasavartin, the countless devas of the form and formless realms. “All in the great assembly” means the gods and humans of the ten directions, the eight classes, the asuras, humans and non-humans, all without exception attendant — none being outside the capacities embraced by the Pure Land Dharma gate.

[Note] [Eight classes] The eight kinds of beings: devas, nagas, yaksas (translated “brave ghost”), gandharvas (translated “incense spirit”), asuras (translated “not-gods”), garudas (translated “golden-winged bird”), kimnaras (translated “not-human”), mahoragas (translated “great serpent-spirit” or “great-bellied earth-dragon”). Because human eyes cannot see these eight classes, they are also called the “eight classes of unseen beings”; and because among them the devas and nagas are the most excellent, they are also called “devas, nagas, and the eight classes”. [Asura] Abbreviation of asura. “Asura” is translated “not-god”, because it has the fortune of a god but not its virtue, resembling a god yet not a god. Also translated “un-end”, because its appearance is very ugly; also translated “no-wine”, saying that in its land wine cannot be brewed. Its nature is fond of fighting. [Humans and non-humans, all without exception attendant] Humans and non-humans, all without exception came to the assembly.
[Essential Explanation] The common introduction is finished.
[Note] The common introduction is finished.

blocks.text: II. The Land of Utmost Bliss

inline.s: B2: The special introduction (the introduction of the occasion)

[Note] [Special introduction] After the common introduction comes the special introduction, which is the part in which each sutra’s preface differs. For example, the second passage of this sutra (“At that time the Buddha told the elder Sariputra: From here to the west, passing through a hundred thousand kotis of Buddha-lands, there is a world called Utmost Bliss. In that land there is a Buddha named Amitabha, who is now teaching the Dharma.”) is the special introduction. The special introduction is also called the introduction of the occasion, explaining how this Dharma-assembly was set in motion.

[Essential Explanation] The wondrous gate of the Pure Land is inconceivable; no one is able to ask, so the Buddha himself proclaims the names of the reliance and the dependent to set it in motion. Moreover, the Buddha’s wisdom discerns capacities without error, seeing that this assembly should hear the wondrous gate of the Pure Land and gain the four benefits; therefore without waiting for a question he sets it in motion himself. As the Brahma Net Sutra, in its lower scroll, itself proclaims its titles saying “I am now Vairocana” and so on, which the wise classify as the introduction of the occasion — by analogy this may be understood.

[Note] [Four benefits] These are the benefits of the four siddhantas: first, the worldly siddhanta, gaining the benefit of joy — hearing that there is a Western land of Utmost Bliss, pure and adorned, with a Buddha in that land teaching the Dharma now, one’s mind gives rise to joy; second, the individual siddhanta, gaining the benefit of producing good — hearing that one may be reborn in that land, one knows that hearing the wondrous gate of the Pure Land can produce good; third, the remedial siddhanta, gaining the benefit of destroying evil — by reverently practicing the pure deeds in accordance with the teaching, thought after thought continuing, one destroys the evil of body, speech, and mind; fourth, the highest-truth siddhanta, gaining the benefit of entering the principle — the teaching to uphold the name and recite the Buddha, recited until the days are many and the merit deep, suddenly awakening to the principle of reality and the first truth, gaining the one-mind undivided.

At that time the Buddha told the elder Sariputra: From here to the west, passing through a hundred thousand kotis of Buddha-lands, there is a world called Utmost Bliss. In that land there is a Buddha named Amitabha, who is now teaching the Dharma.

[Essential Explanation] The Dharma gate of the Pure Land universally embraces the three capacities, absolute and perfectly integrated, inconceivable; it perfectly receives and perfectly surpasses all Dharma gates, so deep and so hard to believe. Hence it is specially told to the one of great wisdom
(the elder Sariputra)
; without the foremost wisdom one cannot directly and without doubt believe it.

[Essential Explanation] “West” means running straight across to the due west, marking the place of the present abode. “A hundred thousand kotis”: ten million is one koti; here, accumulating kotis up to a hundred thousand. “Buddha-lands”: a triple-thousand great thousand world is universally the field of one Buddha. Speaking of this world: one Mount Sumeru, with a continent on each of the four sides, illuminated by the same sun and moon, surrounded by one iron ring of mountains, is called one four-continent world. A thousand four-continent worlds form a small thousand world; a thousand small thousand worlds form a middle thousand world; a thousand middle thousand worlds form a great thousand world. Beyond a hundred thousand kotis of such Buddha-lands to the west is the Land of Utmost Bliss.

[Essential Explanation] Question: Why is the Land of Utmost Bliss in the west? Answer: This is not a good question. If the Land of Utmost Bliss were in the east, you would then ask why it is in the east — would that not be idle talk? Moreover, seen from a Buddha-land eleven thousand kotis away, it is again in the east; what is there to doubt?

[Essential Explanation] “There is a world called Utmost Bliss” prefaces the name of the reliant land. Vertically, by the three times, the eons are distinguished; horizontally, by the ten directions, the boundaries are fixed — hence it is called a world. “Utmost Bliss” (Sanskrit Sukhavati, also translated “land of peace and nourishment”, “peace and happiness”, “pure and serene”, and so on) means being forever free from all suffering, the first and foremost peace — as explained in detail below.

[Note] [Preface] To relate, to set forth. [Reliant retribution] The retribution the body relies on to dwell — the land, mountains, rivers, earth, houses and implements — the environment of life. The sutra says: “The reliant retribution turns with the primary retribution.” [Primary retribution] The body and mind of beings, the principal substance of retribution drawn by past karmic causes. The reliant and primary are called the two retributions. [Vertically, by the three times, the eons are distinguished; horizontally, by the ten directions, the boundaries are fixed — hence a world] This explains “world” in the sutra’s “there is a world called Utmost Bliss”. Past, present, and future are “world” (time); east, west, south, north, up, and down are “world” (space). [Three times] Past, present, future, also called the three worlds. [Peace] Tranquil and secure. [As explained in detail below] See the section “D2: detailed explanation” below.

[Essential Explanation] But there are four Buddha-lands, each divided into pure and defiled. In the land of common dwellers of ordinary and sages, where the five turbidities are heavy it is defiled; where they are light, pure. In the land of expedient remainder, one who enters by the clumsy method of analyzing emptiness is defiled; one who enters by the skillful method of contemplating the nature-emptiness is pure. In the land of true retribution free of obstacles, one who enters by the successive three contemplations is defiled; one who enters by the one-mind three contemplations is pure. In the land of eternal stillness and light, one who realizes in part is defiled; one who is ultimately fully realized is pure. Here the Land of Utmost Bliss refers precisely to the pure land of common dwellers, which is also transversely endowed with the three higher pure lands.

[Note] [Five turbidities] First, the eon of turbidity — the age meets evil fortune and calamities arise; second, the turbidity of afflictions — minds are full of greed, anger, ignorance, and so on; third, the turbidity of beings — beings are of inferior quality, much suffering and little joy; fourth, the turbidity of views — wrong views prevail and thought is confused; fifth, the turbidity of life — beings, receiving retribution for evil karma, are exhausted in body and mind and their lives are short. [Clumsy method] The clumsy one of the methods of salvation. [Skillful method] The skillful one of the methods of salvation. [Successive three contemplations] The Tiantai three contemplations of emptiness, provisional, and middle: first from the provisional enter emptiness, then from emptiness enter the provisional, then transcend both and enter the first-truth contemplation of the Middle Way. [One-mind three contemplations] The contemplative method of the Perfect teaching: all things have the three truths of emptiness, provisional, and middle, mutually endowed and fused, so that a single mind contemplates them together. [One who realizes in part] A bodhisattva of the grounds who has not exhausted ignorance. [Ten grounds] In the fifty-two stages of bodhisattva practice, the fifth group of ten is the ten grounds, where one opens the Buddha-realm and perfects the wisdom of all modes, already among the sages, hence also called the “ten sages”.

[Now the Land of Utmost Bliss refers precisely to the pure land of common dwellers, which is also transversely endowed with the three higher pure lands] The Land of Utmost Bliss now spoken of refers precisely to the land of common dwellers of ordinary and sages. And the land of common dwellers is transversely endowed with the land of expedient remainder, the land of adorned true retribution, and the land of eternal stillness and light: the Buddha in the land of common dwellers — that land is the land of eternal stillness and light; the bodhisattva in the land of common dwellers — that land is the land of adorned true retribution; the hearer in the land of common dwellers — that land is the land of expedient remainder.
[Essential Explanation] “There is a Buddha named Amitabha” prefaces the name of the primary-retribution teacher; the translation is explained in detail below.
[Note] [The translation explained in detail below] The meaning of “Amitabha” is seen in the section “D2: detailed explanation” below.

[Essential Explanation] The Buddha has three bodies, each discussed as single and as multiple. The single dharmakaya refers to the realized principle-nature; the single sambhogakaya to the realized merit and wisdom; the single nirmanakaya to the manifested marks and forms. The multiple dharmakaya: the pure self-nature dharmakaya and the most-sublime dharmakaya free from defilement. The multiple sambhogakaya: the self-enjoyment and the other-enjoyment sambhogakaya. The multiple nirmanakaya: the nirmanakaya of manifestation and of response; again, the Buddha-realm nirmanakaya and the nirmanakaya that conforms to beings. Though the single and multiple three bodies are distinguished, they are truly neither one nor three, yet three yet one. Here “Amitabha Buddha” refers precisely to the nirmanakaya of manifestation in the land of common dwellers, which is still simultaneously the sambhogakaya and the dharmakaya.
[Note] This sets forth the three bodies of the Buddha: dharmakaya, sambhogakaya, and nirmanakaya.

[Essential Explanation] Further, that both the world and the Buddha are spoken of as existing has four meanings: to mark out the real object, causing aspiration; to instruct with truthful words, causing single-mindedness; to distinguish that it is not a city of gandharvas nor a mirage, not a provisional manifestation nor a roundabout display, not a false reflected image, not attachment to true, to the partial, or to the one-sided — destroying the wrong of Mara and the provisional and lesser; and to fully reveal that it is inherent in the nature, causing deep realization.

[Note] Further, that the Land of Utmost Bliss and Amitabha Buddha are spoken of as existing has four meanings: first, to definitively mark that the Western reliance and primary (the Land of Utmost Bliss and Amitabha Buddha) is a real object present now, causing beings to long for it; second, Sakyamuni and the Buddhas of the six directions, with truthful words, instruct the Dharma gate of upholding the name and reciting the Buddha, enabling single-mindedness and pure thought after thought; third, to distinguish that this is not an illusion, not a provisional or roundabout manifestation, not a false reflected image, not the attachment to true or partial true of the Tripitaka school nor the one-sided middle of the Distinct school, but the wonderful existence of the perfect middle, destroying the wrong of Mara and the provisional and lesser; fourth, to fully reveal that the two retributions are inherent in the self-nature, causing deep realization.

[Distinguish] To select and differentiate. [City of gandharvas] Also called ghost city, a mirage tower; the gandharvas are India’s musicians, who deftly conjure towers, hence the mirage in the sky is called the gandharva city. [Mirage] The wandering vapor of the fields; from afar it looks like water, but near at hand there is none; a thirsty deer pursues it mistaking it for water. [Provisional manifestation] An expedient manifestation. [Attachment to true, to the partial, and to the one-sided] “Attachment to true” is the Tripitaka school’s attachment to a true nirvana; “partial” is its partial true; “one-sided” is the one-sided middle of the Distinct school. These two existences of the Western reliance and primary are the wonderful existence of the perfect middle, so they are neither attachment to true, nor partial, nor one-sided. [Tripitaka school] The teaching of the three baskets, one of the four teachings of the method of transformation of the Tiantai school. [Four teachings of the method of transformation] The Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect schools: the first teaches the four truths of arising-and-ceasing dependent origination, chiefly for hearers and pratyekabuddhas; the second teaches the four real truths of emptiness and non-arising, shared by the three vehicles; the third teaches bodhisattvas the immeasurable Mahayana Dharma, not shared by the two vehicles; the fourth teaches bodhisattvas of the sharpest capacity the middle-Way reality of the integration of phenomena and principle. [Provisional and lesser] The provisional teaching and the lesser vehicle. [Inherent in the nature] Existing from the beginning.

[Essential Explanation] “Who is now teaching the Dharma” distinguishes the above two existences of the reliance and primary — not past and already extinguished, nor future and not yet accomplished, but present now; hence one should rightly resolve to seek rebirth, personally draw near and hear the Dharma, and speedily attain right enlightenment.

[Note] “Who is now teaching the Dharma” means that the Land of Utmost Bliss and Amitabha Buddha spoken of above are not past and already extinguished, nor future and not yet accomplished, but present now; hence one should rightly resolve to seek rebirth, personally draw near and hear the Dharma from Amitabha Buddha, and speedily realize the Buddha-fruit!
[Two existences of the reliance and primary] Refers to the sutra’s phrase “there is a world called Utmost Bliss. In that land there is a Buddha named Amitabha”.

[Essential Explanation] Further, the two existences present now are the preface of the encouragement to faith; the world named Utmost Bliss is the preface of the encouragement to the vow; the Buddha named Amitabha is the preface of the encouragement to the wonderful practice of upholding the name.
[Note] [Two existences present now] Refers to the sutra’s phrase “there is a world called Utmost Bliss. In that land there is a Buddha named Amitabha, who is now teaching the Dharma”.

[Essential Explanation] Further, Amitabha prefaces the Buddha, “now teaching the Dharma” prefaces the Dharma, and “the assembly now present” prefaces the sangha. Buddha, Dharma, and sangha are one reality — this prefaces the essence; from this arise faith, vow, and practice — this prefaces the purpose; when faith, vow, and practice are accomplished, one is sure to be reborn and to see the Buddha and hear the Dharma — this prefaces the function; the single Buddha-realm as the object of attention, without mixing other matters — this prefaces the teaching and characteristics. The words are brief but the meaning is complete.

[Note] Further, in the sutra’s phrase “In that land there is a Buddha named Amitabha, who is now teaching the Dharma (in the assembly)”: “Amitabha” prefaces the Buddha, “now teaching the Dharma” prefaces the Dharma, and “the assembly now present” prefaces the sangha. Buddha, Dharma, and sangha being one reality prefaces the essence of the sutra; from this arise faith, vow, and practice — this prefaces the purpose; when faith, vow, and practice are accomplished, one is sure to be reborn and see the Buddha and hear the Dharma — this prefaces the function; the single Buddha-realm as the object of attention, without mixing other matters — this prefaces the teaching and characteristics. The words, though brief, make complete the meaning of the fivefold profound purport.
[Essential Explanation] The first part, the introduction, is finished.
[Note] The first great part, the “introduction”, ends here. Below begins the second great part, the “main body”.

A2: The main body: B1: widely setting forth the wonderful fruits of the reliance and primary of that land to arouse faith; B2: specially urging sentient beings to seek rebirth to arouse the vow; B3: rightly showing the practicer to uphold the name to establish the practice.

[Essential Explanation] Faith, vow, and upholding the name — this is the essential purport of the whole sutra. Faith and vow are the practice of wisdom; upholding the name is the practice of practice. Whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether faith and vow are present; the high or low of the grade depends entirely on the depth of upholding the name. Hence the practice of wisdom is the guide, and the practice of practice is the proper cultivation, like the eye and the foot operating together.

[Note] "Faith, vows, and holding the Name: the essential purport of the whole sutra" means that faith, vows, and practice are inseparable: this is the essential purport of this sutra and also the essential path of Pure Land cultivation. "Faith and vows are the practice of wisdom; holding the Name is the practice of practice," and "therefore the practice of wisdom is the guide ahead, the practice of practice is the true cultivation, like eyes and feet working together" mean that faith and vows are the guide ahead, like the eyes, while holding the Name is the true cultivation, like the two feet. Without eyes one stumbles about at random, and without feet one cannot advance at all. Therefore, in the context of "whether one is born there depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and vows; the height of one's grade depends entirely on the depth of holding the Name," the meaning of these two lines is this: to be born there one must have faith and vows, and one must also have the skill of holding the Name; with deep skill one is born in a high grade, with shallow skill in a low grade.
The questioner: "Whether one is born there depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and vows" ought to mean that so long as one has faith and vows, one attains rebirth.
Answer: Understood that way, there are three problems.

1. If it were understood this way, then "whether one is born there depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and vows; the height of one's grade depends entirely on the depth of holding the Name" would mean: so long as one has faith and vows, one attains rebirth; so long as one has the skill of holding the Name, one attains rebirth (with deep skill, rebirth in a high grade; with shallow skill, rebirth in a low grade). In that case the first half says that so long as one has faith and vows one attains rebirth, while the second half says that so long as one has the skill of holding the Name one attains rebirth. Then is rebirth attained merely by having faith and vows, or merely by having the skill of holding the Name? Consider: how could Master Ouyi ever have uttered such self-contradictory words? Therefore one must pay close attention to the difference in meaning between the two expressions "depends entirely on" and "rests entirely on": "depends entirely on" states a necessary condition (an indispensable condition), while "rests entirely on" states a sufficient condition (the mere presence of that condition suffices).

2. In this passage Master Ouyi speaks with perfect clarity: faith and vows are the guide ahead (the pathfinder), and holding the Name is the true cultivation (the actual walking). How could the guide alone, without the true cultivation, possibly suffice? Moreover, the Master gives a vivid simile: faith and vows are like the eyes, holding the Name is like the feet. Then a practitioner who would reach the destination (the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss) must have his eyes watch the road and his feet walk it (eyes and feet working together). How could he reach the destination merely by having eyes to watch the road while his feet do not walk? As Master Ouyi teaches in the section "Clarifying the Essential Tenet" earlier in this Essential Explanation: "The essential tenet is the crucial path of cultivation.... This sutra takes faith, vows, and the holding of the Name as the essential tenet of cultivation. Without faith, vows cannot be aroused; without vows, practice cannot be guided; without the wondrous practice of holding the Name, one cannot fulfill one's vows and realize what one has believed.... Faith means believing in oneself and believing in others, believing in cause and believing in effect, believing in the phenomenal and believing in the principle; vows mean loathing the Saha world and joyfully seeking the Pure Land; practice means holding the Name single-mindedly without distraction."
3. This passage of Master Ouyi's teaching reads:

"Faith, vows, and holding the Name: the essential purport of the whole sutra. Faith and vows are the practice of wisdom; holding the Name is the practice of practice. Whether one is born there depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and vows; the height of one's grade depends entirely on the depth of holding the Name. Therefore the practice of wisdom is the guide ahead, and the practice of practice is the true cultivation, like eyes and feet working together."

Before the line "whether one is born there depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and vows; the height of one's grade depends entirely on the depth of holding the Name" stand the words "faith and vows are the practice of wisdom; holding the Name is the practice of practice," and after it come the words "therefore the practice of wisdom is the guide ahead, and the practice of practice is the true cultivation, like eyes and feet working together." By your understanding, one could reach the destination with the practice of wisdom, the guide, and the eyes alone, dispensing with the practice of practice, the true cultivation, and the feet. How could that be Master Ouyi's intent? What is more, Master Ouyi was annotating the Buddha Speaks of Amitabha Sutra, in which the Buddha teaches that faith, vows, and holding the Name with single-mindedness can ensure rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. How could Master Ouyi have said in his annotation that faith and vows alone ensure rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss?
Furthermore, note this: when Master Ouyi explained faith, vows, and practice above, he stated plainly:
"Without the wondrous practice of holding the Name, one cannot fulfill one's vows and realize what one has believed.... Practice means holding the Name single-mindedly without distraction."
He sets forth with perfect clarity the relation among faith, vows, and practice and the requirements of practice.

The reason Buddha-recitation must be single-minded is that "only where there is a Pure Land of the mind can the Western Pure Land be born; it is through the pure mind of Buddha-recitation that one elicits birth in the Western Pure Land" — this is the principle of rebirth through Buddha-recitation.

Master Yinguang's original words in this passage are: "Only where there is a Pure Land of the mind can the Western Pure Land be born. If one's own mind is not pure, how could one attain rebirth at once? Even a sinner of vile and rebellious deeds who attains rebirth with ten utterances of the Buddha's Name does so because the pure mind of Buddha-recitation elicits birth in the Western Pure Land." (Collected Writings of Master Yinguang: Answers to Layman Qu Tianxiang's Twenty-Seven Questions) Master Yinguang also said: "With a scattered mind, Buddha-recitation seldom attains rebirth. This method can gather the mind to one place: recite the Buddha's Name single-mindedly, and rebirth is certain." (Collected Writings of Master Yinguang: A Letter to Layman Chen Xizhou) He also said: "Since one has true faith and earnest vows, one should cultivate the true practice of Buddha-recitation. Take faith and vows as the guide ahead, and Buddha-recitation as the true practice. Faith, vows, and practice, these three, are the essential tenet of the Buddha-recitation dharma-gate. Practice without faith and vows cannot attain rebirth. Faith and vows without practice likewise cannot attain rebirth. When faith, vows, and practice are all complete and lacking in nothing, rebirth is certain. Whether one is born there depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and vows; the height of one's grade depends entirely on the depth of holding the Name." (Collected Writings of Master Yinguang: A Letter to Layman Chen Xizhou)
So the essential key that ensures rebirth is:
true faith, earnest vows, single-mindedness without distraction.

This too is the guiding principle of the Buddha-reciter's study and practice. Because of true faith, the eye clearly perceives the scene before it, seeing goal and road unmistakably; because of earnest vows, the driving force is matchless in strength, like a river bursting its banks, sweeping on with nothing able to withstand it. With true faith and earnest vows, one will surely follow the World-Honored One's earnest teaching to "practice in accordance with the teaching," and so bring forth the wondrous practice of single-mindedness without distraction, and by this wondrous practice realize what one has believed and fulfill what one has vowed: "Now, since the mind is single and undistracted, (at the approach of death) one will
inwardly congeal right mindfulness, outwardly evoke the Buddha's welcome
, cast off this karmic body, and at last be born in that land." (Master Lianchi, Commentary and Subcommentary on the Amitabha Sutra)
[Peiran mo zhi neng yu] Sweeping on in vast torrents, with nothing able to withstand it.

Concerning the relation among true faith, earnest vows, and vigorous practice, Master Chewu (the Twelfth Patriarch of the Pure Land school) teaches: "As for those without faith, let them be for now (those who do not believe, let us set them aside and not speak of them). Even among those who believe, to believe without vowing is still not to believe; to vow without practicing is still not to vow; to practice without fierceness is still not to practice. The reason practice is not fierce is that the vow is not earnest. The reason the vow is not earnest is that the faith is not true. In sum, it is hard to give rise to true faith. If faith is truly there, the vow will of itself be earnest. If the vow is truly earnest, the practice will of itself be fierce. With true and earnest faith and vows, joined to brave and vigorous practice, one will certainly be born in the Pure Land, certainly see Amitabha Buddha, certainly realize the three non-retrogressions, and certainly reach the stage of one lifetime from Buddhahood." (The Collected Works of Master Chewu)

Master Shengan, the Eleventh Patriarch of the Pure Land school, says: "Again, there are those who speak of the Pure Land with their lips while their hearts yearn for the Saha world; this too is not a vow. Moreover, the single word 'vow' encompasses both faith and practice. Faith means that self and others, cause and effect, the phenomenal and the principle, are all without falsity (believing that one's own mind is Buddha and that others are likewise; Buddha-recitation is the cause, rebirth and Buddhahood are the fruit. The West is the phenomenal; the nature beyond the mind is the principle; each and every one is real, and so it is called 'without falsity'); practice means devoting oneself solely to holding the Name, without mixture or distraction; vow means that mind after mind delights in it and thought after thought longs for it. These three matters, not one may be lacking. There are those who have faith and practice but no vow; there has never been one who had a vow but no faith and practice. Question: If someone hears of the Western Pure Land and his mind gives rise to delight, yet he does not recite the Buddha's Name, can he attain rebirth? Answer: If delight truly arises in his mind, he will certainly give rise to longing; if longing arises, he will certainly recite the Buddha's Name. To delight without longing is certainly not delight; to long without reciting, how could that be longing? That one who delights, longs, and recites the Buddha's Name should fail to attain rebirth has never been. Question: Suppose someone here both delights, longs, and recites, but his worldly mind is heavy and he clings to the dust of toil, can he attain rebirth? Answer: So long as the general is fierce, the strength of the bandits need not be feared. If the longing mind is truly urgent and the mind that holds the thought is truly focused, then however heavy the clinging, it will of itself gradually grow lighter, and he too will attain rebirth. It is like giving up silver for gold, or giving up fish for bear's paw: what difficulty is there in that? The only fear is that the power of the vow prove no match for the power of craving, and the thought of the Buddha fail to overcome the thought of desire, so that one drifts vague and heedless, half-believing and half-doubting; then there is nothing I can do for such a person." (Annotated Text of the Essay on the Western Pure Land)
[Di kong] One only fears. [Ze wu mo ru zhi he ye yi yi] (Toward such a person) there is truly nothing I can do. The word mo means "there is none."

Therefore, whether the power of the vow can match the power of craving, and whether the thought of the Buddha can overcome the thought of desire, is the standard by which we test whether faith and vows are true and earnest.
Question: How can one attain single-mindedness without distraction in Buddha-recitation?

Answer: The greatest obstacle to attaining single-mindedness without distraction in Buddha-recitation is deluded thought. In the practice textbook of the Practice According to the Teaching Online Buddhist Academy,
Mindful Buddha-Recitation

the causes of deluded thought are analyzed in detail, along with how to overcome it effectively; and the concrete steps and methods of study and practice for attaining single-mindedness without distraction in Buddha-recitation are explained in detail. So long as one has true faith and earnest vows, works hard, advances step by step, and perseveres, one will certainly attain single-mindedness without distraction in Buddha-recitation.

Shariputra! Why is that land called Ultimate Bliss?
E2. The explanation: F1. Explained in terms of the one who enjoys; F2. Explained in terms of what is enjoyed
F1. Explained in terms of the one who enjoys

[Note] [Explained in terms of the one who enjoys] Explained with respect to the one who enjoys. Here "in terms of" has the sense of "with respect to." [Explained in terms of what is enjoyed] Explained with respect to what is enjoyed.
The sentient beings in that land endure no suffering but receive every joy; therefore it is named Ultimate Bliss.

[Essential Explanation] "Sentient beings" refers to those who enjoy; all from Equal Enlightenment downward may be so named. Here we speak with respect to the people of that land, using the lowest of the low to illustrate the highest of the high.

[Note] "Sentient beings" are those who enjoy. Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment and all below them may be called sentient beings. Here we speak of the bliss of the people of the Land of Sages and Commoners Together; if even the lowest of the low are thus, then the bliss of the highest of the high needs no saying.

[Essential Explanation] In the Saha world suffering and bliss are mixed. In truth, suffering is the suffering of suffering, because it presses upon body and mind; bliss is the suffering of decay, because it does not abide for long; neither-suffering-nor-bliss is the suffering of conditioned formation, because its nature is to flow on. That land is forever free of these three sufferings; unlike the bliss of this land, which is bliss only in contrast to suffering, it is therefore named Ultimate Bliss.

[Note] Though the Saha world is said to mix suffering and bliss, in truth all of it is suffering. Suffering is of course suffering: because it presses upon body and mind, it is called the suffering of suffering. Bliss too is suffering: because it does not abide for long, it is called the suffering of decay. Neither-suffering-nor-bliss is also suffering: because its nature is to flow on, it is called the suffering of conditioned formation. The Land of Ultimate Bliss is forever free of these three sufferings; unlike this land (the Saha world), where bliss is spoken of in contrast to suffering, it is therefore called Ultimate Bliss.

[The three sufferings] The suffering of suffering, the suffering of decay, and the suffering of conditioned formation. "The suffering of suffering": people in the world have bodies subject to birth and death, which is suffering enough; when the many sufferings press upon them besides, it is suffering upon suffering, and so it is called the suffering of suffering. "The suffering of decay": the suffering felt when a blissful state that has occasionally appeared is lost. "The suffering of conditioned formation": the suffering of all formations being impermanent, flowing on without cease, and never at rest.

[Essential Explanation] A general distinction: in the Land of Sages and Commoners Together the five turbidities are light, there is no eightfold suffering of fragmentary birth-and-death, and one enjoys only such bliss as freedom from sickness and aging, roaming at will, heavenly food and heavenly garments, and gathering with all good beings; in the Land of Expedient Liberation with Remainder the contemplation of essence is skilful, there is no suffering of sinking into emptiness and stagnating in quiescence, and one enjoys only such bliss as the play of spiritual powers; in the Land of Real Reward and Adornment the contemplation of mind is perfect, there is no suffering of separation and non-fusion, and one enjoys only the unobstructed and inconceivable bliss; in the Land of Eternally Quiescent Light, which is ultimate and equal, there is no suffering of dharmakaya leakage and outflow of the true eternal, and one enjoys only the perfect and ultimate bliss that accords with nature.

[Note] A rough comparison of the suffering and bliss of the four lands of the Saha world (the Land of Sages and Commoners Together, the Land of Expedient Liberation with Remainder, the Land of Real Reward and Adornment, and the Land of Eternally Quiescent Light) with those of the four lands of the Land of Ultimate Bliss (the Land of Sages and Commoners Together, the Land of Expedient Liberation with Remainder, the Land of Real Reward and Adornment, and the Land of Eternally Quiescent Light): In the Land of Ultimate Bliss's Land of Sages and Commoners Together the five turbidities are light, there is no fragmentary birth-and-death and none of the eight sufferings; rather one is free from sickness and aging, and enjoys only such bliss as roaming at will, heavenly food and heavenly garments, and gathering with all good beings. In the Land of Ultimate Bliss's Land of Expedient Liberation with Remainder all uphold the contemplation of the Perfect Teaching; there is no suffering of sinking into emptiness and stagnating in quiescence, and one enjoys only such bliss as the play of spiritual powers. In the Land of Ultimate Bliss's Land of Real Reward and Adornment all enter by upholding the threefold contemplation of one mind; because the contemplative wisdom is perfect and fused, there is no suffering of the three contemplations being separated in sequence and the three truths failing to fuse, and one enjoys only the unobstructed and inconceivable bliss. In the Land of Ultimate Bliss's Land of Eternally Quiescent Light enjoyment is equal to the Buddha's; therefore there is no suffering of dharmakaya leakage and outflow of the true eternal, and one enjoys only the perfect and ultimate bliss that accords with nature.

[The eight sufferings of fragmentary birth-and-death] The eight sufferings of fragmentary birth-and-death. [The two kinds of birth-and-death] Fragmentary birth-and-death and transformational birth-and-death. Fragmentary birth-and-death is the bodily birth and death of ordinary beings within the three realms; transformational birth-and-death is the birth and death of mental moments, in the minds of bodhisattvas beyond the three realms. [The eight sufferings] 1. The suffering of birth, the pain of being born; 2. The suffering of aging, the pain of old age and frailty; 3. The suffering of sickness, the pain of illness; 4. The suffering of death, the pain of dying; 5. The suffering of parting from the beloved, the pain of separation from those one loves; 6. The suffering of meeting the hated, the pain of encountering an enemy; 7. The suffering of not getting what one seeks, the pain of unfulfilled desires; 8. The suffering of the blazing five aggregates, that is, the workings of the five aggregates blazing up and covering the true nature, so that after death one must again be reborn. [In the Land of Expedient Liberation the contemplation of essence is skilful] In the Land of Expedient Liberation with Remainder of this land (the Saha world) there are those who enter by the clumsy path of the Tripitaka Teaching's analytic contemplation of emptiness, and those who enter by the skilful path of the Shared Teaching's essential contemplation of emptiness; all of them sink and stagnate in the phantom city and suffer the extinction of one-sided emptiness. But in the Land of Expedient Liberation with Remainder of the Land of Ultimate Bliss all uphold the contemplation of the Perfect Teaching and enter by realizing that form itself is emptiness; not stagnating in empty quiescence, they can at once issue from the true into the conventional, play with spiritual powers, purify Buddha-lands, and bring beings to maturity. Therefore it is said that they enjoy only such bliss as the play of spiritual powers. [In the Land of Real Reward the contemplation of mind is perfect] In the Land of Real Reward and Adornment of the Land of Ultimate Bliss all enter by upholding the threefold contemplation of one mind; because the contemplative wisdom is perfect and fused, there is no suffering of the three contemplations being separated in sequence and the three truths failing to fuse. Therefore it is said that they enjoy only the unobstructed and inconceivable bliss. [In the Land of Quiescent Light, ultimate and equal] In the Land of Eternally Quiescent Light of the Land of Ultimate Bliss enjoyment is equal to the Buddha's; therefore there is no suffering of dharmakaya leakage and outflow of the true eternal, but only the perfect and ultimate bliss that accords with nature.

[Essential Explanation] Yet the beings of the Land of Sages and Commoners Together, because in holding the Name their roots of goodness and their merit are the same as the Buddha's, perfectly purify the four lands and perfectly enjoy every bliss. Furthermore, what is most excellent in the Land of Ultimate Bliss lies not in the upper three lands but in the Land of Sages and Commoners Together. The reason is that, looking upward, the Lands of Sages and Commoners Together of the ten directions yield to its singular excellence, and looking downward, it can be measured against this land. Therefore ordinary beings enter it with ease and at leisure, transcend horizontally and pass over. The Buddha's teaching on suffering and bliss has its point here.

[Note] Yet the beings born in the Land of Sages and Commoners Together of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, since in holding the Name they reveal the virtue of the fruit through the mind of the cause, have roots of goodness and merit the same as the Buddha's, perfectly purify the four lands, and perfectly enjoy every bliss. Furthermore, what is most excellent in the Land of Ultimate Bliss lies not in the upper three lands (the Land of Expedient Liberation with Remainder, the Land of Real Reward and Adornment, and the Land of Eternally Quiescent Light) but in the Land of Sages and Commoners Together. The main reason is this: looking upward, the Lands of Sages and Commoners Together of the Buddha-lands of the ten directions do not match the Land of Sages and Commoners Together of the Land of Ultimate Bliss in such singular excellence and wonder; looking downward, it can be measured against this land (the Saha world). Therefore ordinary beings who hold the Name and recite the Buddha's Name enter it with ease and at leisure, transcend horizontally and pass over. The Buddha's meaning in speaking of suffering and bliss lies precisely in the Land of Sages and Commoners Together.

[You ru] One who is born in the Land of Sages and Commoners Together of the Land of Ultimate Bliss rises from ordinary being to roots of goodness and merit equal to the Buddha's, perfectly purifies the four lands, and perfectly enjoys every bliss; hence it is called superior entry. [Cong rong] The road is broad and travelers are few. The Sutra of Immeasurable Life says: "The path ascended knows no limit; easy to go, yet none goes." Master Yinguang says: "It is only that you do not return; return, and you have it. The wind and moon of the old home, who will contend for them?" [Heng chao] One who cultivates by self-power must cut off all view-delusions and thought-delusions before leaving the Land of Sages and Commoners Together and entering the Land of Expedient Liberation; must cut off all dust-and-sand delusions and additionally break through ignorance before entering the Land of Real Reward; and must cut off all ignorance before entering the Land of Quiescent Light. This is called vertical transcendence. The Buddha-reciter, relying on the power of Amitabha Buddha's vows, can leave the impure Saha land and be born in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss without having cut off view-delusions and thought-delusions; and on arriving in the Land of Ultimate Bliss he can, from the Land of Sages and Commoners Together, without casting off one body and taking another, directly realize entry into the Land of Expedient Liberation, the Land of Real Reward, and even the Land of Quiescent Light. Hence it is called horizontal transcendence. [Du yue] To cross over from this shore to the other shore, meaning that one born in the Land of Sages and Commoners Together of the Land of Ultimate Bliss attains Buddhahood in one lifetime.
F2. Explained in terms of what is enjoyed

Moreover, Shariputra! In the Land of Ultimate Bliss there are sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all made of four treasures, encompassing and surrounding it; therefore is that land named Ultimate Bliss.

[Essential Explanation] The sevenfold rows represent the seven categories of the aids to the path. The four treasures represent the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. "Encompassing and surrounding" means the immeasurable dwelling places of Buddhas and bodhisattvas. Being all of four treasures means one's own merit is deep; encompassing and surrounding means the wise and holy are everywhere around; these are the true causal conditions of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[Note] [Railings] Horizontal pieces are called lan (rails), vertical pieces are called shun (posts); commonly called balustrades. [The four treasures] Gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. [The seven categories of the aids to the path] That is, the thirty-seven aids to the path. Because the thirty-seven aids to the path can be divided into seven categories (the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of spiritual power, the five roots, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold right path), the thirty-seven aids to the path are also called the seven categories of the aids to the path. [The thirty-seven aids to the path] That is, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of spiritual power, the five roots, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold right path, thirty-seven items in all; they are important provisions for cultivating the path, and hence are called the "thirty-seven aids to the path." Their content is as follows:
1. The four foundations of mindfulness, also called the four mindful abidings. (
) The foundation of mindfulness of the body: contemplating that this physical body is altogether impure. (
) The foundation of mindfulness of feeling: contemplating that all feelings, whether painful or pleasant, are suffering. (
) The foundation of mindfulness of mind: contemplating that this knowing mind arises and perishes moment by moment, with nothing that abides. (
) The foundation of mindfulness of dharmas: contemplating that all dharmas arise from causes and conditions and have no nature of self-mastery or autonomy; this is the no-self of all dharmas.
2. The four right efforts, also called the four right severances. (
) Cause evil already arisen to be forever cut off. (
) Cause evil not yet arisen not to arise. (
) Cause good not yet arisen to arise. (
) Cause good already arisen to increase.
3. The four bases of spiritual power, also called the four bases of miraculous power. (
) The base of desire: aspiring that the dharmas one cultivates be fulfilled according to one's wish. (
) The base of vigor: with respect to the dharmas one cultivates, focusing single-mindedly without intermixture, so that they are fulfilled according to one's wish. (
) The base of mindfulness: with respect to the dharmas one cultivates, remembering without forgetting, so that they are fulfilled according to one's wish. (
) The base of contemplation: contemplating the dharmas one cultivates without letting them be forgotten, so that they are fulfilled according to one's wish.
4. The five roots. "Root" means that which can produce; these five roots can produce all good dharmas. (
) The root of faith: firmly believing in the right path and the dharmas that aid it, one can bring forth all taintless meditative concentrations and liberations. (
) The root of vigor: cultivating the right Dharma without interruption or intermixture. (
) The root of mindfulness: remembering the right Dharma without forgetting. (
) The root of concentration: gathering the mind so that it is not scattered, single-mindedly still and settled; this is the root of concentration. (
) The root of wisdom: clearly perceiving and understanding all dharmas; this is the root of wisdom.
5. The five powers. "Power" means the capacity to function, able to destroy evil and accomplish good. (
) The power of faith: as the root of faith grows, it can destroy all doubts. (
) The power of vigor: as the root of vigor grows, it can destroy bodily and mental idleness. (
) The power of mindfulness: as the root of mindfulness grows, it can destroy all deviant thoughts and accomplish the virtue of supramundane right mindfulness. (
) The power of concentration: as the root of concentration grows, it can destroy all scattered thinking and bring forth the meditative concentrations. (
) The power of wisdom: as the root of wisdom grows, it can check and halt the delusions of view and thought within the three realms.
6. The seven factors of enlightenment, also called the seven branches of enlightenment or the seven enlightenment factors. (
) The enlightenment factor of discriminating dharmas: able to discern the true from the false among all dharmas. (
) The enlightenment factor of vigor: cultivating all path-dharmas without intermixture. (
) The enlightenment factor of joy: apprehending the true Dharma, the mind attains joy. (
) The enlightenment factor of discarding: able to cut off and remove all views and afflictions. (
) The enlightenment factor of renunciation: able to let go of the objects of thought and attachment that one has seen. (
) The enlightenment factor of concentration: able to perceive clearly the meditative concentration that has arisen. (
) The enlightenment factor of mindfulness: able to contemplate the path-dharmas one cultivates.
7. The eightfold right path, also called the eight noble paths or the eight truths of the path. (
) Right view: able to see the truth. (
) Right thought: the mind free of deviant thoughts. (
) Right speech: speech free of falsehood. (
) Right action: abiding in pure and good karma. (
) Right livelihood: living by begging for food in accordance with the Dharma. (
) Right vigor: cultivating all path-practices without intermixture. (
) Right mindfulness: able to focus the mind in remembrance of good dharmas. (
) Right concentration: body and mind still and quiet, rightly abiding in the principle of true emptiness.

[Essential Explanation] As for these adornments: the Pure Land of Sages and Commoners Together is elicited by supreme good karma and also by the fivefold contemplation of the Perfect Teaching, taking as its substance the supremely wondrous five dusts born of conditions; the Pure Land of Expedient Liberation is elicited by the wisdom of the contemplation of emptiness and also by the contemplation of the three truths in similitude, taking as its substance the wondrous taintless five dusts of the true truth; the Pure Land of Real Reward is elicited by the wisdom of the wondrous contemplation of the provisional and also by the contemplation of the three truths in partial realization, taking as its substance the inexhaustible five dusts of the wondrous conventional truth; the Land of Eternally Quiescent Light is elicited by the wisdom of the contemplation of the middle and also by the contemplation of the three truths in ultimate realization, taking as its substance the five dusts of the wondrous middle truth that accord with nature. To make this easier to understand, such a distinction is drawn; in truth the adornments of the four lands are none other than dharmas born of causes and conditions, and there is none that is not at once empty, provisional, and middle. Therefore the pure realm of the Land of Ultimate Bliss's Sages and Commoners Together is perfect and fused in truth and convention, and cannot be measured. The following passages all follow this pattern.
[Note] This separately explains the eliciting causes and the elicited fruits of the four lands.

[The five dusts] Form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. [The fivefold contemplation of the Perfect Teaching] The stage of "contemplation and practice" among the six stages of identity, the six stages of practice of Perfect Teaching bodhisattvas as established by the Tiantai school. This is the stage in which, having already known the name, one gives rise to contemplation and practice; the mind's contemplation is clear, and principle and wisdom correspond. At this stage one can accomplish the fivefold merit: (1) the grade of rejoicing, (2) the grade of reading and reciting, (3) the grade of expounding the Dharma, (4) practicing the six perfections in addition, (5) properly practicing the six perfections. [The contemplation of the three truths in similitude] Cultivating the threefold contemplation of one mind and realizing entry into the stage of similitude. [The contemplation of the three truths in partial realization] Cultivating the threefold contemplation of one mind and realizing entry into the stage of partial realization. [The contemplation of the three truths in ultimate realization] Cultivating the threefold contemplation of one mind and realizing entry into the ultimate stage. [The threefold contemplation of one mind] "One mind" is the contemplating mind; the "three contemplations" are the contemplations of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. To understand that "a single moment of mind" is unattainable and inexpressible, and to be able to cultivate perfectly within one mind the three truths of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, is called the threefold contemplation of one mind, the contemplative method of the Perfect Teaching. [None is not at once empty, provisional, and middle] There is none that is not at once empty, at once provisional, and at once middle. [The following passages all follow this pattern] Wherever principle is revealed below, all follow this pattern.

[The six stages of identity] Also called the six stages of identity with Buddhahood, established by the Tiantai school to show the stages from the practice of ordinary beings up to the fruit of Buddhahood. 1. Identity with Buddhahood in principle. Though all sentient beings revolve through the six paths and dwell day after day in the dust of toil and affliction, turning their backs on the essence of enlightenment, nevertheless the virtue of the Buddha-nature remains complete in them. Hence it is called "identity with Buddhahood in principle." 2. Identity with Buddhahood in name. Whether from a good teacher or from the scriptures, one hears of the unborn and undying Buddha-nature inherently possessed by this very mind; one penetrates and understands it through the name, knowing that all dharmas are Buddha-dharmas and that all sentient beings can become Buddhas; one nods and grasps the meaning, suddenly awakening. Hence it is called "identity with Buddhahood in name." 3. Identity with Buddhahood in contemplation and practice. This is the stage of the five grades of the Perfect Teaching, the stage of outer ordinary beings; not only does one understand the name, one goes further and cultivates contemplation according to the teaching, knowing that all dharmas are Buddha-dharmas, the mind's contemplation clear and principle and wisdom corresponding. Hence it is called "identity with Buddhahood in contemplation and practice," which is the stage of the five grades. (Principle and wisdom corresponding: principle is the contemplated realm of principle, wisdom is the contemplating wisdom. "Corresponding" means matching; that is, when realm and wisdom match, word and deed are one. The five grades are the grade of rejoicing, the grade of reading and reciting, the grade of expounding the Dharma, the grade of practicing the six perfections in addition, and the grade of properly practicing the six perfections.) 4. Identity with Buddhahood in similitude. This is the stage of the ten faiths of the Perfect Teaching, the stage of inner ordinary beings. At the first faith one cuts off view-delusions; at the seventh faith one cuts off thought-delusions; at the eighth, ninth, and tenth faiths one cuts off dust-and-sand delusions. A practitioner at this stage, in contemplation and practice, contemplates more and grows clearer, stills more and grows more quiescent; though he has not truly awakened or truly realized, he resembles the principle, as if truly realizing it. Hence it is called "identity with Buddhahood in similitude." 5. Identity with Buddhahood in partial realization. This is, after the ten faiths, breaking through one portion of ignorance and realizing one portion of the three virtues, whereupon one enters the first abiding and realizes the dharmakaya, from which point one becomes a great being of the dharmakaya. From the first abiding onward, each stage breaks through ignorance and realizes the three virtues, and up to Equal Enlightenment there are forty-one stages in all, breaking through forty-one portions. Hence it is called "identity with Buddhahood in partial realization." 6. Identity with Buddhahood in ultimate realization. This is, from Equal Enlightenment, breaking through the final portion of ignorance, whereupon delusion is exhausted and the true alone remains; one thoroughly realizes the true suchness Buddha-nature inherently possessed by this body, enters the stage of wondrous enlightenment, and becomes a Buddha. Hence it is called "identity with Buddhahood in ultimate realization."
