[The stage of outer ordinary beings] The mind dwells outside the principle (one has not yet even a similar understanding of the right principle). [The stage of inner ordinary beings] Though one has not realized and seen the right principle, one has given rise to a similar understanding of it.

[Essential Explanation] Question: The Land of Quiescent Light is nothing but the nature of principle; how can it have these adornments? Answer: Each and every adornment is the whole body of the principle-nature, and each and every principle-nature is replete with adornments; only this is the Buddhas' ultimate circumstantial fruit. If the Land of Quiescent Light did not possess the supremely wondrous five dusts, how would it differ from a one-sidedly true dharma-nature?

[Note] Master Ouyi, fearing that readers would not understand that the Land of Quiescent Light is the principle that is identical with phenomena, and would fall into a one-sided view, therefore set up this question and answer to make it clear.
Question: The Land of Quiescent Light is solely the essence of principle; how can it have these adornments?

Answer: Each and every adornment of the three lands is not outside the Land of Quiescent Light; the whole body of the three lands is the principle-nature of the Quiescent Light. Each and every principle-nature is inherently replete with immeasurable adornments; phenomena abide within principle, and principle pervades along with phenomena. Nor is the Land of Quiescent Light outside the three lands; only thus is it the Buddhas' ultimate fruit-land of circumstantial reward. The sutra says: "The dwelling place of all Buddhas is called the Eternally Quiescent Light." From the standpoint of the Tathagata, the whole of the three lands becomes the Quiescent Light; from the standpoint of sentient beings, the whole of the Quiescent Light becomes the three lands. This is a difference in one's own karma; what has it to do with the lands being high or low? Ordinary people see only the Land of Sages and Commoners Together and do not see the upper three lands (the Land of Expedient Liberation, the Land of Real Reward, and the Land of Quiescent Light); shravakas see only the Land of Sages and Commoners Together and the Land of Expedient Liberation and do not see the upper two lands; bodhisattvas can see the lower three lands (the Land of Sages and Commoners Together, the Land of Expedient Liberation, and the Land of Real Reward) and partially see the Land of Quiescent Light; only the Buddha sees all four lands perfectly. If one holds that the Quiescent Light is outside the three lands and does not possess the supremely wondrous adornments and five dusts of the three lands, then how would it differ from the one-sidedly true (leaning toward emptiness) dharma-nature of the Lesser Vehicle?

E1. Explaining separately what is enjoyed: F1. Explaining the place of birth; F2. Concluding by showing the Buddha's power
F1. Explaining the place of birth

Moreover, Shariputra! In the Land of Ultimate Bliss there are pools of seven treasures, filled with water of eight excellent qualities. The bottom of each pool is spread wholly with golden sand, and the stairways on the four sides are made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. Above them are towers and pavilions, adorned with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, mother-of-pearl, red pearls, and carnelian. In the pools are lotus flowers as large as carriage wheels: blue ones with blue light, yellow ones with yellow light, red ones with red light, and white ones with white light, wondrously subtle, fragrant, and pure.

[Essential Explanation] Above, the dwelling place was explained; now the place of birth is explained. The jeweled pools are made of gold, silver, and the like, unlike the earth and stone of this world.

[Essential Explanation] The eight excellent qualities are: 1. Clear and pure, unlike the turbidity of this world; 2. Cool and refreshing, unlike heat and cold; 3. Sweet and delicious, unlike the salty, insipid, and inferior tastes; 4. Light and soft, unlike heaviness; 5. Moistening and nourishing, unlike shrinkage, rot, and fading; 6. Calm and harmonious, unlike violence and suddenness; 7. Removing hunger and thirst, unlike causing chill; 8. Nourishing all the faculties, unlike damaging the faculties, and unlike pestilence, causing illness, and drowning.

[Note] The water of the Land of Ultimate Bliss has eight excellent qualities: 1. Clear and pure, unlike the turbidity of the water of this world (the Saha world); 2. Cool and refreshing, unlike the heat and cold of the water of this world (the Saha world); 3. Sweet and delicious, unlike the salty, insipid, and inferior tastes of the water of this world (the Saha world); 4. Light and soft, unlike the heaviness of the water of this world (the Saha world); 5. Moistening and nourishing, unlike the shrinkage, rot, and fading of the water of this world (the Saha world); 6. Calm and harmonious, unlike the violence and suddenness of the water of this world (the Saha world); 7. Removing hunger and thirst, unlike the chill of the water of this world (the Saha world); 8. Nourishing all the faculties, unlike the water of this world (the Saha world), which damages the faculties and brings pestilence (spreading plague), illness (making people sick), and drowning (causing death by water).

The Sutra of Praise of the Pure Land of the Buddha's Reception says: "Moreover, Shariputra! In the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, there are everywhere seven kinds of wondrous jeweled ponds, filled with the water of eight qualities. What is named the water of eight qualities? First, clear and pure; second, cool and refreshing; third, sweet and delicious; fourth, light and soft; fifth, moist and lustrous; sixth, calm and harmonious; seventh, when drunk it removes hunger, thirst and countless other afflictions; eighth, when drunk it is certainly able to nurture the faculties and the four elements and to increase all manner of supreme good roots. Sentient beings of abundant merit ever delight in its enjoyment."

Filled to the brim, it differs from the dried-up and the overflowing. The bottom is pure golden sand, unlike mud. The steps and paths are of four treasures, unlike brick and stone. Tiered steps are called stairs, level ways are called paths, layered chambers are called towers, lofty
(high pavilions)

are called pavilions. Jeweled towers and pavilions differ from this world's timber-and-painted structures. The towers and pavilions are dwelling places, and also places of the Dharma assembly. Only when the lotus calyxes of the jeweled pond unfold in bloom may one ascend the four banks, enter the Dharma assembly, and see the Buddha and hear the Dharma.

[Note] [Tridacna, the giant clam] According to the Expanded Compendium of Materia Medica, volume forty-six, the giant clam is a large sea clam whose outer shell bears furrow-like patterns, like the ruts of a cartwheel (the tracks a wheel leaves on the ground); its shell within is white as jade, so it is often mistaken for jade. Later generations mostly take objects made of white coral and shell as tridacna. [Lofty tower] a high pavilion. [Painted colors] colored decoration. [Timber and painted colors] timber buildings adorned with colored decoration.
[Essential Explanation] As for the flower wheels, the wheel-turning king's golden wheel is forty li across, and here the smallest is cited. If we rely on the Contemplation Sutra
(the Sutra of Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life)
and the Immeasurable Life Assembly
(the fifth assembly of the Great Jewel Heap Sutra, translated by Bodhiruci in the Tang dynasty as the Assembly of the Tathagata of Immeasurable Life)

, their size is truly incalculable, because the bodies within the land of common residence are not equal. The blue is called utpala, the yellow kumuda, the red padma, the white pundarika. Because the birth-body has light, so too the lotus calyx has light. Yet the lotus flowers of the Land of Ultimate Bliss have immeasurable light and colors; this is but a brief word. Subtle, wondrous, fragrant and pure - these briefly extol the four virtues of the lotus. That which is substantial yet without form is called subtle; that which is unobstructed is called wondrous; without form there is no dust, hence pure. Since the calyx is thus, the birth-body may be known.

[Note] [Wheel-turning king] the sage king who turns the wheel. This king's body is endowed with the thirty-two marks; upon his enthronement he receives from heaven the wheel-jewel, and turning it he subdues the four quarters, hence he is called the wheel-turning sage king. [Since the calyx is thus, the birth-body may be known] Since the lotus calyx is bright in color and lustrous, subtle, wondrous, fragrant and pure, the splendor and supremacy of the birth-body may be known.
6.2 Concluding summary of the Buddha's power
Shariputra! The Land of Ultimate Bliss is endowed with such meritorious splendor.

[Essential Explanation] This makes clear that the manifold splendor of the dwelling-place and birth-place above are all accomplished by Amitabha Buddha's great vows and great practices as the merit of his essential nature. Therefore he is able to adorn all four kinds of pure lands and universally gather all beings, ordinary and sagely, of the ten directions and three times so that they may be reborn there. Moreover, the Buddha takes his great vows as the cause of sentient beings' many good roots, and his great practices as the condition of their many blessings and virtues. He enables those who, with faith and vow, hold the Name, in thought after thought, to accomplish this merit - yet all already accomplished, neither now nor future. Hereby, by means of Amitabha's manifold splendor as the supporting essential nature, the manifold splendor of the sentient being's own mind is called forth: the whole Buddha is the being, the whole other is the self. Hence it is said, endowed with such meritorious splendor.

[Note] [All already accomplished, neither now nor future] The manifold splendor of the Land of Ultimate Bliss is the merit accomplished in thought after thought at the moment I conceive faith and vow and hold the Name; it is not something to be accomplished now or in the future. [The whole Buddha is the being, the whole other is the self] When sentient beings, in faith and vow, hold the Name, they take the manifold splendor of Amitabha Buddha as the supporting essential nature and call forth the manifold splendor of their own mind; thus the splendor of Amitabha Buddha becomes the splendor of the sentient being (the whole Buddha is the being), and Amitabha Buddha becomes oneself (the whole other is the self). The Sutra of Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life says: "When the mind is made the Buddha, then this mind is the Buddha." The Zhongfeng Three-period Contemplation says: "Consider this: then Amitabha Buddha is my own mind, and my own mind is Amitabha Buddha." [Supporting] to strengthen its upward tendency. [Essential nature] a doctrine of the Consciousness-only school; the counterpart of the 'image', and that on which the image depends. When mind and mental factors cognize an object, they present within the mind the semblance of the object cognized, which is the immediate object of cognition, called the 'image'. Conversely, the substantial basis of the image and the self-nature of what it depends upon are called the 'essential nature'.

5.2 Combined explanation of the one who receives and the received: 6.1 Illustrating enjoyment by way of the five faculties and five objects; 6.2 Illustrating enjoyment by way of the ear faculty and the sound object
6.1 Illustrating enjoyment by way of the five faculties and five objects: 7.1 Direct explanation; 7.2 Concluding summary
7.1 Direct explanation

Moreover, Shariputra! In that Buddha-land, celestial music constantly plays, and the ground is of gold. Through the six periods of day and night, mandarava flowers rain down. The sentient beings of that land, at early dawn, each with their flower-garment, gather these manifold wondrous flowers and offer them to the Buddhas of the other directions, as many as a hundred thousand myriad kotis. At the time of the meal they return to their own land, and after eating walk in meditation.

[Essential Explanation] Music is the sound object, the ground is the form object, flowers are the form and fragrance objects, food is the taste object, and gathering flowers, scattering flowers and walking in meditation are the touch object - thus the five faculties of sentient beings encountering the five objects may be known. 'Ever playing' means throughout the six periods. As for the ground being of gold, the realm adorned by the seven jewels has gold as its substance.

[Essential Explanation] The day is divided into the early, middle and late, called the three periods of day; the night is divided into the early, middle and late, called the three periods of night. Hence it is said, six periods of day and night. Yet in that land both the circumstantial and the true retributions each have their own light, not depending on sun and moon - how then to divide day and night? Merely following this world's convention do we speak of divisions. Mandarava, here rendered 'pleasing to the mind', is also called the white flower. The flower-garment is a vessel for holding flowers. 'Manifold wondrous flowers' shows it is not of one kind only - they should be like the four flowers of the Wondrous Sutra, signifying the four stages of cause. Offering to the Buddhas of the other directions signifies that the true cause converges upon the ultimate fruit, and the merit of the fruit is nowhere absent. Moreover, speaking in terms of the Saha world of a hundred thousand myriad kotis of Buddhas means to show that, once reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, one can still offer to Shakyamuni and Maitreya, all without difficulty. If the power of Amitabha is applied, what distance is there to which one cannot go!

[Note] [Flower-garment] also written flower-garland. In India, when offering to a noble person, one used it to hold flowers and present them. The Illustrated Biography of Master Yuanguang, volume ten, records: 'The flower basket is used when scattering flowers; it is made of the back bamboo or of copper, hung with deep-red threads, filled with flowers and scattered at the proper time - this imitates the flower-garment spoken of in the sutras.' The Zen Grove Implements describes it: 'The basket for scattering flowers among the monks is called the flower-garment, a small bamboo cage in which flowers are stored and scattered, following the old story of the Buddha Mahabuddha.' [Should be like the four flowers of the Wondrous Sutra] As the four flowers of the Lotus Sutra - mandarava, great mandarava, manjushaka and great manjushaka fall from heaven - so offer these four flowers to the Buddhas of other directions. [The true cause converges upon the ultimate fruit] With the true cause that destroys ignorance and realizes the Dharma-body, one converges upon the Buddha-fruit of supreme wondrous awakening.

[Essential Explanation] The time of the meal is early dawn, hence it says 'at that time'. This shows that his supernormal powers are inconceivable - not leaving that land, yet ever present throughout the ten directions, without a moment's delay in returning. This passage shows that a single sound, a single object, a single instant - even a step or a snap of the fingers - in the Land of Ultimate Bliss interpenetrates the Three Jewels of the ten directions without obstruction. It also shows that in the Saha world, with its turbid, heavy and evil obstructions, one is separated though not separated from the Land of Ultimate Bliss; and once reborn there, with such deep merit, one is separated from the Saha world yet not separated. 'Walking in meditation after eating' means that when one thinks of food, food arrives, needing no arrangement; when the meal is done, the bowl departs, needing no wiping. One merely walks in meditation on the golden ground, amid flowers and music, and freely advances in practice.

[Note] [At the time of the meal] within the space of one meal. The Sutra of Praise of the Pure Land of the Buddha's Reception says: "At early dawn each day, bearing these celestial flowers, within the space of one meal one flies to the immeasurable worlds of other directions and makes offerings to the Buddhas of a hundred thousand kotis."
7.2 Concluding summary
6.2 Illustrating enjoyment by way of the ear faculty and the sound object

[Essential Explanation] Because in this world the ear faculty is the keenest, he singles out and expounds at length the sounds of the Dharma. In fact, the Land of Ultimate Bliss gathers the capacity of the whole Dharma-realm; each of the five objects is perfectly wondrous and gives rise to all Dharma-gates.

[Note] [In this world the ear faculty is the keenest] In the Surangama Sutra, Manjushri Bodhisattva says: "The true substance of the teachings in this world is pure through the hearing of sound; to attain samadhi, one in truth enters by the ear." [Singling out the Dharma sounds to explain at length] For the moment, by the sound object, he reveals the benefit of the Dharma. In fact, the Land of Ultimate Bliss gathers the capacity of the whole Dharma-realm, and each of the five objects (form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch) is perfectly wondrous, giving rise to all Dharma-gates.
6.2 Illustrating enjoyment by way of the ear faculty and the sound object: 7.1 Separate explanation; 7.2 General summary
7.1 Separate explanation: 8.1 The sound of conscious beings; 8.2 The sound of unconscious things
8.1 The sound of conscious beings: 9.1 The Dharma-benefit of the birds' sound; 9.2 Questioning and explaining, briefly made clear
9.1 The Dharma-benefit of the birds' sound

Moreover, Shariputra! In that land there are always many kinds of wondrously colored birds - white cranes, peacocks, parrots, sari birds, kalavinkas and the two-headed beings of shared life. These many birds, at the six periods of day and night, utter the gentle and graceful sound. Their sound proclaims the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold noble path, and such Dharma. The sentient beings of that land, having heard this sound, all recollect the Buddha, recollect the Dharma and recollect the Sangha.

[Essential Explanation] 'Many kinds of wondrously colored' speaks of both abundance and beauty; below he briefly names six. The sari bird is anciently called the osprey; Master Qi says it is the spring oriole, which is possible. The kalavinka, rendered 'wondrous sound', surpasses all birds in song before it leaves its shell. The two-headed being shares one body with two heads; the consciousnesses are distinct but the reward is shared. These two are found in the Snowy Mountains and elsewhere in the western regions; here they are merely spoken of in terms of the beloved birds of this world. Since sound issues at the six periods, one knows that in the Pure Land night is not marked by birds roosting; indeed the body born in the lotus has no drowsiness by nature and does not need to sleep at night.
[Note] [Consciousness distinct, reward shared] their consciousnesses are each distinct, but their reward and life are the same.

[Essential Explanation] 'The five faculties and so on' are the thirty-seven factors of the path. Meaning, the four stations of mindfulness: first, contemplation of body; second, contemplation of feeling; third, contemplation of mind; fourth, contemplation of Dharma. The four right exertions: first, evil not yet arisen to not bring forth; second, evil already arisen to put an end to it; third, good not yet arisen to make it arise; fourth, good already arisen to make it increase. The four bases of supernormal power: first, desire; second, effort; third, mind; fourth, investigation. The five faculties: faith in the right path and the auxiliary methods is called the faculty of faith; practicing the right path and all auxiliary good methods, ever seeking without rest, is the faculty of vigor; recollecting the right path and the auxiliary good methods, with no other thought, is the faculty of mindfulness; collecting the mind within the right path and the auxiliary good methods, in correspondence without distraction, is the faculty of concentration; for the right path and the auxiliary good methods, contemplating the four truths of suffering and so on, is the faculty of wisdom. The five powers: faith growing, able to break doubt, break all wrong faith, and break afflictions, is the power of faith; vigor growing, breaking all manner of physical and mental sluggishness, accomplishing the great task of transcending the world, is the power of vigor; mindfulness growing, breaking all wrong thoughts, accomplishing all the meritorious right mindfulness of transcending the world, is the power of mindfulness; concentration growing, able to break scattered thoughts and give rise to meditation in both affairs and principle, is the power of concentration; wisdom growing, able to block and pass through all the various delusions and give rise to true undefiled wisdom, is the power of wisdom. The seven factors of enlightenment, also called the seven factors of awakening: when wisdom contemplates all phenomena, able to discriminate true from false, not wrongly taking up false dharmas, is the factor of selecting the Dharma; when vigor practices the paths of the Dharma, able to awaken to it, not wrongly practicing useless austerities, ever diligently practicing in the true Dharma, is the factor of vigor; when the mind gains joy in the Dharma, able to awaken to that joy, not rejoicing in inverted dharmas but abiding in the joy of the true Dharma, is the factor of joy; when cutting off all views and afflictions, able to awaken and remove the false without destroying the true good roots, is the factor of removal; when forsaking objects to which views and thoughts cling, able to awaken that the forsaken objects are false and unreal, never again recollecting them, is the factor of renunciation; when producing meditative concentration, able to awaken that all meditation is false, not giving rise to attachment and false imaginings, is the factor of concentration; when cultivating the transcendent path, able to awaken and keep concentration and wisdom ever in balance - by nature sinking, one should call upon the three factors of selecting the Dharma, vigor and joy to lift it up; by nature floating, one should call upon the three factors of removal, renunciation and concentration to hold it down, harmonized to the mean - is the factor of mindfulness. The eightfold noble path, also called the eight right path factors: cultivating the undefiled contemplation and seeing the four truths distinctly is right view; with the undefiled mind, corresponding thought and deliberation and awakening knowledge and weighing, for the sake of increasing and entering great nirvana, is right thought; with undefiled wisdom removing the four wrong means of livelihood, gathering all verbal karma, and abiding in all right speech, is right speech; with undefiled wisdom removing all wrong bodily karma and abiding in pure right body-deeds, is right action; with undefiled wisdom thoroughly removing the five wrong means of livelihood in the three karmas, and abiding in pure right livelihood, is right livelihood; with undefiled wisdom, correspondingly and diligently practicing the path of nirvana, is right effort; with undefiled wisdom, correspondingly recollecting the right path and the auxiliary methods, is right mindfulness; with undefiled wisdom, correspondingly entering concentration, is right concentration.

[Essential Explanation] These factors of the path, cultivated in dependence upon the four truths of arising-and-ceasing, are the factors of the Store-teaching path. Cultivated in dependence upon the four truths of non-arising, they are the factors of the Common-teaching path. Cultivated in dependence upon the four truths of immeasurability, they are the factors of the Distinct-teaching path. Cultivated in dependence upon the four truths of non-doing, they are the factors of the Perfect-teaching path. The Store path factors are called the half-word Dharma-gate; the Pure Land is lightly turbid, so they seem not to be needed, though for those of small capacity who ripen first they may be used for a while. The Common path factors are called the first gate of the Great Vehicle, shared by the three vehicles, and are much spoken of in the land of common residence. The Distinct path factors are called the Dharma of the bodhisattvas alone, and are much spoken of in the land of common residence and expedient pure lands. The Perfect path factors are called the unsurpassed Buddha-Dharma; those of keen faculties hear them in all the four pure lands. 'And such Dharma' - such as the foregoing stations of mindfulness, right exertions and bases of supernormal power, and the remaining four means of gathering, six perfections, ten powers, fearlessness, and immeasurable Dharma-gates.

[Note] [Factors of the path] the categories of the path-Dharma. [Four truths] namely the four noble truths: suffering, arising, cessation, the path. The truth of suffering explains the truth that life is full of suffering; there is the three sufferings and the eight sufferings and immeasurable sufferings; suffering is the true state of the real universe and of life. The 'arising' of the truth of arising means gathering - it explains the truth of how life's pain comes about: the pain of life comes from the ignorance and dullness of ordinary beings themselves, and from the stirring of afflictions such as greed, desire and anger, whereby they create all manner of unwholesome karma, and only then do they gather all manner of pain. The truth of cessation explains that the state of nirvana is the most ideal and ultimate home of this suffering-laden life, for nirvana is the state of permanence, ease and stillness. The truth of the path explains that people must cultivate the path to realize nirvana. These four noble truths encompass both the worldly and transcendent twofold causes and results: arising is the cause and suffering the result, the cause-and-result of the deluded realm; the path is the cause and cessation the result, the cause-and-result of the awakened realm. [Called the half-word Dharma-gate] Because the Small Vehicle is partial in truth and not perfect, it is called the half-word Dharma-gate, in contrast to the full-word Dharma-gates of the Great Vehicle's Common, Distinct and Perfect teachings.

[Essential Explanation] Although the thirty-seven factors gather the Dharma exhaustively, the capacities and conditions are not equal; they make various openings and combinations, their names and meanings are different, and according to what one wishes to hear there is nothing not proclaimed. Therefore the hearer recollects the Three Jewels, gives rise to the bodhi-mind, and subdues and extinguishes afflictions. Seeing clearly the inconceivable majesty and compassion, he recollects the Buddha. Joy in the Dharma enters the mind and the flavor of the Dharma is abundant, so he recollects the Dharma. Hearing together and sharing the teaching, with one mind he cultivates and realizes, so he recollects the Sangha. That which recollects is itself the three contemplations. The recollected Three Jewels have the meanings of separate marks, of oneness, and of the four teachings, with the different expedient and ultimate meanings of the three truths.

[Note] [That which recollects is itself the three contemplations] the mind that recollects is by nature empty and still, which is the contemplation of emptiness; in function it is perfectly illuminating, which is the contemplation of provisionality; at the very moment of being empty and still, it is still yet ever illuminating, and at the very moment of being perfectly illuminating, it is illuminating yet ever still, which is the contemplation of the middle. [Separate marks] the marks of difference. [Oneness] the same single true substance. [The meaning of the four teachings] separate marks and oneness are each divided into the Store, Common, Distinct and Perfect four teachings. [Three truths] the truth of emptiness, the truth of provisionality, and the truth of the middle. The truth of emptiness says that things are empty and without self-nature; the truth of provisionality says that there is only a provisional form arising from conditions; the truth of the middle says that all phenomena are neither empty nor provisional, yet also both empty and provisional - the real principle of the middle way. [Expedient and ultimate] a teaching suited to a particular time is called 'expedient'; a teaching that is ultimate and unchanging is called 'ultimate'.
9.2 Questioning and explaining, briefly made clear

Shariputra! You should not say that these birds are in truth born of retribution for offenses. Why? Because that Buddha-land has no three evil destinies. Shariputra! In that Buddha-land there is not even the name of an evil destiny, how much less its reality. These many birds are all created by the transformation of Amitabha Buddha, who wishes the sound of the Dharma to flow abroad.
[Essential Explanation] The questioning and the explaining may be known.
[Note] Through the questioning and the explaining in the sutra, the doubt whether these birds of the Land of Ultimate Bliss are born of retribution for offenses has been resolved.

[Question] pursuit of inquiry. [Explanation] answer and explanation. [In that Buddha-land there is not even the name of an evil destiny, how much less its reality. These many birds are all created by the transformation of Amitabha Buddha, who wishes the sound of the Dharma to flow abroad] The Land of Ultimate Bliss does not even have the names of the hells, hungry ghosts and animals, so how could it have beings of the evil destinies? All these birds have no consciousness, and are all the lifeless 'birds' manifested by Amitabha Buddha's wish that the sound of the Dharma flow abroad.

[Essential Explanation] Question: are the white crane and the rest not names of evil destinies? Answer: since they are not born of retribution, then each and every name here expresses the Tathagata's ultimate merit. What is meant by the ultimate white crane and the rest is nothing but the beautiful names of essential virtue - how can they be evil names?

[Note] Question: the sutra says 'in that Buddha-land there is not even the name of an evil destiny' - are the names of the white crane and the rest not names of evil destinies? Answer: since these birds are not born of retribution for offenses, all these names express the Tathagata's ultimate merit. Therefore, in the end what are called the names of the white crane and the rest are nothing but the beautiful names of essential virtue - how could they be the names of evil destinies?

[Essential Explanation] Question: what is the meaning of transforming into many birds? Answer: there are the four bases of universal accessibility. Ordinary feelings delight in these birds, so he transforms in accordance with their feelings, to give them joy; the birds still speak the Dharma, so that the hearers give rise to good; he does not incite low thoughts toward the birds, to counteract the discriminating mind; the birds are at once Amitabha, to awaken one to the equality of the Dharma-body, in which nothing is not possessed and nothing is not made. In this passage the sounds of the gentle breeze, the trees and the nets, and all circumstantial and true, provisional and real phenomena, are in themselves the three bodies and four virtues of Amitabha Buddha, without the least difference.

[Note] Question: what is the meaning of transforming into many birds? Answer: this is due to the four bases of universal accessibility. First, the worldly basis: the benefit of joy. Because ordinary feelings delight in these birds, Amitabha, in accordance with their feelings, transforms and gives them joy. Second, the personal basis: the benefit of producing good. The transformed birds speak the Dharma, a matter of singular wonder, so that all who hear recollect the Three Jewels and produce good. Third, the corrective basis: the benefit of extinguishing evil. The birds can speak the Dharma and must not be lightly regarded; not conceiving low thoughts of karmic retribution toward them, one extinguishes evil. Fourth, the supreme-ultimate basis: the benefit of entering principle. Since the birds are made by Amitabha's transformation, the birds are Amitabha's Dharma-realm Treasury body - no dharma is not possessed, no dharma is not made; affairs and principle are perfectly fused, and one enters principle. The sounds of the gentle breeze, the jeweled trees and the nets shown in the sutra, and all circumstantial and true, provisional and real phenomena, are in themselves the three bodies and four virtues of Amitabha Buddha, without the least difference.
[Three bodies] the Dharma-body, the reward-body, the responsive body. [Four virtues] the four virtues of great nirvana: permanence, bliss, self, purity.
8.2 The sound of unconscious things

Shariputra! In that Buddha-land, the gentle breeze stirs the rows of jeweled trees and the jeweled nets, producing a subtle and wondrous sound, as if hundreds of thousands of kinds of music were playing all at once. Those who hear this sound naturally all give rise to the mind of recollecting the Buddha, recollecting the Dharma, and recollecting the Sangha.

[Essential Explanation] The conscious and the unconscious alike proclaim the wondrous Dharma. The path factors of the four teachings and the immeasurable Dharma-gates are taught simultaneously, and each is understood according to its kind, so that hearers recollect the Three Jewels. To recollect the Three Jewels is to benefit by the bases of universal accessibility. The ordinary being, on first hearing, leaps with joy through his whole body - this is the benefit of joy; with the infusion of the Three Jewels he is certain to give rise to the bodhi-mind - this is the benefit of producing good; thereby he subdues and extinguishes afflictions - this is the benefit of destroying evil; and realizing the oneness of the Three Jewels - this is the benefit of entering principle.
[Essential Explanation] The first, the separate explanation, is now complete.
7.2 General summary
Shariputra! That Buddha-land is endowed with such meritorious splendor.

[Essential Explanation] He concludes again and again, so that we deeply believe that all splendor is accomplished by the guide's vows and practices, and manifested by his seed-wisdom; it is all sensed by the pure karma of us beings and transformed by consciousness-only. The Buddha's mind and the sentient being's mind are mutually image and essential nature, like the light of many lamps, each pervading the whole yet appearing as one. The whole principle becomes the matter, the whole matter is at once the principle; the whole nature rises into practice, and the whole practice is in the nature. This too may be deeply pondered! How can one forsake this Pure Land and speak apart of a mind-only Pure Land, content to fall into the mockery of the squeaking rat and the empty cry of a strange bird!

[Note] [Seed-wisdom] an abbreviation for the wisdom of all seeds, one of the three wisdoms. [Three wisdoms] the wisdom of all aspects, the wisdom of the paths, and the wisdom of all seeds. The wisdom of all aspects is the wisdom by which the sravaka and pratyekabuddha know the general mark of all dharmas, and the general mark is the mark of emptiness; the wisdom of the paths is the wisdom by which a bodhisattva knows the various practices of cultivation; the wisdom of all seeds is the wisdom by which a Buddha penetrates general and particular marks of all dharmas, guiding beings and cutting off delusion. In other words, the wisdom of all aspects is the wisdom of contemplating emptiness, the wisdom of the paths is the wisdom of contemplating existence, and the wisdom of all seeds contemplates both emptiness and existence - knowing emptiness on the one hand and existence on the other - the union of the former two. [Mutually image and essential nature] mutually image and essential nature. [The squeaking rat and the empty cry of a bird] a reproach of those who recklessly speak of perfect principle, saying it is like the squeak of an odd rat and the empty cry of a strange bird. The Four Teachings Manual says: "We, foolish ones, upon merely hearing of immediate emptiness, immediately abandon practice, not knowing the reason for the immediacy - the squeak of a rat, the empty cry of a bird. The expositions are many in the sutras and treatises; seek them and ponder them."
[Essential Explanation] The first, the excellence of the circumstantial retribution, is here concluded.
3.2 The excellence of the true retribution: 4.1 Questioning and explaining the name; 4.2 Separate explanation of the principal and the attendants
4.1 Questioning and explaining the name: 5.1 The question; 5.2 The explanation
Shariputra! What do you think - for what reason is that Buddha called Amitabha?

[Essential Explanation] Because this sutra points directly to the wondrous practice of holding the Name, he therefore questions and explains the name, wishing people deeply to believe that the all-virtuous Name is inconceivable, and to grasp it wholeheartedly, without further doubt or duality.
5.2 The explanation: 6.1 Explained in terms of light; 6.2 Explained in terms of lifespan

[Essential Explanation] Amitabha, properly translated 'immeasurable', is originally beyond speech. The master teacher, by the two meanings of light and lifespan, gathers all immeasurableness. Light spreads across the ten directions; lifespan extends through the three times. The horizontal and the vertical interpenetrate, which is the substance of the Dharma-realm. He takes this substance as Amitabha's body and land, and also as Amitabha's name. Therefore the name of Amitabha is the inherently-awakened principle of sentient beings. To hold the Name is the beginning-awakening uniting with the original awakening. Beginning and original are not two, the being and the Buddha are not two. Hence one thought in accord is one Buddha, and thought after thought in accord is Buddha after Buddha.

[Note] [Three times] past, present and future. [Beginning-awakening uniting with the original] the beginning-awakening uniting with the original awakening. [Original awakening and beginning-awakening] 'Original awakening' is the pure self-nature mind that all sentient beings originally possess. 'Beginning-awakening' is when, after the original awakening is obscured by ignorance, one again awakens; all the awakening in the process from sentient being to Buddhahood is beginning-awakening. [One thought in accord is one Buddha] if a single thought's beginning-awakening unites with the original awakening, then in that very thought one is Buddha - when the mind is made the Buddha, this mind is the Buddha.
6.1 Explained in terms of light
Shariputra! That Buddha's light is immeasurable, shining on the lands of the ten directions without obstruction, for which reason he is called Amitabha.

[Essential Explanation] The mind-nature is still yet ever illuminating, hence it is light. Now having fully realized the immeasurable substance of the mind-nature, his light is immeasurable. All Buddhas fully realize the essential nature, all shine on the ten directions, all could be called immeasurable light. But their vows in the causal stage being different, they are given different names according to conditions. Being the bhikshu Dharmakara, Amitabha made forty-eight vows, including the vow that his light should shine constantly on the ten directions; now that his fruit is accomplished, the vow is fulfilled. The light of the Dharma-body has no bounds; the light of the reward-body is proportionate to true nature - in this all Buddhas are the same. The light of the responsive body may shine one yojana, ten, a hundred or a thousand yojanas, one world, ten, a hundred or a thousand worlds. Only Amitabha shines universally, and is therefore distinctly named immeasurable light. Yet the three bodies are neither one nor different; for the sake of giving sentient beings the four benefits is this distinction made. One should know that 'without obstruction' is said with reference to the people. Because the beings' relation to the Buddha is deep, wherever the Buddha's light reaches, all the worlds without exception see it fully.

[Note] [Three bodies] the Dharma-body, the reward-body and the responsive body. The Dharma-body, also called the self-nature body or Dharma-nature body, is the ever-abiding, undying true nature originally possessed by everyone, though we beings are deluded and do not manifest it, while the Buddha, being awakened, has realized it. The reward-body is formed by the Buddha's wisdom and merit; there is the self-rewarding reward-body and the other-rewarding reward-body: the self-rewarding reward-body is the body with which the Buddha himself enjoys the bliss of inner realization, while the other-rewarding reward-body is the body the Buddha manifests to teach the bodhisattvas of the ten grounds. The responsive body, also called the transformation body or the manifest body, is the Buddha-body manifested in response to the capacities and circumstances of beings. [Four benefits] the benefits of the four bases of universal accessibility.
6.2 Explained in terms of lifespan
Moreover, Shariputra! That Buddha's lifespan, and his people's, is immeasurable, boundless, an asankhya number of kalpas, hence he is called Amitabha.

[Essential Explanation] The mind-nature is illuminating yet ever still, hence it is lifespan. Now having fully realized the immeasurable substance of the mind-nature, his lifespan is immeasurable. The lifespan of the Dharma-body has no beginning and no end; the lifespan of the reward-body has a beginning but no end. Here too all Buddhas are the same and could be called immeasurable life. The responsive body, following vows and capacities, is long or short, not equal. The vow-king Dharmakara had the vow that the Buddha and his people should all have immeasurable life; now that his fruit is accomplished, the vow is fulfilled, and he is distinctly named immeasurable life. Asankhya, undecaying and immeasurable - these are all names of numbers, in reality a measured immeasurableness. Yet the three bodies are neither one nor different; the responsive body too may be the immeasurable-of-the-immeasurable. 'And' means together. 'The people' refers to those from the stage of equal enlightenment and below. It means that the Buddha's lifespan and that of his people alike are immeasurable and boundless. One should know that the names of light and lifespan are both established on the basis of sentient beings. Because the being and the Buddha are equal, those who hold the Name may have light and lifespan the same as the Buddha's, without difference.

[Note] [That Buddha's lifespan, and his people's, immeasurable, boundless, asankhya kalpas] the lifespan of that Buddha, and the lifespan of his people, are immeasurable, boundless, asankhya kalpas. [Asankhya kalpa] in Chinese translation, a kalpa of incalculable number. [The people, those from equal enlightenment and below] the people refers to the bodhisattvas at the stage of equal enlightenment and below. That is, within the ten Dharma-realms, excluding the Buddha, all beings of the other nine realms are called the people, also called sentient beings.

[Essential Explanation] Again, because of the meaning of immeasurable light, sentient beings reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are reborn in the ten directions, see Amitabha Buddha and so see the Buddhas of the ten directions, and being able to save themselves, are able to benefit all universally. Because of the meaning of immeasurable lifespan, the people of the Land of Ultimate Bliss are all of the state of one more birth, all certain to accomplish Buddhahood in this life, without falling into another birth. One should know that apart from this present single thought of the mind of immeasurable light and life, where is there the name of Amitabha Buddha? And apart from the name of Amitabha Buddha, from what is one to fully realize the present single thought of the mind of immeasurable light and life? Ponder it deeply, ponder it deeply.

[Note] [One more birth] the meaning of being able in this one life to reach the seat of Buddhahood; it is another name for the bodhisattva of the last body. Such as Maitreya Bodhisattva now dwelling in Tushita Heaven, who is a bodhisattva of one more birth.
4.2 Separate explanation of the principal and the attendants: 5.1 Separate explanation; 5.2 Concluding summary
5.1 Separate explanation: 6.1 The principal; 6.2 The attendants
6.1 The principal
[Essential Explanation] This too explains the sentence in the separate preface, 'now abiding and preaching the Dharma'.
[Note] The following sentence likewise explains the phrase 'now abiding and preaching the Dharma' in the separate preface.
Shariputra! Since Amitabha Buddha attained Buddhahood, ten kalpas have now passed.

[Essential Explanation] This shows the accomplishment of the lord-teacher of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Yet the Dharma-body has no becoming and no not-becoming, and one should not speak of kalpas. The reward-body, when the cause is full and the fruit complete, is called accomplished; the responsive body, manifesting birth for beings, is called accomplished - for both one may speak of kalpas. Again, the Dharma-body, revealed by cultivated virtue, may also be spoken of as accomplished and in terms of kalpas. The reward-body has nothing newly gained, the responsive body is like the moon reflected in a river, and there is also no becoming and no not-becoming, so for these one should not speak of kalpas. But the Buddhahood of all Buddhas each has its local origin and its manifest traces, and the local origin cannot be fathomed. Speaking now only of the manifest trace of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, it is that the three bodies, one accomplished, all are accomplished - it is also a speaking of accomplishment in terms of neither accomplishment nor non-accomplishment.

[Note] [Local origin and manifest traces] the original ground and the manifested traces. The substance of the Buddha and bodhisattvas is called the local origin; from the manifestation of this substance in various bodies to save beings, this is called the manifest traces.

[Essential Explanation] Again, the Buddha's life is immeasurable, and it is only now ten kalpas. Then, preaching the Dharma now, the time is not yet half gone. He universally exhorts beings of the three times to seek rebirth quickly, to share the Buddha's lifespan, and to accomplish in one life. Again, the text below - countless sravakas, bodhisattvas and those of one more birth - are all accomplished within ten kalpas. This plainly shows that those of the ten directions and three times who are reborn there and never retreat are many and it is easy.
[Note] [Not yet half] not yet half-worn. [One more birth] that is, one more birth.
6.2 The attendants
Moreover, Shariputra! That Buddha has immeasurable, boundless sravaka disciples, all arhats, whose number is beyond calculation. His assemblies of bodhisattvas are likewise.

[Essential Explanation] The fixed two-vehicle beings of other directions are not reborn there. If one first practiced the lesser practice, and at death turned one's merit toward bodhi and made the great vow, then once reborn in that land, the Buddha, in accordance with his capacity, teaches the Dharma, causing him to cut off views and thoughts; hence he is called an arhat. An instance is the distinct teaching's seventh abiding cutting off views and thoughts - not really a sravaka. The Store and Common teachings do not hear the names of the Buddhas of other directions; now having heard the name of Amitabha, and with faith and vow being reborn, they all belong to the capacities gathered by the Distinct and Perfect teachings.

[Note] 'Other directions' means all the worlds beyond the Land of Ultimate Bliss. 'Fixed two-vehicle beings' are the fixed sravaka and the fixed pratyekabuddha; because they are determined to dwell in the two-vehicle lineage and do not wish to become Buddhas, they are called the fixed two-vehicle beings; since they refuse to recollect the Buddha, they cannot be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The boundless sravaka disciples of the Land of Ultimate Bliss are those who, though first practicing the lesser-vehicle path factors, at the approach of death, urged on by a good teacher, turn from the small to the great and vow to recollect the Buddha, seeking rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Once reborn there, the Buddha, following their past good roots, teaches them the Store and Common path factors, causing them to cut off views and thoughts, reaching the level of the arhat; hence they are provisionally called arhats, but in truth they are bodhisattvas.
5.2 Concluding summary
Shariputra! That Buddha-land is endowed with such meritorious splendor.

[Essential Explanation] The Buddha, the sravakas and the bodhisattvas are all accomplished by Amitabha's vows and practices in the causal stage, and likewise in the fruit stage, one accomplished, all are accomplished. Thus the Buddha, the bodhisattvas and the sravakas are each neither self nor other; self and other are not two, and therefore it is said, 'accomplished with such meritorious splendor.' Those who have faith and vow and hold the Name are in every thought likewise thus accomplished.
[Essential Explanation] First, the extended setting forth of the wondrous circumstantial and true retribution of that land, in order to awaken faith - here concluded.
2.2 In particular urging beings to seek rebirth in order to arouse the vow: 3.1 Revealing the supreme causal condition; 3.2 In particular urging the excellence of the Pure Land

[Essential Explanation] The excellence of the Pure Land means this: rebirth carrying one's karma, crossing beyond the three realms horizontally; the co-dwelling land horizontally containing the four lands, opening and revealing the Dharma-wheel of the four teachings; beings perfectly purifying the four lands, perfectly seeing the three bodies, perfectly realizing the three kinds of non-retrogression; and its people all attaining Buddhahood in one life. Such surpassing excellence and transcendence are pointed out entirely in these two sections; one must carefully examine them.

[Note] [Four teachings] the Store, Common, Distinct and Perfect four teachings. [Dharma-wheel] a figure for the Dharma spoken by the Buddha: it can crush all the afflictions of sentient beings, just as a great wheel can crush all rocks and gravel. It also means being handed on from one to another in turn, like the turning of a wheel, reaching everywhere without limit.
3.1 Revealing the supreme causal condition

Moreover, Shariputra! Those beings who are born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are all avaivartika, no longer subject to retreat. Among them many are of one more birth, and their number is so great that it cannot be known by calculation, but can only be expressed as immeasurable, boundless asankhya.

[Essential Explanation] Avaivartika is here rendered 'non-retrogression'. 1. Non-retrogression of position: entering the stream of the sages, one does not fall back to the ground of ordinary beings. 2. Non-retrogression of practice: constantly saving living beings, one does not fall back to the ground of the two vehicles. 3. Non-retrogression of thought: thought after thought flows into the ocean of sarvajna.
[Note] [Sarvajna] rendered in Chinese as 'the wisdom of all seeds'; it is the great wisdom of the Buddhas' ultimate and perfect fruit-stage.
[Essential Explanation] If measured against this Saha world: the Store teaching's first fruit
(in the Store teaching the first fruit is called srotaapanna)
, the Common teaching's Insight Ground
(the fourth ground of the Common teaching; one sees the principle of the true truth, hence 'Insight Ground')
, the Distinct teaching's first abiding
(the Distinct teaching's abiding of the first arousal of the mind)
, the Perfect teaching's first faith
(the first mind of the ten faiths of the Perfect teaching)
, is called 'non-retrogression of position'. The Common teaching's bodhisattva
(the bodhisattva of the Common teaching, namely the ninth bodhisattva ground)
, the Distinct teaching's ten practices
(the stage of the ten practices of the Distinct teaching)
, the Perfect teaching's ten faiths
(the stage of the ten faiths of the Perfect teaching)
, is called 'non-retrogression of practice'. The Distinct teaching's first ground
(the Distinct teaching's first Ground of Joy)
, the Perfect teaching's first abiding
(the Perfect teaching's abiding of the first arousal of the mind)

, is called 'non-retrogression of thought'. Now in the Pure Land, even those of the five rebellious acts and the ten evil deeds who accomplish ten recitations, are reborn carrying their karma, and dwell in the lowest of the lowest grade, all attain the three kinds of non-retrogression.

[Note] This passage explains the corresponding stages in the Saha world of the three kinds of non-retrogression and how hard they are to attain, whereas beings of the five rebellious acts and the ten evil deeds, provided only that ten recitations at the point of death succeed, likewise perfectly realize these three kinds of non-retrogression.

[Five rebellious acts] five offenses utterly contrary to principle, namely killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an arhat, shedding the Buddha's blood, and causing division in the harmonious Sangha. Because these five are acts of extreme evil, to commit any one of them brings a fall into the Avici Hell. [Ten evil deeds] killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, frivolous speech, harsh speech, divisive speech, greed, anger, and foolishness. [Srotaapanna] the sravaka vehicle has four fruit-stages, namely the fruit of srotaapanna, the fruit of sakridagamin, the fruit of anagamin, and the fruit of arhat. The first fruit, srotaapanna, is rendered in Chinese as 'stream-enterer', meaning one who has first entered the stream of the sages. [Fifty-two stages] from ordinary being to Buddhahood a bodhisattva must pass through fifty-two stages in all, namely: the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wonderful enlightenment.

[Essential Explanation] Yet according to the teachings: if one is an ordinary being, then one is not a first fruit and so on; if one is of the two vehicles, then one is not a bodhisattva and so on; if one is of different birth, then one is not of the same-birth nature and so on.

[Note] Yet according to the teachings: if one is an ordinary being, then one is not a srotaapanna (the first fruit), sakridagamin, anagamin, arhat or pratyekabuddha of the two vehicles, and so on; if one is a person of the two vehicles, then one is not a bodhisattva of the various stages; if one is a bodhisattva who has not realized the Dharma-body (different birth), then one is not a bodhisattva who has realized the Dharma-body (same-birth nature).

[Different-birth nature] not yet having broken ignorance or realized the Dharma-body, and not sharing the same substance as the Tathagata, one is said to be of the different-birth nature. [Same-birth nature] having broken ignorance and realized the Dharma-body, and sharing the same substance as the Tathagata, one is said to be of the same-birth nature.

[Essential Explanation] Moreover, one of non-retrogression of thought is no longer of different birth; one of non-retrogression of practice has not merely seen the Way; one of non-retrogression of position is not one of the people. To overstep the stages is to fall into great falsehood; having advanced and gained a new realization, one sets aside the former designation.

[Note] Moreover, a bodhisattva of non-retrogression of thought has already attained the same-birth nature and is no longer of the different-birth nature; a bodhisattva of non-retrogression of practice has already aroused the great mind and is not merely a lesser fruit of one who has seen the Way; a sage of non-retrogression of position is not one of the people who are full of afflictions. To overstep the stages is to fall into great false speech; and having advanced and gained a new realization, one sets aside the former designation.
[Essential Explanation] Only in the co-dwelling land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss
(the co-dwelling and the land of expedient remainder of the Land of Ultimate Bliss)

, is all neither, and all both. In the buddha-lands of the ten directions there is no such name or mark, no such stage, no such Dharma-gate. Were it not for the utmost reach of the mind-nature, the wondrous merit of holding the Name, and the great vows of Amitabha, how could this be! One of one more birth is one who has only one life left before succeeding to the Buddha's place, such as Maitreya and Avalokitesvara. The people of the Land of Ultimate Bliss all attain Buddhahood in one life, and every one of them will truly realize the stage of one more birth. Therefore among them there are many such supreme good beings, beyond number or knowing.
[Note] Master Ouyi praises in the highest terms the incomparable excellence of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[Essential Explanation] Furthermore, among the teachings Shakyamuni gave in one lifetime, only the Avatamsaka Sutra makes clear the perfection of one life. And the cause of that perfection in one life is that in the Practices and Vows of Samantabhadra at the end of that sutra, the king of the ten great vows leads one back to the Land of Peace and Nourishment, and with this urges onward the assembly of the Huazang ocean.

[Note] Furthermore, among all the teachings Shakyamuni Buddha gave in one lifetime, only the Avatamsaka Sutra clearly reveals the cause of perfecting Buddhahood in one life. And that cause of perfection in one life is that in the Practices and Vows of Samantabhadra at the end of the Avatamsaka Sutra, the king of the ten great vows leads one back to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and with this urges onward the assembly of the Huazang ocean.

[The teachings of one lifetime] the teachings spoken by the World-Honored One during the single lifetime from his attainment of the Way to his entry into nirvana, namely the three baskets, the twelve divisions of the sutras, the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates, and so on. [Twelve divisions of the sutras] the content of all the sutras and teachings is divided into twelve categories, called the twelve divisions of the sutras. Namely: 1. Prose discourse: setting forth the marks of the Dharma directly in prose, without fixing the number of words or sentences; because its lines are long, it is called prose discourse. 2. Repeated verses: what has already been proclaimed above is again gathered up in verse at the end; as it repeats the proclamation, it is called repeated verses. 3. Unprompted verses: verses that do not depend on the meaning of the prose preceding them but arise independently. 4. Causes and conditions: recounting the causes and conditions of seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, or of the Buddha's preaching and teaching. 5. Past lives of disciples: sutra passages that record the Buddha's account of the past-life causes and conditions of his various disciples. 6. Past lives of the Buddha: sutra passages that record the Buddha's account of his own past-life causes and conditions. 7. The unprecedented: sutra passages recording the Buddha's manifestation of various spiritual powers and inconceivable matters. 8. Parables: sutra passages in which the Buddha tells various parables to make it easy for beings to awaken. 9. Discussions: sutra passages of questions and answers reasoning about the Dharma. 10. Spoken without being asked: as in the Amitabha Sutra, which the Buddha spoke of his own accord with no one asking. 11. Vaipulya: sutra passages in which the Buddha speaks the true principle that is square and vast. 12. Prophecy or bestowal of the prediction: the prophecy in which the Buddha records the name a bodhisattva or sravaka will bear when attaining Buddhahood.

[Peace and Nourishment] another name for the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. [Huazang] that is, the Huazang world (short for the Lotus Treasury world), the name of the pure land of Vairocana, the true body of Shakyamuni Tathagata. The sutras say that in the fragrant-water ocean above the wind-circle there is a great lotus, and within this lotus are contained worlds as numerous as motes of dust; hence it is called the 'Lotus Treasury world'. This world has twenty tiers in all, and the Saha world we dwell in lies in the middle of the thirteenth tier of the Huazang world. [Ten great vows] the ten great practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, namely: to revere all Buddhas, to praise the Tathagatas, to make abundant offerings, to repent of karmic obstacles, to rejoice in others' merit, to request the turning of the Dharma-wheel, to request the Buddhas to remain in the world, to follow the Buddhas in study always, to accord with all living beings constantly, and to dedicate all merit universally. [Ocean assembly] a name for the assembly of monks gathered in a monastery. Also called the great ocean assembly, the pure great ocean assembly, a figure for the harmony of the monks, like a hundred rivers entering the sea.

[Essential Explanation] Alas! That ordinary beings should by rule ascend to the stage of one more birth is a wondrous proposal and a discourse of the utmost, beyond all measure. What the Avatamsaka Sutra hands down is found, after all, in this sutra. Yet throughout the world, from ancient times to now, few have believed and many have doubted; words have multiplied and the meaning has been eroded. I can do no more than lay bare my heart and shed my blood.

[Note] Master Ouyi sighs and says: that ordinary beings should by rule ascend straight to the bodhisattva stage of one more birth is truly a wondrous proposal and a discourse of the utmost subtlety, utterly inconceivable; and the purport of attaining Buddhahood in one life, which the assembly of the Huazang ocean received, is in fact in this sutra (the Amitabha Sutra Spoken by the Buddha). Yet throughout the world, from ancient times to the present, those who believe are few while those who doubt are many; words having multiplied, the meaning of the sutra has been eroded. I can do no more than lay bare my heart and shed my blood to proclaim the great meaning of this sutra to others.
3.2 In particular urging the excellence of the Pure Land
Shariputra! Beings who hear this should make the vow, vowing to be born in that land. Why is this? Because they may gather together in one place with such supreme good beings.

[Essential Explanation] The arhats and bodhisattvas spoken of before can only be called 'good beings'; only those of one more birth, dwelling at the summit of the causal stages, are called 'supreme'; and because their number is very great they are called 'many'.
[Note] [All the supreme good beings] refers to the many bodhisattvas of one more birth.

[Essential Explanation] 'Gather together in one place' is another way of saying that ordinary beings and sages dwell together. Ordinarily, because the actual sages still have defiled karma from the past and the provisional sages have their great compassionate vows, ordinary beings can dwell together with the sages. But when the actual sages' bodies are reduced to ashes and the provisional sages' opportunities are exhausted, then rising and sinking are utterly different, and suffering and bliss are far apart. This is only a temporary dwelling together, not an ultimate one.

[Note] 'Gather together in one place' means that ordinary beings and sages dwell together in one place. Usually, because the actual sages (practitioners of the first, second and third fruits who are about to realize the fruit of arhat) still have past defiled karma not yet exhausted, and because the provisional sages (sages manifested for the occasion) have their great compassionate vows, ordinary beings can dwell together with the sages. When the actual sages realize the fruit of arhat (reducing the body to ashes and extinguishing consciousness) and the provisional sages' opportunities for saving beings are exhausted, then rising and sinking are utterly different, and suffering and bliss are far apart. This co-dwelling land is only a temporary togetherness, not an ultimate one.

[Defiled karma] 'outflow' is another name for affliction; 'with outflows' means having afflictions. It is the counterpart of 'undefiled karma'. 'Defiled karma' refers to all the various good and evil karmas that have not yet departed from the various afflictions. [Reducing the body to ashes and extinguishing consciousness] after the persons of the two vehicles cut off the afflictions of the three realms, they enter the samadhi of the fire-light, burning up body and mind, and return to the empty, still, unconditioned state of nirvana. [Rising and sinking utterly different] 'rising' means the provisional sages return to the land of real reward and adornment and the land of eternal stillness and light, and so are blissful; 'sinking' refers to the actual sages, who sink into emptiness and stagnate in stillness, and so suffer.

[Essential Explanation] Moreover, between heaven and earth, those who see and hear are few. Even those fortunate enough to see and hear, few draw near and follow in the footsteps. Moreover, in the Buddha's time, however many the sages, they were like precious gems and auspicious rarities, unable to fill the whole land as the stars fill the sky and motes of dust fill the earth. Moreover, though their dwelling is the same, what they do and accomplish is utterly different. Now, however, by the same undefiled and inconceivable karma they are born together by response and gather in one place as teachers and friends, like the xun and the chi answering each other, together exhausting ignorance, together ascending to wonderful enlightenment.

[Note] Moreover, between heaven and earth, those who see and hear are few. Even among those fortunate enough to see and hear, still fewer can long receive the clear teaching and follow and take refuge in it. Moreover, when the Buddha was in the world, however many the sages, they were like rare jewels and hard-to-find auspicious signs, and could not fill the land as the Land of Ultimate Bliss does, like the stars arrayed in the sky and motes of dust spread over the earth. Moreover, though their dwelling is the same, what they do and accomplish is utterly different: the sages cultivate the undefiled karma of the Way, while ordinary beings have only the toil of dust and birth and death. But the co-dwelling of the Land of Ultimate Bliss is a sharing of the same undefiled and inconceivable karma, born together by response and gathered in one place as teachers and friends, where all that is done and accomplished is the same: together exhausting the delusion of ignorance, together ascending to the stage of wonderful enlightenment (Buddhahood).
[Like the xun and the chi] the xun (
xun
) and the chi (
chi

) are both musical instruments. When these two instruments play together, the xun leads and the chi responds, a figure for the mutual accord of two things. Here it figures the gathering of all the good beings of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, whose deeds and accomplishments are all the same.

[Essential Explanation] Thus ordinary beings of the lowest grade, within non-retrogression of thought, leap beyond all forty-one causal stages. If you call them ordinary beings, yet they do not pass through different birth and are certain to succeed to the Buddha's office, no different from Avalokitesvara and Mahasthamaprapta. If you call them bodhisattvas of one more birth, yet they may be called ordinary beings and cannot be called bodhisattvas of equal enlightenment. All this the net of the teachings cannot gather in, and the net of the lands cannot reduce to rule. One should know that for us, in the great matter and its causal conditions, the single barrier of co-dwelling is the hardest to break through. Only the co-dwelling of the Land of Ultimate Bliss transcends the co-dwelling of the ten directions.

[Note] [Forty-one causal stages] forty-one stages of the causal ground. They refer to the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, and equal enlightenment. [Different birth] another name for ordinary beings, because ordinary beings transmigrate through the six paths and are born receiving various different retributions. Here, 'not passing through different birth, certain to succeed to the Buddha's office' means no longer undergoing fragmentary birth and death but directly realizing the Buddha-fruit. [Net of the teachings] the teachings spoken by the Buddha: the Dharma-gates are immeasurable, as numerous as the meshes of a net; hence 'net of the teachings'. [Net of the lands] the buddha-lands of the ten directions are as many as the meshes of a net; hence 'net of the lands'. [The great matter and its causal conditions] namely opening, revealing, awakening to and entering the Buddha's knowledge and vision; this is the great matter and causal condition for which all Buddhas appear in the world. [The single barrier of co-dwelling, the hardest to break through] for ordinary beings in an ordinary land of co-dwelling of sages and ordinary beings, the delusions of views and thoughts are extremely hard to cut off. [Only the co-dwelling of the Land of Ultimate Bliss transcends the co-dwelling of the ten directions] only the land of co-dwelling of sages and ordinary beings of the Land of Ultimate Bliss can perfectly cut off all delusions (the delusion of views and thoughts, the delusion numerous as dust and sand, and the delusion of ignorance) and perfectly accomplish the Buddha-way in one life; this far surpasses the lands of co-dwelling of the ten directions.

[Three delusions] the delusion of views and thoughts, the delusion numerous as dust and sand, and the delusion of ignorance. The 'delusion of views and thoughts' is the delusion of ordinary beings: the delusion of views is error in knowledge and understanding, and the delusion of thoughts is error in thought. If sravaka and pratyekabuddha practitioners cut off these two delusions, they can realize the fruit of arhat and escape the three realms. The 'delusion numerous as dust and sand' is the delusion of bodhisattvas: if a bodhisattva who transforms and saves beings does not thoroughly understand the immeasurable Dharma-gates, numerous as dust and sand, he cannot complete the work of teaching and converting beings; hence it is called the delusion numerous as dust and sand. The 'delusion of ignorance' is fundamental ignorance; it can obscure the principle of the true appearance of the middle way, and when it is utterly cut off one attains Buddhahood.

[Essential Explanation] Only by understanding this can one deeply believe in the power of Amitabha's vows; believing in the Buddha's power, one can deeply believe in the merit of the Name; believing in the holding of the Name, one can deeply believe that our own mind-nature is fundamentally inconceivable. Only with this deep faith can one arouse the great vow. The word 'should' in the text refers precisely to deep faith. Deep faith and the making of the vow are supreme bodhi. Faith and vow joined together are truly the guide for the Pure Land. Holding the Name on this basis is then the true practice. If faith and vow are firm, then ten recitations or even one recitation at the end of life will certainly bring rebirth; but without faith and vow, though one hold the Name until the wind cannot enter and the rain cannot wet one, like a wall of silver or iron, there is still no principle by which one may be reborn. Those who cultivate the Pure Land karma cannot fail to know this. The larger Amitabha Sutra likewise takes the arousing of the bodhi-vow as essential, exactly in accord with this.

[Note] [Supreme bodhi] namely anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; this bodhi can be realized only by a Buddha. [Deep faith and the making of the vow are supreme bodhi] such deep faith and vow-making is the supreme bodhi-vow, that is, the arousing of the supreme bodhi-mind. [The larger Amitabha Sutra] refers to the Sutra of Immeasurable Life.
2.3 Directly showing the practitioner's holding of the Name as the establishing of practice: 3.1 Directly showing the supreme cause and effect; 3.2 Repeated exhortation
3.1 Directly showing the supreme cause and effect

[Note] Above, the World-Honored One spoke of the various excellences of the Land of Ultimate Bliss and called on beings to give rise to faith and make the vow. Now he further reveals how to ensure rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss: faith, vow and holding the Name, with one mind undisturbed. Earlier in this sutra it is said that to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss is to attain Buddhahood in one life. From this one may know the cause and effect by which an ordinary being of the Saha world attains Buddhahood in one life: the cause is faith, vow and holding the Name with one mind undisturbed; the effect is the attainment of Buddhahood in one life. Therefore Master Ouyi judges this section to be: directly showing the supreme cause and effect.

Shariputra! One cannot be born in that land with few roots of goodness and few causes and conditions of merit. Shariputra! If there is a good man or good woman who hears of Amitabha Buddha and holds fast to the Name, for one day, or two days, or three days, or four days, or five days, or six days, or seven days, with one mind undisturbed, then when that person is about to die, Amitabha Buddha together with the assembly of holy ones will appear before them. When that person ends, their mind not inverted, they will at once be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitabha Buddha.

[Note] [One cannot be born in that land with few roots of goodness and few causes and conditions of merit] this means that one cannot be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss with few roots of goodness and few causes and conditions of merit. In the Sutra on the Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddha's Reception, the Buddha says: 'No sentient beings of few roots of goodness can be born in the pure buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life.' In the Sutra of Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, the Buddha says: 'Those who wish to be born in that land should cultivate three blessings. First, to be filial and care for one's parents, to serve one's teachers, to have a compassionate mind and not kill, and to cultivate the ten good deeds. Second, to receive and uphold the three refuges, to be complete in the precepts, and not to transgress the rules of demeanor. Third, to arouse the bodhi-mind, to believe deeply in cause and effect, to read and recite the Great Vehicle, and to encourage those who practice. These three matters are called pure karma.' Therefore those who recite the Buddha's name must observe and cultivate the three blessings of pure karma, so as to be complete in the causes and conditions of many roots of goodness and much merit; this is the foundation of study and practice in the Pure Land school. [Roots of goodness] the goodness of the three karmas of body, speech and mind; because it can produce wondrous fruit it is called roots of goodness.

Question: The sutra says, 'When that person ends, their mind not inverted, they will at once be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitabha Buddha.' Does this mean that a reciter who has already attained one mind undisturbed must still have a mind not inverted at the point of death before they can be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss?

Answer: This passage of sutra text follows on from the preceding sentence, and means: when that person is about to die, Amitabha Buddha together with the assembly of holy ones appears before them, and by compassion and blessing causes their mind to be not inverted, and they at once attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitabha Buddha. Master Xuanzang's translation, the Commentary on the Sutra on the Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddha's Reception, says: 'When this good man or good woman is about to die, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, together with his immeasurable sravaka disciples and the assembly of bodhisattvas, surrounds them before and behind and comes to stand before them, and by compassion and blessing causes their mind to be undisturbed. When their life has been given up, they follow the Buddha's assembly and are born in the pure buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Immeasurable Life.' As for the death of one who has already accomplished one mind undisturbed, Master Lianchi's Commentary and Subcommentary on the Amitabha Sutra says: 'Now since the mind is already undisturbed, within, right mindfulness is consolidated; without, the Buddha is sensed and comes to welcome one; casting off this retribution-body, one is straightway born in that land.' (Translation: now, since one has already accomplished Buddha-recitation with one mind undisturbed, at the point of death, within, right mindfulness is consolidated and without, the Buddha is sensed and comes to welcome one; casting off this retribution-body, one is born directly in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.)

Question: 'Holding fast to the Name, for one day, or two days, or three days, or four days, or five days, or six days, or seven days, with one mind undisturbed' - does this mean that from one day up to seven days one must maintain Buddha-recitation with one mind undisturbed day and night?

Answer: Buddha-recitation with one mind undisturbed is a state of practice, that is, in reciting the Buddha's name one is clear and distinct throughout, neither dull nor scattered. This passage of sutra text means: by holding fast to the Name for one day up to seven days, one accomplishes the state of Buddha-recitation with one mind undisturbed. One who accomplishes this state, at the point of death, has right mindfulness consolidated within and, without, senses the Buddha coming to welcome them; casting off this retribution-body, they are straightway born in that land.
Question: Setting aside one day, can one, even in seven days, accomplish Buddha-recitation with one mind undisturbed?

Answer: Here, 'for one day, or two days, or three days, or four days, or five days, or six days, or seven days' is an abbreviated way of giving examples. The full account is as in the Mahasatipatthana Sutra, where the World-Honored One says: 'Monks! Anyone who cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness correctly in this way for seven years may expect one of two fruits: to attain the highest wisdom in this present life, or, if the five aggregates still remain, to attain the fruit of non-returning. Monks! Not to speak of seven years - if anyone cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness correctly in this way for six years, they may expect one of the two fruits: to attain great wisdom in this present life, or, if the five aggregates still remain, to attain the fruit of non-returning. Monks! Not to speak of six years,'
'Monks! Not to speak of five years,'
'Monks! Not to speak of four years,'
'Monks! Not to speak of three years,'
