'Monks! Not to speak of two years,'

'Monks! Not to speak of one year - if anyone cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness correctly in this way for seven months, they may expect one of the two fruits: to attain the highest wisdom in this present life, or, if the five aggregates still remain, to attain the fruit of non-returning. Monks! Not to speak of seven months,'
'Monks! Not to speak of six months,'
'Monks! Not to speak of five months,'
'Monks! Not to speak of four months,'
'Monks! Not to speak of three months,'
'Monks! Not to speak of two months,'
'Monks! Not to speak of one month,'

'Monks! Not to speak of half a month - if anyone cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness correctly in this way for seven days, they may expect one of the two fruits: to attain the highest wisdom in this present life, or, if the five aggregates still remain, to attain the fruit of non-returning.' Therefore the length of time needed to accomplish Buddha-recitation with one mind undisturbed depends on each person's foundation and degree of diligence. If one already has good concentration - for instance, if through actual practice according to the Mahasatipatthana Sutra one can already gather the mind to one point - then one may reach the state of Buddha-recitation with one mind undisturbed in one day or up to seven days.

[To attain the highest wisdom in this present life, or, if the five aggregates still remain, to attain the fruit of non-returning] in this present life one realizes the fruit of arhat; but if the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness) still remain, one realizes the fruit of anagamin (the fruit of non-returning, the stage next below the arhat).

[Essential Explanation] The right path of bodhi is called roots of goodness, which is the direct cause. The various aiding paths - giving, precepts, meditation and the rest - are called merit, which is the contributing condition. The sravakas and pratyekabuddhas have few roots of goodness of bodhi, and humans and gods have few roots of goodness in their defiled blessed karma; neither can be born in the Pure Land. Only by faith and vow and holding the Name does each single recitation become complete in many roots of goodness and much merit. Even reciting the Name with a scattered mind brings immeasurable blessing and goodness, how much more with one mind undisturbed! Thus response and the Way intertwine: the imprint forms as the seal is consumed. Amitabha and the holy assembly, not coming, yet come, and personally extend their welcome. The practitioner's mind-consciousness, not going, yet goes, and is lodged in the jeweled lotus. As for 'good man or good woman': whether monk or lay, noble or low, old or young, in the six destinies and four kinds of birth, one who merely hears the Buddha's name has roots of goodness matured through many kalpas, and even the five rebellious acts and ten evil deeds are then called good.

[Note] [Direct cause] this cause can itself give birth to its own fruit, hence it is called the direct cause. [Giving, precepts and meditation] that is, the six paramitas: giving, observing precepts, patience, diligence, meditation and prajna. [Defiled] 'outflow' is another name for affliction; 'defiled' means having afflictions. [The imprint forms as the seal is consumed] 'the imprint forms' means rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; 'the seal is consumed' means the end of the physical body. 'The imprint forms as the seal is consumed' means that the moment of death is the moment of rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Master Daochuo's Collection of Peace and Bliss says: 'As when a wax seal is pressed on clay, the seal is consumed and the imprint forms; when this life is cut off, that is the time of birth in the Land of Peace and Bliss.' [As a wax seal is pressed on clay, the seal is consumed and the imprint (pattern) forms] a wax seal carved with a pattern is pressed onto a clay mold. When the mold is heated and dried, the wax seal melts away and the pattern imprinted on the clay mold takes form. The clay mold is a mold used for casting metal vessels. The Nirvana Sutra says: 'As when a wax seal is pressed on clay, the seal and the clay meet, the seal perishes and the imprint forms.' Master Daochuo's use here of 'as a wax seal is pressed on clay, the seal is consumed and the imprint forms' is a figure for our cultivating with this physical body until, at the end of life, ten recitations continue without interruption; when the breath stops, though the physical body dies (the seal is consumed), the great matter of rebirth is accomplished at the same time (the imprint forms) - 'when this life is cut off, that is the time of birth in the Land of Peace and Bliss'. [Six destinies] 'destiny' means the direction of tending. Beings receive retribution always by tending from cause to fruit; hence the six paths (gods, humans, asuras, animals, hungry ghosts and hells) are also called the 'six destinies'. [Four kinds of birth] womb birth, egg birth, moisture birth and transformation birth. Womb birth is life born after taking form within the mother's womb, as human beings are; egg birth is life born after taking form within an eggshell, as birds are; moisture birth is life that receives form relying on moisture, as insects are; transformation birth is life that arises suddenly by the power of karma alone, without support, as the gods, the hells and human beings at the beginning of a kalpa are.

[Essential Explanation] Amitabha Buddha is the vast Name of ten thousand virtues; by the Name one summons the virtues, and nothing is left out. Therefore the holding of the Name is taken as the true practice, and there is no need to involve oneself further in such practices as visualization or investigation. It is of the utmost simplicity and the utmost directness.
[Note] [By the Name one summons the virtues, and nothing is left out] by the Buddha's Name one summons the Buddha's virtues, and none is left out.

[Essential Explanation] Hearing, one believes; believing, one vows; only then is one willing to hold the Name. Not believing and not vowing is the same as not hearing; though it may serve as a distant cause, it cannot be called the wisdom of hearing.

[Note] Hearing, one believes; believing, one vows; only then is one willing to hold the Name - complete in the three provisions, one may then be said to have the wisdom of hearing. Not believing and not vowing is, for the present, equal to not hearing; though the Buddha's Name, once passing the ear, can serve as a seed of the Way, it becomes only a distant cause and cannot be called the wisdom of hearing.

[Essential Explanation] Holding the Name means remembering the Buddha's name in every thought, hence it is the wisdom of thought. There is, however, holding in terms of phenomena and holding in terms of principle. Holding in terms of phenomena is believing that there is a Buddha Amitabha in the West, without yet understanding that 'this mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha'. One simply vows decisively to seek rebirth, as a child remembers its mother, never forgetting even for a moment. Holding in terms of principle is believing that the Buddha Amitabha of the West is inherent in my mind and made by my mind; one takes the vast Name, inherent in and made by one's own mind, as the object to which the mind is tied, so that one does not forget it even for a moment.

[Note] Master Ouyi explains here: holding the Name means remembering the Buddha's name in every thought. Moreover, 'one simply vows decisively to seek rebirth, as a child remembers its mother, never forgetting even for a moment'. 'Remembering the Buddha's name in every thought' and 'never forgetting even for a moment' mean that among the Buddha-thoughts (the thoughts of reciting the Buddha) there is no stray thought. Therefore, in reciting the Buddha's name one must be focused: one must recite single-mindedly and gather the mind in recitation, striving to make pure thoughts continue without interruption.

[Remembering the Buddha's name in every thought] this is what Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva calls 'pure thoughts continuing in succession', and what Master Shandao (the second patriarch of the Pure Land school) calls 'thought after thought continuing without interruption'. Master Shandao says: 'Therefore the Great Sage (Shakyamuni Buddha), in his compassion, directly urges us to recite the Name exclusively; precisely because recitation is easy, continued recitation brings rebirth. If one can continue thought after thought, taking the end of life as the term, then ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn. ... May all people reflect well on this: walking, standing, sitting or lying down, one must brace the mind and master oneself, and day and night never slacken; when the former thought dies, the latter thought is born, and one forever enjoys the bliss of the unconditioned Dharma, until Buddhahood itself - is this not joyous?' (Quoted from the Essentials of Buddha-Recitation.) Therefore, to have thoughts continue without interruption in ordinary times is the guarantee of clear right mindfulness at the point of death; and clear right mindfulness at the point of death is in turn the key to rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Master Shandao wrote in his Essay on Right Mindfulness at the Point of Death: 'Zhiguizi asked: Among the world's affairs none is greater than birth and death. When a single breath does not come, one belongs to the next life; when a single thought errs, one falls into transmigration. I have repeatedly received your instruction on the method of reciting the Buddha's name for rebirth, and its principle is very clear. Yet I fear that when illness comes and death arrives, my mind-consciousness will be scattered, and I further fear that others may disturb my right mindfulness and make me lose the pure cause. I humbly beg you to show again the way of return, so that I may escape the suffering of sinking down. The master said: Excellent, this question! For anyone who at the end of life wishes to be born in the Pure Land, the one thing needful is not to fear death. Always reflect that this body is full of suffering, entangled in various defiled and evil karmas. If one can cast off this foul body and be born beyond into the Pure Land, receiving immeasurable bliss and released from the bitter destinies of birth and death, that is a matter for rejoicing - like taking off a worn-out garment and receiving a precious robe in exchange. One should simply let go of body and mind and not give rise to attachment. ... If one is gravely ill and near the end, relatives must not shed tears or weep, nor utter sounds of sighing and grief, which confuse the mind and spirit and cause one to lose right mindfulness. They should simply recite the Buddha's name aloud together; only when the breath has ceased may they mourn and weep. As soon as there is the slightest thought of clinging to the world, it becomes an obstruction, and one cannot be liberated. ... I have often seen people who in ordinary times recite the Buddha's name and make prostrations and praises, vowing to seek rebirth in the West, and are most earnest and sincere about it. Yet when illness comes, they fear death and will not speak at all of rebirth and liberation. They wait until the breath has faded and life is spent, and consciousness has entered the dark realm, and only then recite ten times. That is exactly like shutting the gate after the thief has gone - what use is it? Birth and death are a great matter, and one must exert oneself in one's own case. If a single thought errs, one suffers for kalpas - who can suffer in one's place? Think on this, think on this!' (Quoted from Longshu's Essays on the Pure Land.)

[Essential Explanation] 'From one day to seven days' is a matter of accomplishing the task within a fixed term. The sharp-rooted attain being undisturbed in one day; the dull-rooted become undisturbed only in seven days; the middling-rooted vary between two, three, four, five and six days. Again, the sharp-rooted can be undisturbed for seven days, the dull-rooted only for one day, and the middling-rooted vary between six, five, four, three and two days.

[Essential Explanation] One mind is likewise of two kinds. Whether one holds in terms of phenomena or in terms of principle, when one holds until one subdues and removes afflictions, and even until views and thoughts are utterly exhausted, that is one mind in terms of phenomena. Whether one holds in terms of phenomena or in terms of principle, when one holds until the mind opens and one sees the Buddha of one's own nature, that is one mind in terms of principle. One mind in terms of phenomena is not disturbed by views and thoughts; one mind in terms of principle is not disturbed by the two extremes - this is the wisdom of cultivation.

[Note] One mind undisturbed is of two kinds: one mind undisturbed in terms of phenomena and one mind undisturbed in terms of principle. In terms of the depth of one's practice, one mind undisturbed has three grades. 1. Subduing afflictions, like a stone pressing down grass, not following delusion in turning, one is born in the land where ordinary men and sages dwell together. 2. Cutting off afflictions, pulling them out by the root, with deluded feeling utterly exhausted, one is born in the land of expedient remainder. 3. One mind undisturbed in terms of principle, which is the mind opening to see the Buddha of one's own nature, breaking through one to forty-one grades of ignorance, and being born in the land of real reward and adornment.

To end birth and death and escape transmigration, all the other eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates require cutting off afflictions, whereas the Pure Land Dharma-gate requires only subduing them; and subduing afflictions is far easier than cutting them off - this is the incomparable excellence and subtlety of the Pure Land Dharma-gate. Master Ouyi says in the Lingfeng Zonglun

Fangshi Outan (Occasional Talks from the Brahma Chamber): 'One mind in terms of phenomena means being clear and distinct throughout, neither dull nor scattered; one mind in terms of principle means silently agreeing with the unborn and clearly understanding one's own nature.'

Master Ouyi, in the Preface to the Pure Land Repentance and Release of Life Society, says: “Now, with the single mind undisturbed — even if one has not cut off the delusions (severed afflictions), can one fail to subdue them (repress afflictions)? If the affairs of this Sahā world bind in every direction — when one meets the five desires one clings like gum and lacquer; when one meets adverse conditions one nurses hatred and resentment — then to wish that at the end of life Amitabha will come to receive one, this is a thing that can never be obtained.”

[Subduing and severing the afflictions] To subdue the afflictions, and even to sever them. [See-thought] The wrong views and the wrong thoughts. The wrong views are the confusions and errors of ordinary people in their views — such as the five wrong views of self-view, boundary-view, heterodox view, view-attachment, and precept-attachment. The wrong thoughts are the confusions and errors of ordinary people in their thought — the afflictions of greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt. These two confusions (what is commonly called “afflictions”) are the root of sentient beings’ falling into the three realms and suffering birth and death in vain; cut them off and one can be done with birth and death and leave the three realms. [See-thought already severed] The wrong views and wrong thoughts cut off before one cultivates the Pure Land method: this refers to those who cultivated another method (e.g., Chan) and, having cut off the afflictions, turned to the Pure Land. Because the afflictions are already cut off, from the very start of the Pure Land practice they attain the single-mindedness-without-confusion that is the single point of the practice. For example, the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, Master Chewu, cut off the afflictions through Chan illumination, and became the thirty-sixth patriarch of the Linji school. Yet he always thought of the Chan master Yongming Yanshou, a great craftsman of the Chan school, who still returned his heart to the Pure Land, reciting the Buddha’s name a hundred thousand times daily, seeking birth in Ultimate Bliss. And now, being in the age of the Dharma’s end, all the more should one follow the legacy of Master Yongming. Thereupon he bent his heart to the Pure Land, championed the Lotus school, and became a reciter whose “see-thought was already severed.” [Phenomenal single-mindedness] Although “subduing and severing afflictions, up to see-thought already severed” is one-pointedness, it has not yet reached the principle, so it is judged as phenomenal single-mindedness. [Not disturbed by the two extremes] Not disturbed by the two extremes of existence and non-existence. The deluded, relying on existence, speak of non-existence, and so there arises the opposition of the two extremes, existence and non-existence. For example, a cow has horns; a rabbit has none. But viewed in the light of the true aspect of all dharmas, all dharmas are empty, with nothing whatsoever, all being illusions. Where in truth is a cow? Where a rabbit? Where horns? Needless to speak of having horns or not. One who attains the single-mindedness of principle realizes that “all that is marked by form is false,” and so is not disturbed by the two extremes.

[Key Explanation] Because one is not disturbed by see-thought, therefore one attracts the transformation-body Buddha and the holy assembly to appear before one; the mind no longer gives rise to the three-existence inversion of the Sahā world, and one is reborn in the two kinds of Bliss-world — the Co-dwell and the Expedient. Because one is not disturbed by the two extremes, therefore one attracts the reward-body Buddha and the holy assembly to appear before one; the mind no longer gives rise to the two-view inversion of birth-and-death and nirvāṇa, and one is reborn in the two kinds of Bliss-world — the Real Reward and the Still Light.

[Note] [Three existsences] The birth and death of the three realms, having cause and having fruit: first, desire-existence, the birth and death of the desire realm; second, form-existence, the birth and death of the form realm; third, formless-existence, the birth and death of the formless realm.

[Key Explanation] Know that holding fast to the name — being at once simple and direct, is yet the most sudden and the most perfect. Because each thought is the Buddha, there is no need of visualized contemplation, no need of meditative inquiry; in the present moment it is perfectly bright, without remainder and without lack. The highest faculties cannot overstep its threshold, and the lowest faculties can also reach its domain. The Buddha one attracts and the land one is born in are often the more excellent and advancing, and are not all uniform. It may be said to encompass horizontally the eight teachings and to penetrate vertically the five periods. Therefore, out of utterly thorough compassion, he spoke it without being asked, and deeply sighed over its being hard to believe.
[Note] [Cannot overstep its threshold] Kǔn (
kǔn

), a threshold. “Cannot overstep its threshold” means that even a bodhisattva at the equal-enlightenment stage cannot transcend its scope. [Eight teachings] The eight teachings established by the Tiantai school: the Sudden, the Gradual, the Secret, the Indeterminate, the Canon, the General, the Distinct, and the Perfect. [Five periods] According to the sequence of the World-Honored One’s teaching, five periods are distinguished: the Avatamsaka period, the Āgama period, the Vaipulya period, the Prajñā period, and the Lotus-Nirvāṇa period.

[Key Explanation] Question: The Contemplation Sūtra deals specially with visualization; why is it said there is no need of visualized contemplation? Answer: This meaning comes out of the Contemplation Sūtra itself. Because the superior contemplation is beyond the power of the ordinary mind, that sūtra separately opens, in the thirteenth contemplation, the contemplation of the inferior image. And those of heavy hindrances still cannot be mindful of that Buddha, so in the sixteenth it broadly opens the gate of name-recitation. Since in this sūtra, in the age of the Dharma’s end, there are many of heavy hindrances, it specially emphasizes the sixteenth contemplation. Know that though the faculties of people are dull, yet the image-body of sixteen and eight feet and the name of Amitāyus are never other than mind-made and mind-is. Therefore, the one who contemplates the inferior form has no need of the superior contemplation, and the one who recites the name is not wearied with visualization.

[Note] Question: The Contemplation Sūtra speaks specially of visualization; why is it said there is no need of visualized contemplation? Answer: The meaning “no need of visualized contemplation” comes just out of the Contemplation Sūtra. Because the contemplation of the superior response-body (the superior contemplation) is beyond the power of the ordinary mind, that sūtra separately, in the thirteenth contemplation, opens the contemplation of the inferior response-body (the inferior image). And those with heavy hindrances and shallow wisdom cannot attain even the inferior response-body contemplation, so in the sixteenth contemplation it broadly opens the gate of name-recitation. This sūtra (the Amitabha Sūtra), because in the Dharma’s end there are many of heavy hindrances and shallow wisdom, specially speaks of the sixteenth contemplation — name-recitation. Know that though the faculties of people are dull, yet the image-body of sixteen and eight feet and the name of Amitāyus are never otherwise than mind-made and mind-is. Therefore, the one who contemplates the inferior response-body has no need of the superior response-body contemplation, and the one who recites the name is not wearied with visualization.

[Mind-made, mind-is] The Contemplation Sūtra says: “The Tathāgatas, all Buddhas, are the body of the dharmadhātu, entering into the thought of all sentient beings. Therefore, when you think of the Buddha, this mind is itself the thirty-two marks and the eighty minor characteristics. This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. The sea of the Buddhas’ right and universal knowledge is born of thought.”

[Key Explanation] Question: The patriarchs Tianqi and Dufeng all advocated probing “who is it that recites the Buddha’s name?”; why is it said there is no need of meditative inquiry? Answer: This meaning comes just from the Tianqi and other patriarchs. Because the earlier patriarchs saw that reciters were not in accord with the Buddha’s utterly thorough compassion, they could not stand it aside, and straightway questioned them, with one fierce reminder — far more than “after the long night, the dawn returns.” We, down to this day, still will not die to the mind and recite the Buddha, but insist on grasping the knocked-door tile to beat our own flesh-and-blood parents inside the house. Toward the patriarchs, this is a wicked rebellion, not a good compliance.

[Note] [Tianqi] Master Benrui. [Dufeng] Master Benshan. [Reciters not in accord with the Buddha’s utterly thorough compassion] The Buddha’s utterly thorough compassion in teaching people to recite was to have them clearly awaken to the meaning that “this mind makes the Buddha, this mind is the Buddha,” but the reciters did not understand this. [Therefore could not stand it aside] Seeing that the reciters did not understand the essential meaning, the patriarchs of old could not stand it aside: the Buddha’s mind being so compassionate, and yet the reciters still dull and unaware, so they added further direction. Master Tianqi showed the assembly: “All day you recite the Buddha, not knowing that it is wholly the Buddha’s recitation. If you do not know, you must look at “who is it that recites the Buddha?” Fix the eyes, raise the mind. Be sure to get the answer.” Through such a direct question and a fierce reminder, the reciters are made to turn the light back upon themselves at the very word, and see in person the Amitabha of their own nature. This teaching of Master Tianqi is directed at those “all-day reciters” who, having recited until it is clear and distinct, neither dull nor scattered, think this is the ultimate and stop advancing. The master wanted them to take one more step from the top of a hundred-foot pole, and accomplish the Buddha-recitation samādhi. Later people, not understanding the patriarchs’ intent, instead use the inquiry “who is it that recites the Buddha?” to negate faith, vow, and name-holding — they have truly turned it upside-down! [More than the dawn returning after the long night] Once one sees in person the Amitabha of one’s own nature, is it not more than the long night’s seeing daybreak! [Knocked-door tile] In old times, because a courtyard lay between the main gate and the dwelling, visitors would knock with a tile or a stone. When the door opened, it was naturally discarded. The Chan school often likens the word-head (huatou) to a knocked-door tile; once one illuminates the mind and sees the nature, the word-head is naturally useless. [Beating one’s parents inside the house] The World-Honored One’s utterly thorough compassion asked us to recite the Buddha, yet we still will not die to the mind and recite the Buddha to seek birth in the Pure Land, but insist on the bitter inquiry “who is it that recites the Buddha?” as a word-head. This is like taking the knocked-door tile and, instead of knocking open the door to see the people in the house, beating one’s own flesh-and-blood parents inside.

[Key Explanation] A further question: this is all very well for one who has a willing mind; but for one who is not yet willing, how can he respond? Answer: Alas! It is precisely because you are not yet willing that you must be brought to a willing mind that responds. Your right faith is not yet opened; you are like raw cowhide, which cannot be bent and folded. Know that one with eyes of course never lights a lamp under the sun. And one without eyes — why must he search bitterly for a lamp in the daylight? The Dharma-prince Mahasthamaprapta says: “Without borrowing any expedients, the mind opens of itself.” This is the flaming-charcoal word in the one-practice samādhi. Who would dare to touch it and not be consumed?

[Note] A further question: This is all very well for one who is willing to die to the mind and recite; but one not yet willing to die to the mind and recite — how can he respond to the World-Honored One’s utterly thorough compassion? Answer: Alas! This is precisely said to those who are not yet willing to die to the mind and recite — to make your willing mind respond. The right faith that “this mind makes the Buddha, this mind is the Buddha” is not opened in you; you are like raw cowhide, which cannot be bent and folded into shape. Know that one who already has that right faith of course has no reason to probe “who is it that recites the Buddha?” (one with eyes never lights a lamp under the sun). But one who does not yet have that right faith — what use is it for him to probe “who is it that recites the Buddha?” (and one without eyes, why must he search bitterly for a lamp in the daylight?) The Dharma-prince Mahasthamaprapta says: “Without borrowing any expedients, the mind opens of itself.” This is the flaming-charcoal word of the one-practice samādhi! Who dares to touch it and not be consumed?

[One-practice samādhi] The mind abiding in one practice and cultivating the right concentration. [Great fire-ball] A great fire gathered in one place; all things that touch it are burned. The Zhongfeng Three-Hour Recitation says: “Raise a single call of the Buddha’s name, and straight down there is no other view. Like the Tai’ē sword laid cross-wise before the hall; like a great wheel of fire, its stars leaping, its flame blazing. All things that brush against it are set alight; all that touch it are wounded.”

[Key Explanation] Question: If the Buddha appears at the end of life, can one be sure it is not a demon? Answer: A mind-cultivator who does not contemplate the Buddha, and then the Buddha suddenly appears — this was not at first expected, so it is called a demonic matter. But a reciter of the Buddha’s name who sees the Buddha is already in accord. Moreover, the end of life is not the time for demons; why the need to doubt?

[Key Explanation] Question: The “seven days without confusion” — is it in ordinary times, or at the end of life? Answer: In ordinary times. Question: If, after the seven days of no-confusion, one again arouses confusions and creates karma, can one still be born there? Answer: One who has truly attained the single-mindedness-without-confusion — for him there is no further matter of arousing confusion and creating karma.
[Note] Master Ouyi clearly shows: the single-mindedness-without-confusion in Buddha-recitation is a skill that should be trained in ordinary times.

[Key Explanation] Question: The ten recitations of the Larger Sūtra and the one recitation of the Jewel-King Treatise — are they in ordinary times, or at the end of life? Answer: The ten recitations span both times. The ten recitations at dawn belong to ordinary times; the “ten recitations attaining birth,” the same as the ten recitations of name-recitation in the Contemplation Sūtra, belong to the time of death. The single recitation is spoken only of the time of death.
[Note]

A student asked: The Larger Sūtra speaks of “ten recitations attaining birth,” and the Jewel-King Treatise speaks of “one recitation attaining birth.” Do these ten and the one refer to ordinary times or to the end of life? Master Ouyi answered: What is commonly called “ten recitations” has two situations, one referring to ordinary times and one to the end of life. The “ten recitations at dawn” advocated by the Repentance-Master Ciyun refer to ordinary times; “ten recitations attaining birth,” the same as the “ten recitations of name-recitation” in the Contemplation Sūtra, all refer to the last ten recitations at the time of death. And the “one recitation attaining birth” spoken in the Jewel-King Treatise refers only to the last thought at the time of death.

[Ten recitations of the Larger Sūtra] Refers to the “ten recitations attaining birth” spoken in the Larger Sūtra. [One recitation of the Jewel-King] Refers to the “one recitation attaining birth” spoken in the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi Jewel-King Treatise, the Ninth Gate, “This Life and the Other Life, One Recitation and Ten Recitations.”

[Key Explanation] Question: Whether ten recitations or one, both attain birth — why then the seven days? Answer: If there is not the ordinary-time work of seven days, how could there be the ten recitations or the one at the end of life? Even the lowest grade of rebellious and evil person is but the ripening of past karmic causes, so that at death he meets a good friend, and hearing, straightway has faith and vow. This is a case of one in a myriad, not something to be gotten by luck! The Questions on the Pure Land refutes this most fully, and people today must read it.
[Note]

The student asked again: Since the ten recitations and the one recitation at death can both attain birth in the Western Pool of Ultimate Bliss, why need one do the work of single-mindedness-without-confusion? Answer: If in ordinary times one does not do the work of single-mindedness-without-confusion, where would the ten or the one recitation at death come from? Even the lowest grade of rebellious and evil person is but the ripening of past karmic causes, so that at death he meets a good friend, and hearing, straightway has faith and vow. This is one in a myriad, not something to be gotten by luck! The Questions on the Pure Land refutes most fully this fallacy that “ten or one recitations both attain birth, so why need the ordinary-time work of single-mindedness,” and people today must read it.
[Why the seven days?] And why need one do the work of single-mindedness-without-confusion?

Here the “seven days” refers to doing the work of single-mindedness-without-confusion. In ancient writing, one liked to use allusions (quoting canonical stories). The allusion of “seven days” comes from the Amitabha Sūtra, in which:

“If there be a good man or good woman who, hearing Amitabha Buddha, holds fast to the name — for one day, for two days, for three days, for four days, for five days, for six days, or for seven days, with a single mind without confusion — then when that person’s life ends, Amitabha Buddha and the holy assembly appear before him. At that person’s death his mind is not inverted, and he is reborn in the Pure Land of Amitabha Buddha.”

As for the question of the ten recitations at death, Master Ouyi, in the Lingfeng Collected Works, Preface to the Pure Land Repentance and Release of Life Society, discusses it: The ten recitations at death must be grounded in deeply planted wholesome roots, and only then can the right thought appear at death. If when present adverse and favorable circumstances come upon one, one no longer has right thought, how much less can one keep right thought at death? Moreover, in the broad daylight of today, with all clearly and brightly before one, one still cannot accept and practice the true admonitions of a bright teacher and good friend; and one imagines that when the suffering of death arises, merely relying on a good friend’s reminder and teaching would be enough to accept and practice them? And further, when dying, how can one be sure a true good friend will appear? Even if a true good friend appears, if at the time of instruction the person’s spirit-consciousness is benumbed, and he seeks his faith and understanding — this too is a thing impossible to obtain. (The original text reads: “The ten recitations at death must be deeply grounded in good roots. Now, when adverse and favorable circumstances come, one no longer has right thought — how much less at death? And when the suffering of death appears, one relies only on a good friend’s reminding; in the broad daylight of today one still cannot accept and practice the true maxims of a bright teacher and friend! When dying, how can one be sure a good friend appears? Even if he appears and instructs, and the spirit-consciousness is benumbed, then to seek his faith and understanding — this again is a thing impossible to obtain.”)

From this it can be known: the ten recitations attaining birth are the last ten recitations at death, and the one recitation attaining birth is likewise the last thought at death — the last resolve at death is the true resolve. At the moment of death, it is like a person arriving at the airport; in ordinary times he says he wants to go here or there, but where he will actually go depends wholly on which airplane he boards last —
this is the final vow, the final resolve.
Even in a muddled state, still it is himself who boards it.)
Therefore, being able at the last moment, with single-minded concentration, to recite one call or ten calls of the Buddha’s name, is utterly crucial.

As for the relation between the ten and the one recitation attaining birth and the single-mindedness-without-confusion, Master Ouyi clearly states: “If there is not the ordinary-time work of seven days (the ordinary-time work of single-mindedness), how could there be the ten or the one recitation at death?”

As for the state of recitation of the person of the five rebellious acts and ten evil deeds who recites ten times at death and is reborn, Master Yinguang instructs: Though he has not personally realized the single-mindedness-without-confusion, yet the mind of the dying one, apart from the thought of remembering the Buddha, is at last without any other thought. (Master Yinguang’s original instruction: “In the Contemplation Sūtra, the five rebellious acts and ten evil deeds, about to die, with the appearances of hell manifest, have a good friend (original note: whether monk or layman, man or woman, only one able to teach them to remember the Buddha is called a good friend) who teaches them to remember the Buddha — perhaps only ten sounds, or not even ten sounds, and they straightway die. They too, relying on the Buddha’s compassionate power, are born there carrying their karma. These ten recitations, compared with ordinary ten recitations, have a force of fierce urgency as different as heaven from the deep, and so they attain birth. Driven by the extreme suffering of hell, the instant they hear the Buddha’s name, they recite it with their whole mind and strength. Apart from this recitation there is absolutely no other thought. Though they have not personally realized the single-mindedness-without-confusion, yet at last their mind is without any other thought.” (From the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, Third Series, Volume Two, Letter in Reply to Layman Chen Xinru))

Question: The passage above said “one must deeply plant good roots, and only then can the right thought appear at death.” The person of the five rebellious acts and ten evil deeds in the Contemplation Sūtra, reborn through ten recitations at death — did he too deeply plant good roots?

Answer: To this, Master Ouyi says: “The sūtra says that the ten evil deeds and five rebellious acts attain birth — they must have in the past planted the seed of bodhi. Without the seed of bodhi, how could they have met a good friend? Even meeting a good friend to rouse them, how could they suddenly give rise to faith and vow, and recite the great name?” (Lingfeng Collected Works
General Discourse at the Tianma Monastery of Shepu)

[Key Explanation] Question: The West is ten trillion Buddha-lands from here — how can one be born there at once? Answer: The ten trillion Buddha-lands are not outside this present single thought of my mind-nature, because the mind-nature has originally no “outside.” And again, relying on the Buddha-power of one’s own mind to lead one, what difficulty is there in being born at once? It is like a mirror reflecting dozens of layers of mountains, rivers, and towers — the layers are distinct, yet there is really no far and near; one reflection reveals all, and seeing has no first and last. “Passing from here through the West over ten trillion Buddha-lands, there is a world called Ultimate Bliss” — it is also like this. “That land has a Buddha named Amitabha, now presently teaching the Dharma” — it is also like this. “When that person’s life ends, Amitabha Buddha and the holy assembly appear before him; at that person’s death his mind is not inverted, and he is reborn in the Pure Land of Amitabha Buddha” — it is also like this. Know that every word is the literary text of the sea-seal samādhi and the great perfect-mirror wisdom.

[Note] [Sea-seal samādhi] The name of a samādhi attained by the Buddha, likening the Buddha’s falsehood exhausted and his mind clear, so that all things appear together, like the surface of a windless, waveless, clear sea, in which not a single form is not reflected. [Great perfect-mirror wisdom] This is what is formed by transforming the defiled eighth consciousness; it is the Buddha’s wisdom by which he contemplates all phenomenal affairs and principles with not the least obscurity. This wisdom, pure, clear, and perfectly bright, sees through to everything within and without, like a great round mirror illuminating all things.
[Key Explanation] Question: Holding the name is judged as the practice-practice; being thus an auxiliary practice, why is it called the right practice?
[Note] Because the preceding text judged faith and vow as the wisdom-practice and upholding the Name as the practice-practice, hence this question.
[Key Explanation]

Answer: Speaking of faith, vow, and practice in terms of the single mind, they have no before and after, and are not fixedly three. For without vow and practice there is no true faith; without practice and faith there is no true vow; without faith and vow there is no true practice. Now, since by faith and vow one holds the name, the three — faith, vow, and practice — are wholly perfect in every sound, and so it is called abundant roots of goodness, merit, and karmic conditions. The Contemplation Sūtra says, “Because of reciting the Buddha’s name, in every thought is wiped away the offenses of birth and death of eighty koṭi aeons” — this is what is meant. If the good merit were not abundant, how could it wipe away offenses so great?

[Note] [No before and after, not fixedly three] Faith, vow, and practice are one body; they have no before and after, and cannot be separated into three matters. For, since there is faith, vow must of necessity arise from faith; since there is vow, practice must of necessity proceed from vow. Therefore, when one speaks of faith, vow and practice are of necessity within it; when one speaks of vow, faith and practice are of necessity within it; when one speaks of practice, faith and vow are of necessity within it. Without vow and practice there is no true faith; without practice and faith there is no true vow; without faith and vow there is no true practice.

Question: Since faith, vow, and practice cannot be separated, why did Master Ouyi say earlier: “If there is no faith and vow, even if one holds the name until the wind cannot blow in and the rain cannot wet it, like a wall of silver and iron, there is still no principle by which one attains birth”?

Answer: If there is no faith and vow, yet one holds the name until the wind cannot blow in and the rain cannot wet it, like a wall of silver and iron — this refers to those Chan practitioners who take the Buddha-name as a word-head (huatou) to probe. They are not cultivating the Pure Land at all; their faith is the Chan faith — illuminate the mind, see the nature, and become Buddha. Their vow is likewise to attain this goal of “illuminating the mind, seeing the nature, becoming Buddha.” So their recitation is not the cultivation of the Pure Land, but Chan practice. Let me ask: if a Pure Land reciter could recite until the wind cannot blow in and the rain cannot wet it, like a wall of silver and iron, could you still say he has no faith and vow? Without faith and vow as the guide, as the motive, as the spur, as the whip, as the supervisor, could the recitation attain such a realm?

Master Ouyi, in speaking these words, intends to warn those Chan practitioners that they should cultivate both Chan and the Pure Land. For “upholding the Name until the wind cannot blow in and the rain cannot wet it, like a wall of silver and iron” is, in the study of the Pure Land school, wholly the realm of single-mindedness-without-confusion; as long as one is complete in faith and vow, one is certain to be reborn in the Western Pool of Ultimate Bliss, ending birth and death and leaving the round. But for Chan practice, to end birth and death and leave the round, one must pass through the ten thousand thoughts returning to one, the one returning to nothing, illuminating the mind and seeing the nature, and then do the work of maintaining and sustaining, until the see-thought and thought-afflictions are wholly cut off, and only then can one end birth and death and leave the round. And “upholding the Name until the wind cannot blow in and the rain cannot wet it, like a wall of silver and iron” is but the elementary work of Chan — the ten thousand thoughts returning to one — still far from ending birth and death and leaving the round. Therefore, Master Yongming, the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, and many patriarchs and great masters, have time and again urged Chan practitioners to cultivate both Chan and the Pure Land.
As for cultivating both Chan and the Pure Land, Master Ouyi says:
“If a Chan practitioner wishes to be born in the West, he need not change to reciting the Buddha; as long as he is complete in faith and vow, then the Chan practice is itself the Pure Land practice.”
(From the Pure Land Collection of Master Ouyi
Casual Talks in the Brahma Chamber)

[Master Yongming, the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha] Master Yongming is the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, so his birthday, the seventeenth day of the eleventh lunar month, was taken as the anniversary of Amitabha Buddha. As for Master Yongming, Master Yinguang praises him, saying:
“Master Yongming is the incarnation of Amitabha Buddha. With great compassion, he opens and transforms sentient beings.”
(From the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Discourse at the World Buddhist Laymen’s Forest)

[Key Explanation] Question: At death, fiercely and urgently, one can wipe away many offenses; in ordinary times, reciting the name with a whole mind — does that too wipe away offenses? Answer: As when the sun rises, the manifold darkness vanishes; reciting the great name, the ten-thousand offenses are extinguished.

[Note] [Reciting the name with a whole mind] Apart from the thought of remembering the Buddha, absolutely no other thought. Master Yinguang says: “In the Contemplation Sūtra, the five rebellious acts and ten evil deeds, about to die, with the appearances of hell manifest, have a good friend (original note: whether monk or layman, man or woman, only one able to teach them to remember the Buddha is called a good friend) who teaches them to remember the Buddha — perhaps only ten sounds, or not even ten sounds, and they straightway die; they too, relying on the Buddha’s compassionate power, are born there carrying their karma. These ten recitations, compared with ordinary ten recitations, have a force of fierce urgency as different as heaven from the deep, and so they attain birth. Driven by the extreme suffering of hell, the instant they hear the Buddha’s name, they recite it with their whole mind and strength. Apart from this recitation there is absolutely no other thought. Though they have not personally realized the single-mindedness-without-confusion, yet at last their mind is without any other thought.” (From the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, Third Series
Volume Two
Letter in Reply to Layman Chen Xinru)

[Key Explanation] Question: Does reciting the name with a scattered mind also wipe away offenses? Answer: The merit of the name is inconceivable; how could it not wipe away offenses? But [with a scattered mind] one does not definitely attain birth, because the drifting, shallow good is no match for the accumulated offenses of the beginningless. Know that were the accumulated offenses to have a bodily form, the whole realm of space could not contain them. Though through a hundred years, day and night, one recited “Amitabha” a hundred thousand times, and every sound wiped away the birth-and-death offenses of eighty koṭi aeons, yet the offenses wiped away are like the earth on a fingernail, while the offenses not wiped away are like the earth of the great lands. Only when one recites to the single-mindedness-without-confusion is it like a strong man breaking through a siege and coming out, no longer to be checked by a camp of troops. Yet the recitation of the name is itself the seed of becoming Buddha, like the diamond, which can never be destroyed. In the Buddha’s time, an old man sought to leave the household; five hundred sages all said he had no good roots. The Buddha said: “This man, countless aeons ago, being pressed by a tiger, cried out in terror ‘Namo Buddha.’ Now that this good root has ripened, he has met with my attainment of the Way — this is not within the knower-eye of the two-vehicle sages.” From this it may be seen that the Lotus Sūtra makes clear that those who, in the presence of the Buddhas of the past, scattered-ly recited the name have all become Buddhas — is this not to be believed? I humbly wish that monk and layman, wise and dull, of this simple, direct, unsurpassed, perfect and sudden gate, do not regard it as hard and so give rise to retreat and excuse, nor regard it as easy and so make no effort. Do not regard it as shallow and so rashly despise it, nor as deep and so dare not take it up. For the name that is held is truly inconceivable; the mind-nature that holds it is also truly inconceivable. Recite one sound — that one sound is inconceivable. Recite ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten-thousand, measureless, countless sounds — every sound is inconceivable.

[Note] “The merit of the name is inconceivable; how could it not wipe away offenses? But one does not definitely attain birth, because the drifting, shallow good is no match for the accumulated offenses of the beginningless.” (Translation: The merit of the name is inconceivable; how could it not wipe away offenses? But one does not necessarily attain birth in the Western Pool of Ultimate Bliss, because the drifting, shallow good is no match for the offenses accumulated since the beginningless.)

Master Ouyi here clearly points out: reciting the name with a scattered mind can wipe away offenses, but one does not necessarily attain birth in the Pool of Ultimate Bliss; and he explains the principle: “Know that were the accumulated offenses to have a bodily form, the whole realm of space could not contain them. Though through a hundred years, day and night, one recited “Amitabha” a hundred thousand times (though in a hundred years, day and night, one recited Amitabha a hundred thousand times), and every sound wiped away the birth-and-death offenses of eighty koṭi aeons (every sound wiping away the heavy birth-and-death offense of eighty koṭi aeons), yet the offenses wiped away are like the earth on a fingernail (the offenses wiped away are like the earth on the fingernail), while the offenses not wiped away are like the earth of the great lands (the offenses not wiped away are like the earth of the lands of the ten directions).” What then is to be done? Master Ouyi continues: “Only when one recites to the single-mindedness-without-confusion is it like a strong man breaking through a siege and coming out, no longer to be checked by a camp of troops.” Therefore the way out is “only recite to the single-mindedness-without-confusion.” This is why the World-Honored One expressly showed that one should recite the Buddha to the single-mindedness-without-confusion, and again and again admonished that one should practice as taught.

[Earth on a fingernail] Also rendered “earth on the nail,” the earth on one’s fingernail. In the sūtras and treatises the earth on a fingernail is often compared with the earth of the great lands as a metaphor, describing the former as extremely little and the latter as extremely much. [Monk and layman] Black is purple-black, and plain is white; monks wear purple-black robes and lay people mostly wear white, hence monk and layman are called the black-and-white.
Part C 2: The Second Exhortation
[Note] The matter is of great importance, so the World-Honored One exhorted again.
Śāriputra! Because I see this benefit, I speak these words. If there be sentient beings who hear this teaching, they should make the vow and be born in that land.

[Note] Master Xuanzang’s translation reads: “Śāriputra. Having observed such a great matter of benefit, peace, and joy, I speak words of truth. If there be pure-faith good men or good women who hear the inconceivable meritorious name of this Amitāyus Buddha and the pure Buddha-land of the Pool of Ultimate Bliss, all of them should believe, accept, make the vow, and practicing as said, be born in that Buddha-land.” Please pay special heed to the eight words: “believe, accept, make the vow, practicing as said.”

[Key Explanation] “I see” refers to what the Buddha’s eye sees, exhaustively and clearly. “This benefit” refers to the horizontally passing out of the five turbidities, the perfectly purifying of the four lands, up to the non-retrogressive stage being reached — this is the benefit of inconceivable merit. Again, this benefit is spoken in terms of the mind not being inverted at the end of life. For on the defiled soil, in self-power practice, the critical juncture of birth and death is where one most rarely gains strength. Whether the stubborn cultivator or the wild wisdom, all are of no avail. Even a person of deep awakening whose practice is silent and firm, if a hair’s breadth of habit-energy is not yet purged, cannot but fall with the strong and the biased. What Patriarch Yongming calls “ten men, nine miss the road; if the shadow-realm appears, at a glance one goes with it” — this is truly chilling. A first-fruit sage is benighted in leaving the womb; a bodhisattva is fogged in crossing between births. Here, how can one presume to act the master, and get it by luck and recklessness? Only faith, vow, and name-holding, relying on the other-power — the Buddha’s compassionate vow must not be in vain. Amitabha and the holy assembly appear to comfort and guide, so that one attains the non-inversion and is born freely.

[Note] “I see this benefit” means that the World-Honored One’s Buddha-eye personally sees two great and supremely excellent benefits: first, that sentient beings born in the Pool of Ultimate Bliss at once realize the stage of non-retrogression (“those born there are all avaivartika”) and, in that one life, become Buddha; second, that those who recite to the single-mindedness-without-confusion are born freely. The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Reception by the Praised Pure Land says: “That good man or good woman, at the end of life, with Amitāyus Buddha and his immeasurable host of voice-hearer disciples and bodhisattvas together, before and after surrounding, come to stand before him, with compassionate protection, making the mind not confused. Having cast off this life, he follows the Buddha’s assembly and is born in the pure Buddha-land of the Amitāyus Pool of Ultimate Bliss.”

[Whether stubborn cultivator or wild wisdom, all of no avail] Whether the stubborn cultivator (blind cultivation and reckless practice) or the wild wisdom (understanding without practice), these two kinds of people, at the critical juncture of birth and death, cannot be masters of themselves, and are wholly without effect (all of no avail). [By luck] Here it means pinning hope on one chance in ten thousand (getting lucky success). [Reckless] Muddled and careless.

[Key Explanation] The Buddha, seeing the suffering of sentient beings’ inversion and confusion at death, specially guarantees this matter, and therefore earnestly exhorts again to make the vow, because the vow can guide the practice.

[Note] The World-Honored One, seeing the suffering of sentient beings’ inversion and confusion at death, specially taught a method to ensure birth in the Pool of Ultimate Bliss — reciting the Buddha to the single-mindedness-without-confusion — and earnestly exhorted again to make the vow: to vow that the recitation reaches the single-mindedness-without-confusion and one is born freely in the Pool of Ultimate Bliss. In Master Xuanzang’s translation there are the four words “practicing as said,” which make the meaning clearer. The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Reception by the Praised Pure Land says: “All should believe, accept, make the vow; practicing as said, be born in that Buddha-land.”

Question: Before speaking of the single-mindedness-without-confusion, the World-Honored One said “sentient beings who hear this should make the vow, vowing to be born in that land”; after speaking of the single-mindedness-without-confusion, the World-Honored One again said: “If there be sentient beings who hear this teaching, they should make the vow and be born in that land.” Are the contents of these two vows different?

Answer: They differ. The first vow was spoken by the World-Honored One after he had introduced the many excellences of the Western Pool of Ultimate Bliss, so the vow made is: recite the Buddha to seek birth in the Pool of Ultimate Bliss. The second vow was spoken after the World-Honored One had taught that those who recite to the single-mindedness-without-confusion are born freely in the Pool of Ultimate Bliss, so the vow made is: recite the Buddha to reach the single-mindedness-without-confusion and be born freely in the Pool of Ultimate Bliss.

[Key Explanation] Question: Since the Buddha is mind-made and mind-is, why not speak directly of one’s own Buddha, and must one necessarily take the other Buddha as superior? Answer: This gate lies wholly in realizing that the other is one’s self. If one shrinks from speaking of the other Buddha, then the view of “other” is not yet forgotten. If one emphasizes one’s own Buddha, one falls into the inversion of self-view. Again, of the four siddhānta-gratifications, the three later never arise alone. If one does not, by the worldly, deeply arouse rejoicing faith, then the two gratifications of yearning and of abandoning cannot arise; how much less one’s entering the principle-Buddha? Only through the phenomenal holding reaching the principle-holding, so that Amitabha and the holy assembly appear before one, is one’s own nature manifest. Being born in that land, seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, is the accomplishing of the wisdom-body — not attained through another’s awakening. This gate is profound and subtle, breaking all idle arguments, severing all opinions; only such as Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, Zhizhe, and Yongming can thoroughly take it up. The rest, with worldly wisdom and sharp speech, scholars of the Confucians and Chan guests, exhausting thought and measure, the more they push the farther it recedes; nor are they equal to the honest man and woman who sincerely recite the Buddha, who alone can secretly penetrate the Buddha’s wisdom and tacitly match the mystery of the Way. “Because I see this benefit, I speak these words” — clearly with the Buddha-eye and the Buddha-voice it stamps and fixes this matter. How dare we disobey, and not enter it well and accord?
[Note] In the Sūtra on the Buddha’s Reception by the Praised Pure Land, the corresponding passage here is:

Moreover, Shariputra, if a good man or good woman, whether already having heard, or about to hear, or now hearing this sutra, and having heard it gives rise to profound faith and understanding — having given rise to faith and understanding, they will surely be received and protected by the Tathagatas dwelling in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges rivers. One who practices as taught will surely attain non-regression from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, and will surely be born in the pure Buddha land of the Land of Utmost Bliss of Amitayus Buddha. Therefore, Shariputra, all you beings should faithfully accept and understand the words of me and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions, and earnestly strive, practicing as taught, harboring no doubt.”

Moreover, Shariputra, if a good man or good woman, with regard to the pure Buddha land of the Land of Utmost Bliss of Amitayus and its merits and adornments, whether already having made the vow, or about to make the vow, or now making the vow, they will surely be received and protected by the Tathagatas dwelling in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges rivers. One who practices as taught will surely attain non-regression from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, and will surely be born in the pure Buddha land of the Land of Utmost Bliss of Amitayus Buddha. Therefore, Shariputra, if there are good men and good women of pure faith, all should, with deep faith and understanding in the pure Buddha land of the Land of Utmost Bliss of Amitayus, make the vow to be reborn there, and not act negligently.”
Please note the phrases in the sutra: “one who practices as taught,” and “practice as taught.”
[Ganges sands] That is, the sands of the Ganges River.
[Commentary] Two: the main proper division, concluded.
[Annotation] The second major part, the main proper division, ends here. Next begins the third major part, the division of propagation.

blocks.text: 4. The Buddhas of the Various Directions Praise

inline.s: Jia-3, the division of propagation:
Yi-1, the universal exhortation; Yi-2, the concluding exhortation
Yi-1, the universal exhortation: Bing-1, exhorting faith for propagation; Bing-2, exhorting the vow for propagation; Bing-3, exhorting practice for propagation

[Commentary] The single method of faith, vow, and holding the name perfectly includes and perfectly surpasses all Dharma-doors. In the vertical sense it is the same as all Dharma-doors; in the horizontal sense it is wholly different from them. Since it was taught without being asked, who is able to advocate and to circulate it? Only the Buddhas and the Buddha can fathom the true character of all dharmas. This sutra is exclusively the Buddha's realm; only the Buddhas [and the Buddha] can circulate it.

[Annotation] In the past, the various commentaries classified the passage “When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, Shariputra and the bhikkhus, and all the devas, humans, asuras and so forth of the whole world, hearing what the Buddha said, joyfully believed and accepted it, made obeisance and withdrew” as the division of propagation. So Master Ouyi here specially explains why this place is classed in the division of propagation, in order to remove doubt. The master says: this sutra is the most perfectly and most suddenly round of the round and sudden teachings; it is the Buddha's realm, and no one could ask, so the World-Honored One taught it without being asked. Since no one could ask, who again could take up the duty of advocating and circulating it? Only the Buddhas! Therefore the praise of the Buddhas of the various directions is classed in the division of propagation.
Bing-1, exhorting faith for propagation: Ding-1, briefly citing the title; Ding-2, inquiring and explaining the sutra title
Ding-1, briefly citing the title: Wu-1, the east; Wu-2, the south; Wu-3, the west; Wu-4, the north; Wu-5, the below; Wu-6, the above
[Commentary] The Tang translation has ten directions; the present one condenses.

[Annotation] The Tang translation is the version of Master Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty, the Sutra of the Praise of the Pure Land in Which the Buddha Receives and Upholds; in it are praised the Buddhas of the ten directions: east, south, west, north, below, above, southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast. This version of Master Kumarajiva, responding to the tendency of our people to favor brevity, abbreviates it into six directions.
Wu-1, the east

Shariputra! As I now praise the benefit of the inconceivable merits of Amitabha Buddha. In the east there are likewise Akshobhya Buddha, Sumeru-form Buddha, Great Sumeru Buddha, Sumeru-light Buddha, Wondrous-sound Buddha, and Buddhas such as these, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Each, in his own land, puts forth the broad and long tongue, covering the whole triple-thousand great-thousand world, and speaks the words of truth: You beings should believe in this Sutra on the Praise of Inconceivable Merit, Protected and Remembered by all the Buddhas.

[Commentary] “Inconceivable” has, in brief, five meanings: one, a horizontal transcendence of the three realms without waiting to cut off delusion; two, the West itself horizontally possesses the four lands, not attained through gradual realization; three, merely holding the name, without relying on the expedients of meditation and contemplation; four, with a single seven-day period as the limit, not relying on many kalpas, many lives, many months and years; five, holding the name of one Buddha is already the protection and remembrance of all the Buddhas, no different from holding the names of all the Buddhas. These are all accomplished by the great vows and practices of the guide; therefore it is said, the benefit of the inconceivable merits of Amitabha Buddha.

[Commentary] Moreover, the practitioner who has faith, vow, and holds the name fully draws in the Buddha's merits to become his own merits; therefore it is also called the benefit of the inconceivable merits of Amitabha Buddha. Below it further says the inconceivable merits of the Buddhas and my own inconceivable merits — that is, the Buddhas and Shakyamuni all take Amitabha as their own.

[Annotation] The “benefit of the inconceivable merits of Amitabha Buddha” is the dependent and direct adornments of the Western Land of Utmost Bliss that the World-Honored One spoke of earlier, together with what was stated above: “If there is a good man or good woman who, hearing of Amitabha Buddha, holds his name, whether for one day, or two days, or three days, or four days, or five days, or six days, or seven days, with a single mind and without disturbance, then at the end of that person's life, Amitabha Buddha and the holy assembly appear before him. When that person dies, his mind is not inverted, and he is at once reborn in the Land of Utmost Bliss of Amitabha Buddha.” After the World-Honored One had finished this passage, he at once said, “Shariputra! I see this benefit, and therefore speak these words.”

[Commentary] Akshobhya, which is translated as immovable. The Buddha has immeasurable virtues, and so should have immeasurable names. They are established according to conditions — some take the cause, some the fruit, some the nature, some the characteristic, some the practice and vow. Though one corner is raised, the four means of attraction are still complete. With every name, the virtue it signifies is revealed; were one to speak of them for a kalpa of lifetime, one could not exhaust them. The empty space of the east is inexhaustible, and the worlds too are inexhaustible. As the worlds are inexhaustible, the Buddhas dwelling in them are also inexhaustible; here they are but briefly cited, merely as many as the sands of the Ganges. These Buddhas each put forth the broad and long tongue to exhort faith in this sutra, yet beings still do not give rise to faith — how utterly dull and unawakened! An ordinary person who does not lie for three lives can make his tongue reach his nose. The Buddha at the head of the fruit of the Store teaching, not lying for three great asamkhya kalpas, has a thin, broad, and long tongue that can cover the face. Now, having realized the wondrous gate of the Mahayana Pure Land, therefore it spreads over the whole triple-thousand world. This shows that the principle is truly sincere and accords with the real; the matter is not false.

[Annotation] [Though one corner is raised, the four means of attraction are still complete] Though only one virtue is raised to display the name, the four means of attraction are still complete. [Were one to speak of them for a kalpa of lifetime, one could not exhaust them] Even using a lifespan of a great kalpa to speak of them continuously, one could not finish. [The Buddha at the head of the fruit of the Store teaching] The “fruit-head Buddha” is a term of the Tiantai school, indicating the Buddha at the stage of fruit among the four teachings of Store, Common, Distinct, and Perfect. The “Buddha at the head of the fruit of the Store teaching” is the Buddha of the Store teaching.

[Commentary] It sets forth the sutra title, the basis of circulation. Master [Kumarajiva], conforming to the fondness of this land, abbreviated it to the present title, which happens to accord with the wondrous practice of holding the name. Master Xuanzang rendered it as the Sutra of the Praise of the Pure Land in Which the Buddha Receives and Upholds. In wording there is detail and brevity, but in meaning there is neither increase nor decrease.

[Annotation] In the exhortation to faith, the Buddhas of the six directions set forth the sixteen-character sutra title, the Sutra on the Praise of Inconceivable Merit, Protected and Remembered by all the Buddhas — this is the sutra's original name. The title of the present circulating version was rendered by Master Kumarajiva as the Buddha Speaks the Amitabha Sutra, conforming to this land's inclination to favor brevity, and it happens to accord with the wondrous practice of holding the name, so it is circulated throughout the world. Master Xuanzang, for his part, rendered the title as the Sutra of the Praise of the Pure Land in Which the Buddha Receives and Upholds. These two titles, though differing in the degree of detail of their wording, in meaning are truly neither increased nor decreased.
Wu-2, the south

Shariputra! In the southern world are Sun-moon-lamp Buddha, Name-fame-light Buddha, Great-flame-shoulder Buddha, Sumeru-lamp Buddha, Immeasurable-diligence Buddha, and Buddhas such as these, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Each, in his own land, puts forth the broad and long tongue, covering the whole triple-thousand great-thousand world, and speaks the words of truth: You beings should believe in this Sutra on the Praise of Inconceivable Merit, Protected and Remembered by all the Buddhas.
Wu-3, the west

Shariputra! In the western world are Amitayus Buddha, Immeasurable-form Buddha, Immeasurable-banner Buddha, Great-light Buddha, Great-brightness Buddha, Jewel-form Buddha, Pure-light Buddha, and Buddhas such as these, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Each, in his own land, puts forth the broad and long tongue, covering the whole triple-thousand great-thousand world, and speaks the words of truth: You beings should believe in this Sutra on the Praise of Inconceivable Merit, Protected and Remembered by all the Buddhas.

[Commentary] Amitayus Buddha shares the same name as Amitabha. The Buddhas of the same name throughout the ten directions and various directions are immeasurable; yet it may also be this very guide. To deliver beings, he quite readily in turn praises what the Tathagata Shakyamuni has spoken.

[Annotation] Amitayus Buddha shares the same name as Amitabha Buddha. This has two meanings: one, since the Buddhas of the ten directions are many and the Buddha's virtues are not different, names established by virtue are also many and may be the same; two, this Amitayus Buddha may even be the guide of the Land of Utmost Bliss, and to deliver beings he quite readily in turn praises this sutra spoken by Shakyamuni Buddha.
Wu-4, the north

Shariputra! In the northern world are Flame-shoulder Buddha, Most-supreme-sound Buddha, Hard-to-overcome Buddha, Sun-arisen Buddha, Net-brightness Buddha, and Buddhas such as these, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Each, in his own land, puts forth the broad and long tongue, covering the whole triple-thousand great-thousand world, and speaks the words of truth: You beings should believe in this Sutra on the Praise of Inconceivable Merit, Protected and Remembered by all the Buddhas.
Wu-5, the below

Shariputra! In the below world are Lion Buddha, Name-fame Buddha, Name-light Buddha, Dharma Buddha, Dharma-banner Buddha, Dharma-holding Buddha, and Buddhas such as these, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Each, in his own land, puts forth the broad and long tongue, covering the whole triple-thousand great-thousand world, and speaks the words of truth: You beings should believe in this Sutra on the Praise of Inconceivable Merit, Protected and Remembered by all the Buddhas.

[Commentary] Beneath this world's water-wheel, gold-wheel, and wind-wheel there are likewise lower worlds such as the heaven of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and so forth, endlessly layered. Dharma, which here means “the Dharma.”

[Annotation] [Dharma, which here means “the Dharma”] Dharma is a transliteration of the Sanskrit word; its Chinese meaning is “the Dharma.” It refers to the truth realized by the Buddha and the method of realization.
Wu-6, the above

Shariputra! In the above world are Brahma-sound Buddha, Host-king Buddha, Superior-offering Buddha, Offering-light Buddha, Great-flame-shoulder Buddha, Adorned-with-multicolored-jewel-flower Buddha, Sala-tree-king Buddha, Jewel-flower-virtue Buddha, Sees-the-meaning-of-all-things Buddha, Sumeru-mountain Buddha, and Buddhas such as these, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Each, in his own land, puts forth the broad and long tongue, covering the whole triple-thousand great-thousand world, and speaks the words of truth: You beings should believe in this Sutra on the Praise of Inconceivable Merit, Protected and Remembered by all the Buddhas.
[Commentary] Above this world's heaven of neither-perception-nor-non-perception there are likewise upper worlds with wind-wheel and gold-wheel and the three realms, endlessly layered.

[Commentary] Question: The various directions surely all have Pure Lands; why the partial praise of the West? Answer: This is likewise not a good question. Were I to praise the land of Akshobhya Buddha, you would again doubt the partiality for the east, and so on in endless idle argument.

[Annotation] Question: The ten directions have many Pure Lands; why do you not praise them, but only particularly praise the West? Answer: Such an objection is likewise not a good question. If what is praised were the land of Akshobhya Buddha, you would again ask why the east is particularly praised. Thus in round upon round of questions, all becomes idle argument.
[Land of Akshobhya Buddha] The land of Akshobhya Buddha is in the east of the world in which we dwell. [Idle argument] Playful and impractical talk.
[Commentary] Question: Why not universally contemplate the dharma-realm?

[Annotation] Question: Why not universally contemplate and fix the mind on all the Pure Lands of the dharma-realm? (This question does not understand the principle that “when the contemplated realm is broad, the contemplating mind is sure to scatter”; it is not a good question.)

[Commentary] Answer: There are three reasons. To make it easy for beginners to fix the mind on the object; because Amitabha's original vow is supreme; and because the Buddha has a particular affinity with beings of this land.

[Annotation] Answer: There are three reasons here: one, to make it easy for beginners, who on hearing this sutra praised, believe in the Land of Utmost Bliss, vow to be reborn in the western Pure Land, and hold the name of Amitabha, with mind believing in the Land of Utmost Bliss, mind vowing for the Land of Utmost Bliss, mind mindful of the Land of Utmost Bliss — easy to tie the mind to a single realm. Two, the western Land of Utmost Bliss established by Amitabha Buddha's forty-eight great vows far surpasses the lands of the Buddhas. Three, Amitabha Buddha has a particular affinity with this land.
[Fix the mind on the object] To tie the mind to a single realm.

[Commentary] Generally the Buddha delivers beings and beings are transformed; within it the difficult and the easy, the shallow and the deep all lie in the affinity. Where the affinity is, the grace and merit are vast and deep; the various teachings awaken and lead beings to joyfully believe and enter, can stir the seeds of their past lives, can make demonic obstacles hard to block, and can open and develop their essential nature. The Buddhas originally come forth from the Dharma-body and firmly bind the seeds of affinity; whether worldly or world-transcending, all of it is inconceivable. Honored within the teachings of the vehicles, raised up within the ocean of the assembly, seeping into the sea of suffering, in compassion joined with the still light — for this reason the myriad virtues revere and receive, and all spirits face toward the Ultimate. One should know that the Buddha-seed arises from conditions, and conditions are the dharma-realm. One thought is all thoughts; one birth is all births. One incense, one flower; one sound, one form — even receiving confession and prophecy, the touch of the hand on the head and the lowered hand — throughout the ten directions and the three times, nothing is not completely fused. Therefore this predominant-condition cause is called the dependent arising of the dharma-realm. This is precisely what is meant by universally contemplating the dharma-realm. Those of shallow capacity can then resolve and seek it exclusively; those of deep capacity need not abandon the West and seek the Avatamsaka elsewhere. If one says the West is provisional and the Avatamsaka is ultimate, the West is small and the Avatamsaka is great, one wholly falls into the clinging of beings’ discriminating imagination, because one does not reach the oneness of the provisional and the ultimate, and the non-inherent nature of great and small.

[Annotation] This makes clear the reason for the three meanings stated above and explains the answer: contemplating and binding the mind to the Western Land of Utmost Bliss is precisely universally contemplating the dharma-realm.
Ding-2, Inquiring and Explaining the Sutra Title

Shariputra! What do you think? Why is it named the Sutra Protected and Remembered by all the Buddhas? Shariputra! If there are good men or good women who hear this sutra and uphold it, and who hear the names of all the Buddhas, these good men and good women are all protected and remembered by all the Buddhas, and all attain non-regression from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Therefore, Shariputra! You should all faithfully accept my words and what the Buddhas have spoken.

[Commentary] This sutra exclusively sets forth the supremely essential teaching of the mind and the names of all the Buddhas, and likewise sets forth the supremely perfect, ultimate myriad merits; therefore those who hear it are all protected and remembered by the Buddhas. Moreover, hearing the sutra and upholding it is to hold the name. The name of Amitabha is protected and remembered by all the Buddhas.

[Annotation] This sutra exclusively sets forth the supremely essential teaching of the mind and the names of all the Buddhas, and likewise sets forth the supremely perfect, ultimate myriad merits; therefore those who hear it are all protected and remembered by the Buddhas. Moreover, hearing the sutra and upholding it is to hold the name, and the name of Amitabha Buddha is surely protected and remembered by all the Buddhas.

[Set forth] To explain in detail, to illuminate the facts and the principle. [The names of all the Buddhas] The names of all the Buddhas are precisely the name of Amitabha. Earlier it was said, “Amitabha is the Dharma-body, the treasury of all the dharma-realm; to be mindful of Amitabha, the one Buddha, is to be mindful of all the Buddhas.” Therefore it is said that this sutra exclusively sets forth the names of all the Buddhas.

[Commentary] Question: If one merely hears the names of the Buddhas without having upheld this sutra, does one also receive protection and non-regression? Answer: This meaning has both a restricted and a universal sense. The Sutra of Divining says that a confused and defiled mind, though it recites my name, is not counted as having heard it. Because one cannot give rise to settled faith and understanding, one only obtains worldly good retribution and not the vast, deep, and wonderful benefit; if one reaches the single-practice samadhi, then one accomplishes the vast, subtle, wonderful mind of practice, and is called one who attains the tolerance of non-arising dharmas in resemblance; only then is one counted as having heard the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions. This should likewise be so. Therefore one must, after hearing, hold it until the mind is single and undisturbed, and only then is one counted as having heard the names of all the Buddhas and received the protection and remembrance of all the Buddhas. This is the restricted sense.

[Annotation] [Divining] That is, the Sutra of Divining the Good and Evil Karmic Retribution. [The tolerance of non-arising dharmas] Abbreviated as the tolerance of non-arising.
